Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua press conference LIVE: Heavyweight rivals trade insults and clash over Eddie Hearn
Sports.content:
Right, that's it for today.

The first presser is over and now we have two months to wait until we see both Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua go face-to-face again.

Let's hope the next time they face off and have words, it's a bit more fiery and feisty. That was all too nice for me.

Anyway, thanks for joining us for this live coverage and I will see you all very soon.

Goodnight.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua reveals that Tyson Fury's estranged uncle has joined his camp ahead of £150m mega-fight as Gypsy King claims: 'I've not spoken to him for years'
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua made the startling revelation that he has joined forces with Tyson Fury's uncle, Peter, ahead of their eagerly-anticipated super-fight in Cardiff in December.

Never has the calling of a sporting press conference agitated as much, if not more, attention than the event itself.

Without putting Fury and Joshua into the same room in London on Wednesday evening there would have been no chance of them sharing a ring in Cardiff two months from now.

Never has a promo prompted so many startling revelations, either. We might never have known that Fury’s estranged uncle is advising AJ on how to prevent Tyson beating him. Traveller families are usually bonded by such fierce loyalties that we can only wonder about the tensions around the camp fire.

‘Not to worry,’ said the Gypsy King about the defection. ‘I haven’t spoken to him for years.’

Nor might we have learned that Joshua took a mind-blowing pay cut in order to haul the Battle of Britain back home from the clutches of New York.

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Tyson Fury’s ticket-selling appearances

How much of a purse deduction? ‘Twelve figures’ declared his promoter Eddie Hearn. That’s £10million at least.

AJ shrugged and cited another fringe benefit picked up during the maelstrom of doubt as to whether this fight between a pair of British world heavyweight champions would ever take place. He also added Fury’s former trainer Ben Davison to his team.

Joshua said: ‘Ben’s pinpointing details which will make the difference on the night.’

Fury replied: ‘Ben can’t put muscles on that suspect chin.’

He could not resist reminding everyone that Davison has just returned from Las Vegas where he presided over Conor Benn’s two-round devastation by America’s great Latin hope, Ryan Garcia.

When they took to the stage there were very few of the histrionics which are the trademark of most of Fury’s ticket-selling appearances.

Instead he advertised ‘probably the greatest fight boxing’s ever seen if you factor in the commercial aspect'.

Which includes the US$150million split equally between the two of them as they put an end to 12 years of public waiting for this fight.

Joshua said: ‘Both of us want to do British boxing proud.’

Even though the ritual stare down was lengthy the chatter was amicable and ended in smiles with Fury inviting Joshua to ‘a pint of Guinness as soon as the fight over, win lose or draw'.

Well, they are ten weeks away from them putting on their fight faces.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's £150m mega-fight is back ON: Heavyweight rivals set to meet in London face off TOMORROW after Gypsy King claimed rival 'tried to pull out' amid Eddie Hearn's feud with Dana White

It's on. At last. Finally. Confirmed by the almighty Turki.

Reconfirmed by the late, late word sent out that the face to face stare down between our two heavyweight titans will definitely take place at a press conference launch this Wednesday.

The fight that almost got away. AJ versus the Gypsy King. So close to being another of boxing's lost jewels that we almost gave up hope.

May the lords of the rings be praised.

Whether or not Dana White, the American interloper from UFC cage fighting who is demanding a share of the action, is present despite the protestations of Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn, who won the battle for this fight to take place if not at Wembley but not as far, far west of London as New York.

Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury has been rescued for the British fight fans, by Cardiff. Although like the 70-odd thousand in the Principality Stadium the TV majority will have to stay awake into the wee small hours on the Friday night of December 11.

Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will face each other down at a press conference on Wednesday

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on December 11 in Cardiff with the showdown set to begin at 2am so Netflix subscribers can stream it at peak time in America

Fury against Joshua was almost the fight that got away, with the heavyweights now set to sort out differences that should have been settled a decade ago

First bell about 2am so that the tens of millions of Netflix subscribers can stream at peak time in America.

Assuming they buy into this as being a mega fight for all time. Or are satisfied that it is a spectacle unto itself.

Maybe a world heavyweight title adding spice to the occasion. Maybe not. Maybe just two good old Brits sorting differences that should have been settled a decade ago.

And why not? Fury and Joshua may be past their prime but they are not yet the walking dead.

They have enough fight left in their late 30s to put on a show.

And a future to fight for. For the winner there can be challenges to meet from the new generation of champions and a few million dollars more to add to the 75 million each will receive as an early Christmas present.

Always assuming no more spanners are thrown into these on-off-on works.

Good luck to both. Even more so to the Welsh constabulary who will have to deal with all those fans spilling out into darkened streets on what will already be a typically wild Friday night in Cardiff.

Sports.title: For Scottish boxing, the cupboard is bare. All that remains are memories of better times
Sports.content:
Given the endless nonsense that continues to surround the Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight, it’s no surprise that it has dominated all the recent headlines in boxing.

Will they? Won’t they? Does anyone even really care any more? Is it happening in the UK? America? Saudi Arabia? Maybe on the moon? For a gazillion dollars?

It felt like a degree of certainty had been reached last week with the announcement that the fight will go ahead at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff in December.

That was until Dana White, the UFC supremo and one of the fight’s chief promoters, said only a few days ago that he ‘doesn’t know’ if it will go ahead.

Perhaps we will get a clearer picture tomorrow afternoon, with Fury and Joshua set to face-off at a media conference in London.

Either way, this tiresome circus act involving two fighters long past their prime continues to be pretty much the only thing anyone is speaking about in boxing right now.

Josh Taylor is dominated by Jack Catterall in Leeds as his ring supremacy is left in ruins

Nathaniel Collins had been Scotland's biggest hope until he suffered two successive defeats

Taylor's rise to the top of the fight game was an incredible achievement that will long be lauded

It perhaps escaped your attention, then, that Scotland’s Nathaniel Collins was back in the ring last weekend. Quite an important fight it was, too.

Taking on European featherweight champion Liam Davies in Birmingham, this was supposed to be Collins’ comeback fight after he lost to Spain’s Cristobal Llorente in Glasgow in April in their world title eliminator.

It did not go well. Collins was floored in the first round and never really recovered, before his trainer put a stop to it all and said enough was enough at the end of the seventh round.

There was a sadness to it all. Not only that Collins had suffered a second successive defeat, but also in terms of the wider implications for himself and for Scottish boxing as a whole.

The defeat to Llorente at The Hydro had been the first loss of Collins’ career. It had been a tough night, albeit not disastrous. There was a chance to bounce back and come again.

But, in terms of challenging at world level, he now looks further away than ever. The same would surely apply to Scottish boxing as a whole after this latest blow.

Not so long ago, Scottish boxing felt like it had a pulse. Josh Taylor climbed the mountain and was, in his pomp, one of the best pound-for-pound fighters on the planet.

The Tartan Tornado put together one of the greatest runs by any British fighter in history to become our first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era. Achieving that in just 18 fights was truly phenomenal.

When Taylor’s career then fizzled out due to a combination of burn-out, inactivity and promotional mismanagement, it had been hoped that Collins would be the next cab off the rank.

The late Ken Buchanan won multiple titles at lightweight and fought between 1965 and 1982

The Nightmare, as he’s known, was supposed to be the fighter who kept the lights on and continued to fly the flag in the post-Taylor era.

That’s not to say he was ever going to be quite as good as Taylor. That always looked unrealistic. But there was genuine hope that Collins could at least be a contender for a world title.

The brutal yet stylish manner in which he dismantled fellow Scot Lee McGregor at The Hydro in May 2025 gave the look of a fighter with all the credentials to go on and box at world level.

But the defeat to Davies in Birmingham last weekend has surely ended that conversation. In the post-Taylor era, the cupboard is depressingly bare for Scottish boxing. Completely and utterly empty.

No one is selling out arenas in Scotland. No one is forcing their way on to Sky Sports and the likes. No one is even close to holding box-office appeal or appearing on pay-per-views.

The amateur and club scene are still doing their bit. The numbers are OK, even if a lot of people use boxing clubs as fitness classes these days rather than having any desire to actually enter a ring.

But when you speak to people involved with boxing clubs across Scotland, the majority of them all share a similar concern.

Plainly, that we have no one even remotely close to following in Taylor’s footsteps and fighting at the top level of the sport. The outlook is bleak.

Listen, Scotland is a relatively small country. We do not have an endless pool of talent. Boxing is not a mainstream sport like football or rugby.

The two successive defeats for Collins have signaled a barren period for Scottish boxing

Kids learn to play football in various different ways; at school, at coaching sessions, or with a club. Maybe even down the local park or on the streets in some very rare and old-fashioned instances.

Rugby is a non-negotiable for those in private education. Even golf now has far more reach and appeal with the younger generation than boxing.

With the awareness around long-term brain damage now greater than ever, you can hardly blame any parent if they aren’t overly enthused by the idea of their kids being involved in a sport where they get punched in the head.

When a generational talent like Taylor comes along and then leaves, the gap is enormous. There is no conveyor belt of world-class operators waiting in the wings.

Sadly, it also now appears that Scotland can’t even offer up any fighters in the bracket just below world level either.

Collins has already come through a serious health scare – a life-threatening twisted bowel caused by infant scar tissue – that put much more than just his boxing career at risk. He has shown heart. No one questions that. He gave it a good go.

But his latest defeat is emblematic of the wider malaise that continues to be so prevalent across Scottish boxing as a whole.

There have been lean times in the past. After Ken Buchanan and Jim Watt, there were quiet periods. After Scott Harrison’s turbulent reign at featherweight the scene thinned out again until Ricky Burns and then Taylor arrived.

Cycles exist. The problem now is that the cycle feels stuck in the downward phase with no obvious sign of it moving back up again.

Where is the next boxing superstar in Scotland? It is beginning to feel like the sport is dying a death. That is the uncomfortable truth.

When Collins fought Llorente at The Hydro in April, it wasn’t even close to being a sell-out. The whole top tier of the arena was closed. Make of that what you will.

And that was a world title eliminator involving the guy who was supposed to be our next big hope. Taylor himself has acknowledged the lack of young fighters breaking through.

The Tornado’s retirement left a void. Collins’ latest defeat has made it wider and deeper. The Hydro still stands ready for big nights, but it’s hard to see a major promoter going back there any time soon.

The Scottish public still loves a fighter who will dig in and go to war. But the fighters of genuine world-class pedigree are simply not here at present.

These are the lean years. The barren stretch. And that should worry anyone who cares about the sport north of the border.

The cupboard is bare. The stars have gone. Until someone steps forward and proves otherwise, Scottish boxing is living on memories of Taylor and on nostalgia about some of the other great names of the past.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury enrolls in drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott London press conference ahead of £150m Cardiff bout

Tyson Fury has now enrolled in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (VADA)'s testing programme ahead of his blockbuster showdown with Anthony Joshua, his camp has confirmed.

The development comes just 24 hours after Joshua threatened to boycott Wednesday's first press conference in London unless Fury could prove he had entered the VADA testing pool.

Joshua had already enrolled, while Fury's camp maintained that the terms of their agreement gave him longer to do so.

But with the first face-to-face meeting between the two heavyweights this Wednesday, Fury has now completed his enrolment and provided his whereabouts to VADA.

Fury's manager, Spencer Brown, told Playbook Boxing: 'We are enrolled in VADA. We are enrolled in VADA. Just to confirm that.'

Asked about the timing of Fury's enrolment, they added: 'He did it a bit earlier than when the fight was announced. In our contract, we had more time, but you know, it doesn't matter. We've done it. We've done everything we've been asked to do. Everything.'

Tyson Fury has agreed to join a drug testing programme after Anthony Joshua threatened to boycott their press conference

The Gypsy King's manager also explained that enrolment and testing are separate stages of the VADA process.

Asked whether Fury had already been tested, they said: 'No, you have to enrol first, don't you? That part of it's all been done, then the testing comes second.'

Brown stressed that the nature of VADA's programme means fighters are not given advance warning of when testers will arrive.

'You could be tested in a week, you could be sitting there on your toilet and they knock on the door,' he said. 'That's the way they work. They don't tell you a time. They don't say we're coming round tomorrow. That's the way. That's why it works.'

The dispute had threatened to become an unwanted subplot to a fight more than a decade in the making.

Joshua's camp had raised concerns after it emerged that the two fighters had different timelines under their respective contractual arrangements, with promoter Eddie Hearn subsequently making clear that he expected Fury to enter the programme.

There is now another significant issue to resolve before December 11: exactly when the fight will take place.

The heavyweight blockbuster will be staged at Cardiff's Principality Stadium and streamed globally by Netflix, with organisers targeting the US primetime market. The main event is expected to take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in Britain, with a ring walk potentially as late as 2am.

Fury and Joshua's fight is due to take place on Friday December 11. The pair are set to meet for a press conference on September 30

Brown has now revealed that the precise timing is still being negotiated and made clear that he does not want the fight to start at 2am.

'I think 2am is far too late,' he said.

'I think that the general public in England will want to watch it in the pubs, the clubs, you know, round each other's houses. There'll be a party atmosphere, and I just think it needs to be earlier. Simple as that.'

Brown added: 'It's all in negotiation at the moment, but it shouldn't be at 2 o'clock in the morning. I certainly wouldn't like to sit there at 2 o'clock in the morning, would you?'

And Brown also questioned the experience for the thousands of fans expected to attend in Cardiff.

'I think 99 per cent of the people will probably tell you that if you're in the stadium, you don't want to be sitting in the stadium till 2 o'clock in the morning, freezing your nuts off.'

The late start has been driven by the fact Netflix is looking to maximise its US audience, while Cardiff's Principality Stadium was selected after the proposed venues in London could not accommodate the required late finish.

The venue can accommodate the late finish, but the event's licensing arrangements have also required negotiation because of the proposed early-hours schedule.

Fury and Joshua are due to meet for the first time in public since their long-awaited fight was officially confirmed at Wednesday's press conference in London.

The bout, which will be contested at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11, is the culmination of years of failed negotiations between the former world champions.

Both men have won their respective comeback fights this year, clearing the way for the long-awaited all-British heavyweight showdown.

Now, with Fury's VADA enrolment confirmed, attention can turn back to the build-up and whether organisers can find a start time that works for both the global Netflix audience and the British fans inside and outside the stadium.

Sports.title: Why Malaysia would be the perfect place for F1’s first wet-weather race in 2026
Sports.content:
While Formula 1 has already reached the 16th round of the 2026 season, fans have still not been treated to a wet-weather race under the new regulations – or even a wet session. Rain has threatened on several occasions, but the on-track action has consistently remained unaffected.

Following initial concerns about safety in wet conditions, the FIA has made several changes to this year’s regulations. These include increasing the tyre blanket temperatures for intermediates, capping electrical power and, related to that, banning boost mode in the wet.

Aside from that, there are also concerns about the tyres. Several drivers have said that they struggled to get the intermediates up to temperature – and subsequently keep them there. It meant Pirelli was quite keen to have a wet-weather race in Miami, where ambient temperatures are high, while a potential wet race in Montreal was described as “the perfect storm” due to the low temperatures and a layout where it is difficult to get the tyres up to temperature anyway.

In Canada, McLaren did start on intermediates, although that turned out to be the wrong choice as further rain failed to materialise. And so F1 is still waiting for its first wet-weather race under the new technical regulations.

While drivers still have some concerns about safety even after the FIA’s changes – Isack Hadjar called it “dangerous” – Pierre Gasly sums up the feeling of many in the paddock: the Sepang International Circuit would effectively be the ‘easiest’ location for a wet-weather race in 2026.

“I think out of any track in the season, if one is good for wet, it's probably here,” Gasly said when asked about a potential wet-weather race by Autosport.

“If you'll ask me about Vegas in crazy cold conditions and, well, it still could happen there, but then it is definitely going to be more tricky.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“But here the track is really rough, it's really hot and there's a bit of elevation change as well, so it should be pretty good to clear the track in terms of water quantity. So I think it will be fine.”

Gasly’s experiences with the 2026 car in the wet so far have not been positive, but those conditions were not representative of what drivers could potentially face in Malaysia: “The only time I tried was in January at Silverstone, which was horrendous. And then in Magny-Cours with extremely cold conditions, which didn't feel good at all. But I expect it to be in a much better place here.”

It is a theory shared by tyre supplier Pirelli. Chief engineer Simone Berra acknowledges that Sepang is also the best possible location for them to test the wet-weather tyres.

“I would like to gather some information because it's good to have feedback, not just from our tests, but also from normal running with all the teams and all the drivers,” Berra confirmed when asked about the prospect of rain by Autosport.

“Honestly, as an engineer, I would like to have some more feedback and data to work with. And, yes, this is the perfect circuit to have rain.

“When we went to Montreal, I said it would be the perfect storm because it was cold with a low-energy circuit, but here it's a completely different story.”

Rain is seen on the pitwall Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

It means that if there are problems with the tyres, they will be of a very different nature from those feared in Montreal. There, drivers could have struggled to get the tyres up to temperature, while in Malaysia the opposite could be the case – not only because of the high temperatures, but also due to the extremely rough asphalt.

“The point is that we could end up in a situation where you generate overheating, especially if it's raining and then dries up quite quickly”, Berra said. “So the overheating effect could be important.”

Another atypical factor is that teams generally want to use the full wets as little as possible, but Pirelli expects a different situation in that respect as well at the circuit near Kuala Lumpur.

“When it rains here, it's quite massive and I would see the full wet as the preferred race tyre,” Berra said. “That is probably for once, because we know that usually teams prefer the intermediates. But we also know that here it's often like a monsoon and you need to have proper water dissipation for that.

“But let's first see if it's going to rain or not, because this is probably the first year that we are at round 16 without rain! But if it comes, then I think the full wet is not to be discarded, despite that tyre overheating very quickly. With a high level of standing water, I think it would work quite well.”

Sports.title: "The FIA needs to step in" - Russell's cooling vest comments explained
Sports.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell caused a stir in some quarters by appearing to suggest the FIA should protect teams against themselves by ensuring cooling vests are commonly used in hot races.

Driver comfort in hot climates has been a topic since the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix, when several drivers experienced heat exhaustion symptoms during the Doha race, which was held October before being moved to a more reasonable December climate.

In response, the FIA and all F1 teams conducted research to improve the venting and cooling of drivers in such extreme conditions. The end result was a cooling vest that circulates water through a tube system, which drivers can use in extreme conditions.

The FIA declares a so-called "heat hazard" at the start of a grand prix weekend when ambient temperatures for an on-track session are predicted to exceed 31C.

This weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix, exceptionally held in Malaysia, is the third such heat hazard of the 2026 season, with a fourth one likely following next weekend in nearby Singapore.

It prompted Russell to reveal that he would prefer to use a bespoke cooling solution, but that his Mercedes team had decided against developing one.

Carlos Sainz, Scuderia Ferrari, puts on a cooling vest in the garage Photo by: Mark Sutton / Motorsport Images

"We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough," Russell told The Times in Kuala Lumpur.

“When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me…'look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it [but at the cost of performance]'.”

That's why Russell called on the FIA to get involved again and effectively protect teams against themselves: “I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say, 'Here’s some money extra in the cost cap,' or there’s an external company who’s going to develop it for everybody, you just put the money towards it. Because we should all be wearing it."

In some quarters the story has been construed as Russell going against his team or being forced to suffer in the heat by his engineers, but the real story is slightly more prosaic.

Initially, the FIA did intend to make the use of cooling vests mandatory when a heat hazard is declared, but the standard vest wasn't particularly popular with drivers, with many feeling the vest only provided a benefit for a handful of laps before becoming more of a hindrance than a help. As a result, the vest is still optional, with drivers who don't use it instead being forced to add the corresponding 0.5kg of ballast to the car.

Teams are free to develop their own solution within a certain framework to improve the system's cooling efficiency and ergonomics. But with a heat hazard only declared a limited number of times per season, the majority of teams don't feel it is worth the engineering resources when such conditions are rare, and haven't been as extreme as they were in Qatar 2023.

Logan Sargeant, Williams Racing Photo by: Williams F1

So, with a mandatory system almost universally dismissed by the drivers, the FIA has been happy to keep it optional and let teams make their own decisions. There doesn't appear to be much of an appetite to restart the whole debate.

As Russell mentioned in his explanation, any extra financial and human resources poured into sporadically used vests would not be spent on improving the performance of his W17 car.

So, as Mercedes battles to stay ahead of the pack against advances from McLaren, Red Bull and Ferrari, and the issue revolves around comfort rather than outright safety concerns at this stage, it is clear where the priority is.

Sports.title: McLaren explains recurring Norris straightline speed issue after Bahrain GP qualifying
Sports.content:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has clarified the issues with Lando Norris' current Mercedes power unit, as the reigning champion rued the lack of straightline speed in Formula 1 qualifying for the second week running.

Although McLaren is known to be missing straightline speed versus its other Mercedes-powered counterparts owing to its selected gear ratios being lower, Norris had a deficit on top of that across the Baku weekend. This deficit has resurfaced, although McLaren was losing further time across qualifying when compared to the Red Bulls and Ferraris.

Norris confirmed this, stating: "I'm just down on every single straight, so every time I get a good exit, I'm just slower at the end of the straight. It just hurts seeing this every single time."

Stella explained the mechanics at play with Norris' power unit issue, but added that it was difficult to diagnose given the complexities of the current regulations and the myriad factors that could hold an effect. A deployment issue, for instance, would be easier to spot - but a mechanical issue outside of the reach of sensors would be tough to identify.

The Italian believes that this is costing Norris somewhere between 0.1-0.2s seconds per lap, a not-insignificant deficit given the margins involved in qualifying for this weekend's Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

"I think more precisely we should say that the issue we see on Lando's car is about a lack of straightline speed. So we see that in the power limited section, the car accelerates a little less and develops a little bit less top speed, all the other parameters being the same," Stella explained.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

"We talk about probably between one and two kilometres per hour, they are small quantities, and they are even difficult to see. As soon as Lando, for instance, has a little bit of slipstream from a car four seconds ahead, now you see Lando faster than the other car.

"So, it's a small quantities but that we see statistically and we should more precisely talk about the deficit of straightline speed, which we can quantify in a lap time loss that I would say in excess of one tenth of a second, possibly between one and two tenths of a second.

"A different conversation is about why that is and while we can talk immediately about a lack of power, in reality there can be different reasons.

"As you say, it's in a way more difficult to monitor what is happening from a power unit point of view, because if it was deployment we would be able to see it, possibly has to do with some other parameters."

Stella added that those external factors could be nothing to do with the power unit at all, and was keen to avoid a situation where his comments could be construed as blame on Mercedes' High Performance Powertrains division.

The main issue seemed to be largely restricted to the latter half of the lap, where Piastri found more top speed over Norris between Turns 13 and 14, and then on the back straight towards Turn 15.

"But at the same time there's the areas of the power unit that depend on what's happening on the chassis side and finally there could be parameters that have to do with the drag of the car," Stella continued.

"At no point we are making a point about power unit, we are just making a point about a lack of straightline speed which we want to make a point about - because it's fair to Lando that we take the responsibility for the fact that on his car there's a lap time deficit which at the moment we have not been able to remove in a couple of events.

"But obviously we are definitely looking at all the possible parameters and we will look at further changes but we only can do that now for Singapore."

Additional reporting by Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: From "paper car" to pole – What changed for Verstappen and Red Bull?
Sports.content:
It is less than a month since Max Verstappen qualified sixth at Monza and afterwards spoke about a Red Bull car "made of paper". Admittedly, that comment specifically concerned the "car degradation" issue – components that sometimes deteriorate over the course of a race – and according to Verstappen and team principal Laurent Mekies, that issue can no longer be fully resolved in 2026.

But in terms of pure pace, significant steps have been made since those frustrations at Monza. Verstappen has finished on the podium at every race weekend since his crash at Zandvoort, and in Malaysia he has now secured his first pole of the year.

The latter marks another step forward because, yes, Verstappen made it onto the podium at Monza, Madrid and Baku, but Red Bull was never the benchmark at any point during those race weekends.

And that is precisely what the Milton Keynes-based team has been so far at Sepang. Verstappen already completed impressive long runs on Friday and followed that up with a convincing pole position a day later.

"I think the car has been in a good operating window all weekend," Verstappen told a handful of Dutch journalists in the paddock after qualifying.

"Is that perhaps because it’s the heat here? It could be, but I do think we’ve made good steps with the set-up over the past few weeks as well, and of course with those upgrades on the car."

Verstappen thinks Mercedes is simply having an off-weekend in the Malaysian heat Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

Verstappen thinks Mercedes is simply having an "off-weekend"

There are two sides to the explanation for Saturday’s picture. Verstappen believes other teams – Mercedes in particular – are struggling slightly more with the heat than Red Bull, and secondly, the technical team led by Pierre Wache has undeniably improved the RB22.

As for the former, Verstappen does not want to jump to far-reaching conclusions just yet. According to him, Saturday’s result does not necessarily mean that Mercedes’ long-awaited upgrade is not working: "I think they always struggle more at circuits where it’s very hot, so I think we have to wait and see with their upgrades over the coming races."

In general terms, Verstappen still sees Mercedes as the benchmark: "I think they are generally still very efficient in many areas. We just have to look at it race by race. Last weekend they were obviously faster and actually they have been all season, just not now. They’re having a bit of an off-weekend."

More confidence in the RB22 after Baku upgrade

Verstappen prefers to look at his own team and, in that respect, it is important that the Baku upgrade – the final significant package of the year – has delivered what was expected internally.

"It’s clear that, with the changes we’ve made, we’ve been able to get much more out of the car and the car is also easier to drive," he said. "That’s obviously positive, also for next year. There are a few things we can’t change anymore this season, so we want to address those for next year and I hope it will then move even further in the right direction."

Aside from the outright pace, the Baku upgrade has also made both Red Bull drivers feel more comfortable behind the wheel, Verstappen acknowledged: "It’s nice when you have a car that does a little more of what you want. At the start of the season, I really had weekends where I would turn the steering wheel and strange things would happen. Now it’s all a bit more normal again."

Verstappen says he can make more of a difference again after Red Bull's successful Baku upgrade Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

When asked by Autosport, Verstappen acknowledges that this allows him to make more of a difference as an individual again, although in his view a driver can still only make a limited difference due to the constraints of the regulations.

"That’s still a bit of an issue. But the more our car gets the right balance again, the more I can push and the more I can get out of the car," he said.

As for his frustrations with the regulations and energy management, it is worth noting that this pole position changes nothing in that regard.

"No! That has nothing to do with whether I’m first, sixth or 10th. Those are two separate things," Verstappen stressed.

Is Red Bull's race pace enough for a first win of 2026?

An important caveat is that the starting position is not everything this weekend. Pirelli already explained on Friday that, due to the extremely rough tarmac and very high degradation, everything hinges on tyre management. But Verstappen says he is confident in that respect as well.

"Personally, I’m confident with what I did. If others make bigger sacrifices [for the race], then good luck to them, but I’m ready," the four-time world champion said.

"Ultimately, we need to have a decent start and that’s already difficult enough for us this year. After that, it’s obviously a very long race with the tyres. My race pace did look good, but of course you don’t know what others have changed since Friday, so we’ll have to wait and see."

Sports.title: Why Mercedes' upgrade is still a "big question mark"
Sports.content:
The Mercedes team has taken a big swing by introducing a substantial aerodynamic update package at a circuit Formula 1 hasn't visited since 2017. Has it missed?

Probably not – but, because the upgrade is a major one, Mercedes has committed to it on both cars so it has been unable to run back-to-back comparisons between old and new in identical conditions. This has added to the challenges of understanding why the W17 seems to have coped notably poorly with the Sepang track's abrasive asphalt surface.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli set the fourth-fastest time in qualifying after a mistake in Q2 meant he needed to use another set of the Pirelli C4 soft tyres, leaving him with just one remaining for Q3. George Russell was eighth fastest, though both Mercedes drivers will gain a place on the grid owing to Isack Hadjar's engine penalty.

"That is the big question mark," said Russell when asked by Autosport if the team had found it difficult to extract the potential of the new package.

"If you could have done a direct back-to-back it would have been great to know, but that's the challenge of this sport.

"If I put the upgrade package on last week, even if it was worse, we probably still would have been on pole and we'd have been saying it was fantastic. And equally, if we had the old car here, maybe the result would have been even worse.

"So that's the challenge. As a team we have yet to have, let's say, a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us."

The entire sidepod profile of the W17 has changed, as has much of the architecture underneath Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

The Mercedes upgrade features a new floor with major revisions to the leading edge, diffuser, and furniture around the rear wheels. More significantly it adopts a very different sidepod profile which it's understood has required the internal cooling architecture to be redesigned.

For this reason it is not possible to swap between the two specifications during a race weekend.

What has really provoked puzzlement within the team is the W17's apparent aversion to the unusually rough track surface at Sepang. It is highly unlikely to have been caused by the upgrade package, but it hinders efforts to understand and optimise it because there is no equivalent data set for the previous spec.

"It's very difficult to understand," said team boss Toto Wolff. "We've been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year. But then you can say it's very hot and the tarmac is very different to all the [other] tracks.

"It looked really good in the morning [when Antonelli topped FP3 by 0.278s from Max Verstappen, who later qualified on pole]. We seem to have at least with Kimi made a step in understanding.

"And then qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before. Just no performance.

"It looks like we're very draggy because it's the first time we're losing a lot of time on the straights, especially to Max. And then through the low speed, we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So overall, things we haven't seen all year."

Antonelli's qualifying was compromised by a track-limits violation in Q2 Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Antonelli and Russell certainly appeared to go backwards relative to their competition between final practice and qualifying. Russell was 0.741s off Verstappen's pole time despite having the typical two runs on new tyres in Q3.

Championship leader Antonelli had a lap struck off in Q2 for a track-limits violation, requiring him to go again with a new set of tyres which had originally been destined for him to use in Q3. That left him with just one opportunity to go for a timed lap in Q3 because the C4 hasn't proved resilient enough at Sepang to do more than one.

All the drivers have had to contend with a low-grip surface which is highly abrasive, owing to the more open nature of the aggregate. This has been a feature of the circuit ever since it was opened in 1999; the intention was to make the surface less slippery when wet, and to drain and dry quicker after bouts of rain.

"This circuit is a bit of an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac," said Russell. "The lap times seven years ago were about six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you're driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone. However, it's clearly affecting us more than others.

"All the numbers say it's [the upgrade] an improvement, but obviously it's a sport where we need to follow the lap times and not what the numbers say. So the numbers look absolutely fine and in line with expectations. However, the result wasn't."

Sports.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Verstappen dominates for first pole of 2026 from Hamilton
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen took his first pole of the 2026 Formula 1 campaign to deliver on his early weekend promise by dominating qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The Red Bull driver was fastest in all three sessions after also topping FP1 on Friday to take his first pole since the 2025 Abu Dhabi finale with a 1m35.130s at Sepang.

Verstappen will be joined on the front row by Lewis Hamilton on the weekend Malaysia ends its nine-year hiatus from F1 to host the Bahrain Grand Prix due to conflict in the Middle East.

It comes after the four-time world champion also went fastest in the first runs of Q3, taking the provisional top spot with a 1m35.250s, 0.308s quicker than team-mate Isack Hadjar in second.

Verstappen then failed to improve in the first two sectors of his second lap, before bouncing back with a purple final sector to go 0.120s quicker for the 49th pole of the Dutchman’s career.

His final time was 0.298s faster than Hamilton’s 1m35.428s for Ferrari, which pushed Hadjar down to third after the F1 sophomore failed to improve on his final lap.

Hadjar will serve a five-place grid penalty for an engine change which will see him start the Bahrain GP in Malaysia from eighth place.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli endured a struggle by taking fourth, 0.501s off the pace, after entering Q3 already compromised by what happened in Q2.

The Mercedes driver had to churn through an extra set of new softs after his first Q2 push lap was deleted for track limits at Turn 6, leading to him doing just one lap in the final session.

Antonelli’s 1m35.631s ultimately leaves him on the second row, one spot above Hamilton’s team-mate Charles Leclerc with a 1m35.666s, who will start fourth ahead of Lando Norris.

The reigning world champion was 0.627s off the pace on a weekend McLaren has struggled for speed, with Norris’ team-mate Oscar Piastri set to start sixth with a 1m35.762s.

It was even more of a struggle for Antonelli’s team-mate George Russell, who was 0.741s off the pace in eighth, but will start seventh to due Hadjar's penalty, with Alpine’s Pierre Gasly and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto completing the top 10.

Liam Lawson missed out on Q3 by two tenths to take 11th on the grid after being pushed into the Q2 elimination zone by Bortoleto right at the end.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

The Racing Bulls driver will duly share the sixth row with Aston Martin’s Fernando Alonso, who took his best qualifying result of 2026, while 13th went to Williams driver Carlos Sainz.

Sainz will be joined on the seventh row by Alonso’s team-mate Lance Stroll in the first double Q2 appearance of 2026 for Aston Martin, who confirmed both drivers for 2027 on Tuesday.

Franco Colapinto took 15th, but the Alpine driver will start Sunday’s race at the back due to a 15-place grid penalty: five for his Baku clash and 10 for changing his Mercedes power unit.

Rookie Arvid Lindblad took 16th for Racing Bulls, as he is also set for a grid drop, one spot above Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg who paid the price for starting Q1 on the mediums.

Haas driver Oliver Bearman will join him on the ninth row in 18th ahead of his outgoing team-mate Esteban Ocon in 19th - the Frenchman’s first Q1 exit since Spa.

Alex Albon’s frustrations continued with 20th for Williams ahead of the usual suspects: Valtteri Bottas in 21st, three tenths quicker than Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez at the back.

Sports.title: F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Antonelli recovers from tough Friday to top FP3
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli topped final practice at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to recover from a disappointing Friday for the championship-leading Mercedes outfit.

The Silver Arrows brought a heavily upgraded W17 to Sepang, but only managed second and fifth in FP1 and seventh and eighth in FP2 with other teams looking stronger.

But the dominant outfit of 2026 responded perfectly on Saturday with Antonelli going quickest on a 1m36.302s, two tenths quicker than Max Verstappen who set the pace in first practice.

This comes on the weekend that Sepang is returning to F1 for the first time since 2017, which was the final race of an 18-year stint where mixed weather conditions were characteristic.

Yet F1 is still waiting to see that from the Malaysian track in 2026 as FP3, like FP1 and 2, was dry throughout but did have the first running of the expected main race tyre, the hard.

That’s because tyre degradation played a huge role in Friday practice on the hot, low-grip surface and Charles Leclerc set a 1m37.772s on the white-striped rubber early on.

It put the Ferrari driver in third, respectively 0.611s and 0.289s behind McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who used the mediums with all three compounds shown.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

The softs were used by those in the midfield downwards meaning Leclerc was still the only driver to have the hards, but he was set to be joined by George Russell until the 25th-minute red flag.

That came after debris flew off Oliver Bearman’s Haas at Turn 10 and when the session resumed eight minutes later, with various drivers still yet to set a time, more soft tyre runs instead kicked in.

Championship leader Antonelli vaulted to the top with his first push lap, a 1m36.924s, giving him a 0.129s advantage over team-mate Russell in second.

Leclerc subsequently split the pair with a 1m37.016s to kickstart the final six-minute rush, with Isack Hadjar going top moments later on a 1m36.860s aboard his highly competitive Red Bull.

His lead only lasted for a short while though because, just after Russell had improved to a 1m36.912s, Antonelli displayed his dominance once more by setting a 1m36.302s.

That put the 20-year-old five tenths above Hadjar and both drivers were soon split by the Frenchman’s team-mate Verstappen, who set a 1m36.580s at the end of the qualifying runs.

So Red Bull had both of its cars inside the top three for the second time this weekend after FP1, while Russell took fourth for Mercedes with Leclerc in fifth, 0.714s off Antonelli.

Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton took sixth with a 1m37.041s ahead of seventh-placed Norris, whose best time (1m37.161s) came on the mediums with team-mate Piastri in eighth.

The Australian set a 1m37.366s that put him 1.064s off Antonelli, continuing McLaren’s struggles at Sepang after it finished 11th and 12th in opening practice.

Alpine’s Franco Colapinto and Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad, meanwhile, completed the top 10 in FP3 and were respectively 1.618s and 1.782s off the pace.

Sports.title: Why Verstappen’s unusual run plan highlights F1 teams’ biggest challenge in Malaysia
Sports.content:
Friday practice for the Formula 1 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was atypical in several respects. Lap times turned out to be four and a half seconds slower than expected due to the poor track surface, Mercedes did not impress as much as perhaps expected and the run plans were rather unusual.

The latter was perhaps most evident with Max Verstappen. Normally, drivers complete their qualifying simulations halfway through the second practice session before using the second half for long runs. With the FIA estimating the chance of rain ahead of FP2 at 90%, several teams wanted to play it safe, which in practice meant bringing their long runs forward.

“I wanted to do a long run in case there was some rain coming in,” Verstappen clarified when asked about his unusual Friday run plan.

Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache also explained that the team at least wanted to gather data on what is considered the most important factor of the race weekend at Sepang: tyre degradation.

“We didn't want to compromise the long run, which I think is the most important thing this weekend, in terms of degradation and see how the tyres behave, especially the medium. We didn't have data of the medium, so we prioritised that and afterwards it was too late to run the soft,” Wache said.

F1 teams’ biggest challenge at Sepang explained

It underlines two things. Firstly, this quote perfectly illustrates that looking at individual lap times after Friday in Kuala Lumpur is pointless. Only the long runs provide a valuable picture, meaning even less significance should be attached to Friday’s classification than usual.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Joe Portlock / Getty Images

Secondly, it underlines that F1 teams’ approach in Malaysia differs from a normal race weekend. Usually, it is a balancing act between qualifying performance and keeping the tyres – particularly the rear axle – alive during the race, but this time it is all about the latter.

“We have seen today that the degradation was quite significant, quite high. I remember just one weekend where we had this kind of degradation and that was Barcelona,” said Pirelli’s chief engineer Simone Berra.

“We have recorded around two or three tenths of tyre degradation per lap, on both the medium and the soft. So the level of decay is quite important here. Teams need to manage especially the rear temperatures, but also the front tyres in the high-speed corners.”

Moreover, that can become a vicious circle at Sepang, F1’s tyre supplier explained based on Friday’s data.

“Due to the poor surface, the grip was low on both the medium and the soft. This exacerbated even more thermal degradation because we know that sliding means higher surface temperatures, higher surface temperatures mean lower grip, that means even more sliding, that leads to higher surface temperatures again, and so on.”

Keeping thermal degradation under control is crucial to avoid ending up in this vicious circle, but that is easier said than done. That is because while the rear axle is the primary concern and this track is ‘rear-limited’, the front axle still requires management as well. And those two things are difficult to combine.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

“The point is that for the rear axle especially, there is no rear respite here. It's very difficult to keep the temperatures under control, you have to try to avoid sliding in the high-speed corners and on traction,” Berra explained.

“But meanwhile you have to keep consistency with the pace and you have to avoid overloading the front tyres.

“It's very complicated because you have to protect both axles basically, the front can overheat and degrade as well. It's really not simple. It will be a compromise in the end, which axle you prefer to degrade more. I think all teams will go to protect the rear, because in the end, on the rear axle, you lose much more performance than on the front.”

More qualifying question marks: Is a surprise on the cards?

All of this means that the teams’ work and data analysis on Friday evening is completely different from a week ago during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

“Baku was a circuit with very low degradation levels and very high importance of qualifying on the front rows. Here, qualifying is less important,” Berra continued.

“We know that it's possible to overtake, especially when you have this high degradation. If you are able to keep the performance and the tyre temperatures in the correct window, you can extend or you can push more than other competitors. The position on the grid is less important than in other places.”

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

That said, the extreme focus on race pace does mean that teams head into qualifying with more question marks than usual, even if it takes place in dry conditions.

Berra confirms – understandably without wanting to reveal which teams – that some teams even struggled on Friday to get their tyres up to temperature for the first corner of a flying lap. That may sound remarkable given the extremely high track temperatures, but it is a consequence of the huge focus on protecting the rear axle and therefore on race pace.

An interesting final point is that there are also many question marks for Sunday. As a precaution, all teams have decided to save two sets of hard tyres, meaning nobody – including Pirelli – has data on the C2, the hardest compound available this weekend.

Moreover, given the extreme conditions, the rule of thumb that the harder the compound, the better it is for the race does not necessarily apply.

“I would also expect a high level of degradation on the hard compound, because [a harder tyre] is generating a lower level of grip and therefore a higher level of sliding and higher surface temperature,” Berra explained.

“It's something that we have seen today with the soft and medium as well. We have seen in some back-to-back comparisons for the race that the soft was at a similar level of degradation or even a lower level of degradation than the medium. That’s because the medium was sliding more than the soft and the soft was more controllable, let's call it this way. And so all options are open for Sunday.”

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Photo by: Srinivasa Krishnan

The latter is essentially good news, as it could encourage strategic variation, which is exactly what Pirelli always aims for.

“All three compounds are usable because we are most likely going towards a two-stop race, and possibly even three stops. Everything is, let's say, in play at the moment,” Berra concluded.

“This is generating quite a big amount of possibilities in terms of strategies and that's what we want, also from our side, to generate different combinations.”

Sports.title: “This and golf are probably the two most frustrating fricking sports” – Hamilton | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton was “elated” to claim his second front row start in what he called a “trying year” so far.

The Ferrari driver’s only previous front row start this year came at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, which he went on to win.

Though he was second in the championship just four rounds ago, his deficit to leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli has more than double since then to over 100 points. He said he was “really, really happy” with today’s result after in season which has been frustrating at times.

“It’s definitely been a trying year. Lots and lots of positives, lots of good days [but] for sure more bad days on the race weekends.

“It’s just been a massive challenge. It’s so competitive out here every weekend. Everyone’s doing a really great job across the teams. There’s been some races where we’re all within tenths of each other and getting the most out of these cars and these power units has been, honestly, the bane of probably all of our lives.

“So we didn’t expect to be on the front row, so that’s why I’m so elated, because I thought we’d be like fourth or fifth or something like we usually are, so to be second is pretty awesome.”

Hamilton said he felt vindicated by the result. “We’re in the office, we’re giving it everything, we’re looking at all this data. You’re going through so many different things, you’re focusing on your breathing and your food and your timing and all these different things, your heart rhythm.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Then you get out and mistakes happen or something catches you out and it’s frustrating as hell. This and golf are probably the two most frustrating fricking sports there can possibly be.

“But when you finally calm down, get things aligned and things run smoothly and you get a result like today, it’s really great. It kind of just reinforces the belief you have in yourself

“All the times that you are failing make you question things sometimes. But you just continue to have that belief regardless of what is happening around you. Then, when it finally comes, you’re like ‘see, I knew I had it’. And that’s a great feeling.”

Sports.title: Russell mystified by latest setback after talking up his chances in Sepang | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell admitted he does not know why he was so uncompetitive in qualifying at Sepang following his strong performance in Baku.

The Mercedes driver arrived in Malaysia in a positive frame of mind after winning the Azerbaijan Grand Prix from pole position.

“Now feel in a position that my performances are strong enough to fight for victory week in, week out,” said Russell on Thursday. “Pre-summer break I was missing out in the championship but also I was also missing out on the performance every weekend.

“Whereas now I feel I know what I need from the car, I know from myself and I don’t really feel lost anymore. The confidence is back, it’s growing again. And it’s all coming a bit more naturally, which is how it has been for me in most of my career.”

He had high hopes for the upgrade Mercedes brought for their car this weekend. “I’m enjoying it more than I have done recently just because I feel more at one with the car and hopefully this new upgrade with a few characteristic changes are also going to play into my favourite a bit more,” said Russell.

However he was left disappointed by his performance in qualifying. Andrea Kimi Antonelli qualified ahead of him despite being compromised in Q3, where Russell had one more set of new soft tyres.

Russell will start Sunday’s race from seventh on the grid, four places behind Antonelli.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I really don’t know,” he said after qualifying. “It was a strange one out there today.”

“It’s the most demanding circuit on the tyres [and] we don’t exactly know why we didn’t have the pace. I think from Friday, it was clear we weren’t on the pace of the Red Bulls.

“Then throughout the course of this weekend, we just haven’t really progressed. The others have caught up and overtaken.”

However he remains hopeful he will be able to make progress in the race. “I think tomorrow the race is going to be a totally different story,” he said. “Very high tyre degradation, all three tyre compounds look viable, so I think there will be some opportunities.”

2026 Bahrain Grand Prix

Sports.title: Red Bull ‘pushed the weaknesses out’ says Verstappen after breakthrough pole | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says his first pole position of 2026 demonstrates the progress Red Bull have made with their car in recent races.

“It’s always very hard to say why that is, but I think for us anyway, the last few races we have probably understood the car a little bit better, but also the upgrades have pushed some of the weaknesses out of the car,” he said.

Verstappen was immediately competitive from the first practice in Sepang and unusually opted not to perform a soft tyre qualifying simulation in yesterday’s second session. Red Bull introduced an upgrade to their car at the last race in Baku, where Verstappen finished a close second, and the RB22 has performed well on a very different type of track this weekend.

“There are, of course, always things that you would still like, but we have been adding bits to the car and they have worked,” said Verstappen. “It’s simple as that.

“When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car. So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time.

“Then, on a track probably where it’s all very hot and you want a stable balance or connected balance, then that’s very important. And that’s, I think, what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends.”

His team mate Isack Hadjar, who missed three rounds prior to last weekend due to injury, said their car has clearly improved during his absence.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I definitely feel like I jumped in a car that’s way better than when I left it in Budapest,” he said. “Definitely, when you step out actually for three races and you come back, you actually notice a bigger difference.

“The last two weekends have been surprising. Even though I was following from close, even though I was on the bench, I feel like I’m quite surprised driving this car right now.”

Hadjar said Red Bull have a clear idea where they can make further gains with their car.

“I still believe there are things that need major improvements and still the car is performing okay, so it’s only good news,” he said. “I’m actually surprised it’s performing that well on a Tarmac that has such low grip. Usually it doesn’t really suit our car, but apparently it does.

“So it’s good that it works in Baku and Sepang, two completely different tracks. I think it’s good news.”

2026 Bahrain Grand Prix

Sports.title: Haas admit set-up mistake on Bearman’s car made one session a “total waste of time” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Oliver Bearman revealed his qualifying performance was compromised because Haas set his car up incorrectly for Friday’s second practice session.

“My car, to be honest in FP1 it was okay, in FP2 we really struggled,” he explained. “We did a mistake with the set-up and basically it was as if we didn’t run in FP2. It was totally a waste of time.”

Bearman was 16th in the second practice session, three-tenths of a second slower than team mate Esteban Ocon. He said the mistake with his set-up left him without valuable reference information for the rest of the weekend on his first visit to Sepang.

“Going into FP3 with just pretty much two push laps, you don’t have enough time to fix mistakes that we’ve done in previous days,” he said. “So that meant I went into quali basically like this and just guessing what to do with the car, with my driving and everything.”

The “incredibly high” tyre degradation made it harder to make up for lost time, said Bearman. “It means that every new tyre you get one push lap on it.

“So if you say that I’ve had four push laps on the new soft heading into quali, well the one on FP2 was a total waste of time, so that meant the two on FP3 were also pretty much a waste of time because we were trying to recover. So we’re just very behind.

“That’s not our true pace, that’s not our true potential, but it’s really not far from it, if I’m honest.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

A heavy lock-up at turn one left him heading to elimination in the first round of qualifying. “In my second run I locked the front-left which is the outside front into turn one, which is super-unusual and weird and usually tells you something’s up with the brakes so we need to look into that,” he said. “So I came into my final run with a lack of confidence, I definitely left some lap time on the table.”

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu admitted the team slipped up on Friday. “Operationally, we made a mistake on Ollie’s car in FP2, so that meant in the session he couldn’t get any information, and he couldn’t recover in FP3 with him because the tires only last one lap.

“Unlike Baku, where you could keep running and recovering, it wasn’t the case here, so it goes to show that everything counts. As a team, even though it’s tough, there are lots of specific things we need to look into.

“I’m confident that when we look into it and understand it, we can put a solution in place, like we have done every other time. It’s very tough, but that’s what we’ve got to focus on.”

Sports.title: Mercedes expected to gain three-tenths from upgrade but lost five – Wolff | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes suffered an unexpected setback in Malaysia as their upgrade for the W17 failed to deliver.

The runaway leaders in the constructors’ championship produced one of their weakest qualifying performances of the season at Sepang. Andrea Kimi Antonelli was half a second slower than pole-winner Max Verstappen while George Russell was two tenths of a second further behind.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said they expected the team’s long-awaited upgrade, one of few major packages they have introduced, would be worth around three tenths of a second.

“You’re expecting three tenths to kick in and it looks like [we’ve gone] three or four or five tenths backwards,” he told Sky. “It’s the first time we miss out on the top three, and by quite a chunk. So it’s odd, but I guess we will find a solution.”

Wolff said the unusually abrasive track surface at Sepang has complicated the team’s efforts to understand their new package.

“It’s very difficult to understand,” he said. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn’t see all year.

“But then you can say it’s very hot and the Tarmac is very different to all the tracks. It looked really good in the morning. We seem to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”

He said the team has identified two clear problems with their car performance this weekend. “It looks like we are very draggy because it’s the first time that we’re losing a lot of time on the straights to, especially, Max,” he said.

“Then through the low speed, turn two, we are not able to turn the car. There’s just too much understeer. So overall, things we haven’t seen we haven’t seen all year.”

However he believes there are further problems the team needs to solve. “Something else is going on and we have to understand,” he said. “This is now [about] working through the data and putting our heads together because we still believe that the upgrade works we just need to understand why not here.”

Sports.title: Verstappen takes first pole of 2026 ahead of Hamilton and Antonelli in Sepang | 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia qualifying
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen dominated qualifying at the Sepang International Circuit to claim his first pole position of the season.

Lewis Hamilton will join him on the front row of the grid for Formula 1’s first race in Malaysia for nine years. The pair will start in the same order they finished the last race at this track.

The threat from Mercedes failed to materialise as Andrea Kimi Antonelli compromised his session with his latest track limits breach and George Russell never figured in the fight for pole position.

Antonelli, who has had multiple penalties for track limits breaches this year, made life difficult for himself when he strayed beyond the exit kerb at turn six on his first lap in Q2. With Pirelli’s soft tyres only good enough for a single flying lap on the highly abrasive Malaysian track, Antonelli had to take a second fresh set to ensure he reached Q3, where unlike most of his fellow front-runners he would not have the benefit of a second set.

Verstappen’s first run in Q3 put him comfortably ahead, while Isack Hadjar backed him up in second place. Antonelli did his sole run in the gap between the others taking to the track and initially slotted into third place.

With his final run, Verstappen cut another tenth of a second off his best time so far, leaving the benchmark at a 1’35.130. His original run would have been quick enough for pole, as only Hamilton could get within three tenths of a second of him.

Hadjar qualified third but his grid penalty will drop him to eighth on the grid. Both Mercedes drivers will be among those to benefit, Antonelli moving up to third, Russell seventh. The two championship leaders will be separated by Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari and the two McLarens.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

The two other drivers with grid penalties dropped out in Q2: Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls used Lindblad to give his team mate a tow down the back straight – some compensation for crashing into his team mate in Baku last week – and Liam Lawson duly took 10th place. However he was eliminated by a superb final lap from Gabriel Bortoleto.

The Audi driver claimed a place in the final 10 having been the only Audi driver to progress through Q1. Like Ferrari, both their drivers used the medium rubber, but a poor final lap by Nico Hulkenberg meant he went no further.

The Aston Martin drivers revelled in their latest car improvements to achieve the team’s first double Q2 appearance of the season. It comes five months after the FIA changed its Additional Development Update Opportunity regulations to help its power unit supplier Honda.

Carlos Sainz Jnr, the only Williams driver to reach Q2, split the two AMR26s. Alexander Albon continued his run of Q1 eliminations this season after locking up and running wide at turn 14.

Both Haas drivers went out in the first round. Oliver Bearman went deep at turn one on his first attempt while Esteban Ocon was one of the first drivers to complete his final run and felt he had left the pits too soon. The Cadillac pair were slowest.

Sports.title: 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia grid | Formula 1
Sports.content: The Formula 1 world championship began in 1950 and is considered the world’s leading form of single-seater motorsport. The 2025 F1 season is the 75th time the championship has been held. Sports.title: Featured Comment: Ferrari in Todt’s time had more problems than Vasseur faces | Briefs
Sports.content:
One thing all Ferrari team principals have in common is the intense scrutiny they face from the media and the passionate Italian tifosi.

Current team principal Frederic Vasseur has experienced that again in the past week, prompting the team to reiterate its support for him.

Vasseur is trying to put Ferrari back on the path to victory. The man who most recently achieved this successfully was Jean Todt in the mid-nineties. And as reader @Tifoso1989 explains, he arguably faced a much tougher task:

The management and the way the team was being run were clearly a mess that’s precisely why Vasseur was brought in but I wouldn’t say Ferrari’s underlying technical organisation was collapsing. The F1-75 is the clearest evidence of that. Ferrari produced the best all-round interpretation of the ground effect regulations straight out of the box. It was quick in qualifying, strong in race pace, and competitive across different types of circuits. It was the benchmark early in the season until the TD039 came in and Red Bull got the RB18 down to the minimum weight around Hungary. Whatever happened afterwards, you don’t produce a car like that if the entire technical organization is collapsing. And Ferrari had already spent years, particularly in the period before the budget cap, investing heavily in its infrastructure to sort out the wind-tunnel/track correlation problems that had plagued them. They had also invested in a new state of the art simulator from Bristol-based Dynisma, which was already being used in the development of the F1-75. On top of that, they were making extensive use of AWS for advanced analytics, machine learning and AI, allowing them to run simulations much faster and extract more data from the car development process. So I think there’s an important distinction here. The management was dysfunctional. The technical foundations weren’t. That’s actually part of my argument about Vasseur. He didn’t inherit the Ferrari of the early 1990s that Todt inherited. He inherited a team with enormous resources, modern facilities, a sophisticated simulation and data infrastructure and, as the F1-75 demonstrated, the ability to produce a genuinely excellent F1 car. His job was to take those resources and turn them into a properly functioning championship operation. And that’s why I’m much less sympathetic to the argument that Ferrari simply needed several years to rebuild from the ground up. The foundations were already there when Vasseur arrived.
