World.title: Remembering the Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968
World.content:
The Tlatelolco student massacre of 1968 — one of the most pivotal events in modern Mexican history, one that the renowned National Security Archive organization has called “Mexico’s Tiananmen Square” — all began with a fracas between two rival public vocational high schools that erupted into an out-and-out brawl in a Mexico City marketplace built for the upcoming 1968 Olympics.

The next day, riot police arrived at the two schools, wielding clubs and beating anyone within reach, attacking students and faculty with equal brutality. The following day, students took to the streets in protest of the previous day’s beating, which then, in turn, drew the police out for more violent confrontations.

How protests escalated into the 1968 Tlatelolco Massacre

“Those protests provoked more repression, which provoked more protests,” journalists Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon explained in their 2005 book, “Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy.”

By the fourth day of protests, tensions escalated. To express solidarity with their fellow teenage protesters, the students of the prestigious high school, San Ildefonso Preparatory — officially known as the National Preparatory School — declared a strike. When Mexican President Gustavo Díaz Ordaz learned that the students at the prestigious government-run school were on strike, he ordered the Mexican army to take the campus.

Soldiers in Jeeps and small tanks moved across the city, aiming to confront the students of San Ildefonso. When they arrived at the campus, they found the entrance locked, so soldiers blew the school’s ornate 18th-century wooden door, hand-carved by Indigenous craftsmen, to bits.

The soldiers rampaged through the school, beating anyone they could find. They then turned on other high schools, and even attacked unsuspecting pedestrians they encountered on surrounding streets.

“By the end of the day, 400 people had been hospitalized and 1,000 arrested,” Preston and Dillon noted.



“Through the military occupation of the San Ildefonso School, the government elevated the situation from a local, primarily police matter to an issue of national security,” wrote Mexican historian Enrique Krauze, author of the seminal book “Mexico: Biography of Power.”

A history of government repression

For most Mexicans, government repression was nothing new. In 1959, railroad workers who went on strike, asking for better working conditions and a modest pay increase, were viciously put down, a pattern well-established with striking miners, doctors, nurses and even teachers. Strikers were routinely either beaten into submission or cajoled into joining a newly created government-run union. But this episode — the government violently attacking a high school — stunned most Mexicans.

In response, on July 31, Javier Barros Sierra, the politically moderate rector of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) — which was in charge of San Ildefonso Preparatory and is the largest and most prestigious university in Latin America — led a dignified, peaceful march of 50,000 faculty and students through Mexico City’s leafy suburbs.

That Barros had the temerity to lead such a protest earned him the enmity of Díaz Ordaz; later that summer, it cost him his job. That march, however, moved the center of protests against the government from Mexico’s high schools to its universities.

Taking inspiration from the U.S. civil rights movement and the earlier 1968 student protest movements in Paris, West Germany, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Japan, the Mexican university student activists had happened upon an issue that already deeply resonated with the general Mexican public: government brutality.

Students stand up in dissent

Raúl Álvarez Garín, a 27-year-old physics student from Mexico’s National Polytechnic Institute, emerged as one of the student leaders. Álvarez came from a family steeped in a tradition of protest and of standing up for its beliefs. His grandfather was an aide to Mexican Revolutionary General Álvaro Obregón. His parents were communists. His wife was the daughter of one of the leaders of the aforementioned railroad workers’ strike of 1959.

Álvarez helped draw up a modest list of demands: The government should release the recently jailed students, as well as the railroad union leaders still imprisoned since 1959. They should also compensate the families of injured protesters, disband the riot police and repeal vague laws used to jail anyone who dissented with the government.

Álvarez and his fellow activists weren’t advocating regime change or overthrowing the government. They were advocating that the political process in Mexico become more tolerant, open and democratic. But, for Díaz Ordaz, this was beyond the pale. The government never responded to the demands.

In the face of government silence, the student activists decided to hold a march from the southern suburbs to the Zócalo. They set the date for August 13, hoping to attract a few followers. On that day, by the time they reached the Zócalo, there were 200,000 people in tow. While many were students and families of students, there were also nurses, teachers, and every kind of worker in the city in the crowd. Speeches were delivered, and the event was entirely peaceful. As Preston and Dillon pointed out, “The unexpected size of the crowd proved that the students were voicing frustrations felt by Mexicans of all ages in a modernizing Mexico.”

A warning to protesters

The students then planned another march to the Zócalo for August 27, and this time, 400,000 people showed up. On this occasion, though, some students congregated under the balcony of the National Palace, the building from which Mexican presidents traditionally preside over annual Independence Day celebrations, standing on a balcony. Those students then started chanting, “Sal al balcón, chango hocicón” (“Come out to the balcony, you big-snouted monkey”) — referring to Díaz Ordaz’s pronounced buckteeth and frequent comparisons to a monkey.

As nighttime fell, most protesters left, but at the approach of midnight, a few thousand stragglers continued to mill around. At that point, a dozen armored personnel carriers rolled into the Zócalo; the army mercilessly beat any remaining protesters.

Then on September 1, Díaz Ordaz delivered his annual State of the Union address, essentially offering a warning.

“We can’t allow our legal order to continue to be ruptured so inexcusably,” the president declared in his speech. “We wouldn’t like to find ourselves in a situation where we would have to take measures we don’t want to. But we’ll take them if we must. We’ll go as far as we have to.”

Unfortunately, the students did not recognize the warning.

Politician and ex-education minister of Mexico City Salvador Martínez della Roca, one of the student leaders from UNAM at the time, told U.S. journalist Mark Kurlansky, “It was a threat, but we didn’t really listen.”

By September 24, “Mexico City was living under a barely camouflaged state of siege,” Krauze explains.

Mexican military mobilizes against campuses

On that day, the army seized the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN), known colloquially as the Politécnico; government forces had already occupied the UNAM campus. IPN students fought the army for hours, but there was only so much that unarmed civilians could do against tanks.

Although the army withdrew from both campuses on September 30, the message had been sent. Unfortunately, students failed to recognize that, for Díaz Ordaz’s government, a hard-and-fast deadline was quickly approaching: the 1968 Olympic Games, scheduled to begin in Mexico City on Oct. 12.

The Olympics were seen by many in the nation as Mexico’s moment to shine: The world no longer saw it as a chaotic, strife-ridden backwater nation but as the “Mexico Miracle” — with a powerful economy and a newly minted middle class. From the 1950s through the 1960s, Mexico’s economy had grown at 6% per annum (8% in 1968). In 1968, Mexico had the strongest economy in all of Latin America, with an inflation rate lower than the United States.

Díaz Ordaz was not about to let a bunch of long-haired students, whom he viewed as spoiled, ruin the opening of the Olympic Games and Mexico’s moment of glory.

President Díaz Ordaz sees conspiracies everywhere

Much like former U.S. president Richard Nixon, Díaz Ordaz was a tremendously insecure man, about his appearance and when interacting with others. “Ever since he was a little boy, the sense of being ugly had tortured him,” Krauze explained. “His mother would freely say to anyone, ‘But what an ugly son I have!’ It would take its toll on his life.”

And much like Nixon, Díaz Ordaz saw conspiracies everywhere. If students were protesting, it must be at the behest of French communists or Cuban agitators. In reality, this seems unlikely; even the CIA station chief in Mexico City, Winston Scott, doubted it.

“Although the [Mexican] government claims to have solid evidence that the Communist Party engineered the fracas of 26 July, and reportedly had indications of Soviet Embassy complicity, it is unlikely that the Soviets would so undermine their carefully nurtured good relations with the Mexicans,” Scott told CIA headquarters at the time.

It never occurred to Díaz Ordaz that it was, in fact, his policies — or his overreaction to a minor skirmish — that spurred the student protests.

After a few more protests, at which some buses were set on fire, the student leaders scheduled a rally to be held on October 2 at the Plaza de las Tres Culturas. This plaza sits in the Tlatelolco neighborhood on the north side of Mexico City. Perhaps more than any other site, it best represents Mexican history: Aztec ruins there are flanked by a Franciscan church.

In the 1960s, the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) government built a housing project there, one building of which was Edificio Chihuahua. The third floor of the Edificio Chihuahua had an open-air hallway with a three-foot wall overlooking the plaza. It was from this third-floor balcony that the speakers decided to address the crowd on October 2.

The day of the Tlatelolco Massacre

By 8:30 a.m. that morning, the army had taken up positions in each corner of the plaza — not necessarily unusual — as the army often posted soldiers at protest rallies. But something about this day seemed off: Witnesses later mentioned seeing men with short haircuts in civilian clothes, all wearing a white glove on one hand.

Myrthokleia Gonzáles Gallardo, a 22-year-old Politécnico student, had been chosen to introduce the speakers that day, even though her parents warned her not to go, fearing something might happen with the increased military presence.

Myrthokleia described her entry into the Plaza:

“As I approached the Tlatelolco with the four speakers, I was introduced, and we were warned to be careful, as the army had been seen nearby. But I wasn’t afraid, though we decided to make it a short meeting. There were workers, students, and families coming into the plaza, filling it up. We didn’t see any [soldiers] in the plaza.

“We took our place on the third floor and started our speeches. Suddenly, off to the left, over the church, were helicopters with a green light. Suddenly, everyone down in the plaza started falling. And then men with white gloves and weapons appeared, maybe from the elevator. They ordered us down to the ground floor, where they began beating us.”

Gunfire erupts and continues for hours

Raúl Álvarez Garín was also whisked down to the ground floor and made to stand facing a wall as government forces beat him relentlessly. Álvarez remembered the sound of automatic gunfire continuing for a full two hours. Other witnesses remember sporadic gunfire until 11 p.m.

The next morning, journalist Elena Poniatowska arrived at Tlatelolco at dawn. There were tanks and soldiers everywhere, yet no one tried to impede her strolling around the plaza. She had heard from a friend that bodies covered the plaza, but by morning, they all had been taken away.

In the newspaper Excelsior, Poniatowska learned that Italian journalist Oriana Fallaci was in Mexico to cover the Olympics and had been wounded while attending the rally. Poniatowska tracked down Fallaci in a hospital and interviewed her.

“What savagery!” Fallaci told her. “Police dragging students away by the hair. I saw many people get hit — until I was hit too. I lay in a pool of my own blood for 45 minutes.”

Shocked by what she heard, Poniatowska wrote an article detailing the events. Her editor immediately rejected it.

“There’s an order,” the editor announced, according to Preston and Dillon. “We’re going to concentrate on the Olympic Games. We’re not printing anything more about Tlatelolco.”

The legacy of the Tlatelolco Massacre

The Tlatelolco student massacre was a tragic and immensely consequential event in Mexican history. The Olympic Games may have gone off without a hitch, but at what cost? Over 400 people were murdered in cold blood by government troops. Hundreds more simply disappeared, never heard from again. Hundreds more were imprisoned for years. Hundreds, if not thousands, went into hiding, fearing retaliation for simply expressing their ideas about the nature of their society.

Before 1968, most Mexicans felt proud of their nation’s economic achievements. During the Mexican Revolution, one leader after another had been brutally assassinated. In the wake of the Revolution, the PRI provided stability and economic growth, and Mexico had become a modern nation. In 1959, American academics conducted a poll and found that while most Mexicans were tired of their country’s endemic corruption, they were generally proud of their political system and its achievements and felt their presidents were, for the most part, benign. After 1968, however, most middle-class Mexicans felt disillusioned, resentful and utterly distrustful of their government.

Perhaps the students’ National Strike Council (CNH) final statement, issued in December 1968 upon its dissolution, summed it up best:

“Democracy in Mexico is just a concept, another formalism,” it announced. “Politics is carried out behind the backs of the popular majorities and of their aspirations, interests and demands.”

While the student movement of 1968 was neutralized, the Tlatelolco massacre has had a long-lasting impact on Mexican politics and history: More than 50 years later, October 2 is commemorated every year across Mexico with civilian demonstrations. Films and documentaries and countless books have been written about it — in Mexico and around the world.

Groundwork laid in 1968 also spawned a generation of the nation’s activists and political leaders, who were involved in Mexico’s electoral reform in the 1980s, which ultimately led to the end of the PRI’s uninterrupted rule over Mexico for 70 years in 2000, with Vicente Fox’s election as president.

Kurlansky, in his book “1968: The Year that Rocked the World,” commented: “But very much in the same way that the invasion of Czechoslovakia was the (beginning of the) end of the Soviet Union, Tlatelolco was the unseen beginning of the end of the end of the PRI.”

Robert McLaughlin, Ph.D. is a historian specializing in Cold War Latin American history.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Peso sinks to 18 as school safety, storms and trade talks dominate
World.content:
Listen to this article

Attacks on and by students, a political comeback and the memory of past violence marked the week of Sept. 28 in Mexico. Two 17-year-old students from a prep school affiliated with the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM) were shot dead in Cuernavaca on Saturday night, weeks after the Sept. 12 killing of Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte. That brings to six the number of UAEM students murdered in Morelos this year. After students and members of the Somos party protested Sunday outside the state attorney general’s office, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced a special security plan for Morelos on Monday.

On Friday, the 58th anniversary of the Tlatelolco massacre, students, rural normalistas and parents of the 43 missing Ayotzinapa students marched from Mexico City’s Plaza de las Tres Culturas to the Zócalo. In Cuernavaca, students and families of slain youths marched for justice, and some protesters set fire to the exterior of the state government palace, causing no major damage, according to Animal Político. Morelos ranked first nationally in homicide rates among both 13-to-17-year-olds and 18-to-29-year-olds from January to August, the outlet noted.

Former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador resurfaced Wednesday with an 80-minute video message promoting his new book, “Pueblo,” which he dedicated to Sheinbaum, calling her “the best president in the world.” On Thursday, the second anniversary of her inauguration, Sheinbaum cited approval ratings of up to 75%, pointing to polls by FactoMétrica (74.9%) and El Financiero (70%). Meanwhile, Morena named its 17 presumptive candidates for the governorships up for election on June 6, 2027, including ex-Financial Intelligence Unit chief Santiago Nieto in Querétaro and Clara Luz Flores in Nuevo León.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Ebrard optimistic about trade talks

Bilateral negotiations of the USMCA trade agreement continued in the United States this week. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Thursday that Mexico and the U.S. are getting “closer every day” to new trade terms. Speaking on the sidelines of a G-20 meeting in Milwaukee, Ebrard said he had held a one-hour meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. His priorities are reducing Section 232 tariffs on Mexican autos, steel, aluminum and copper, and preserving preferential treatment for USMCA-compliant goods.

Ebrard said Mexico is in a better position than most countries at the summit, crediting Sheinbaum’s handling of relations with President Donald Trump. An anonymous Mexican official told France 24 that Mexico expects reductions on steel, cars and aluminum and is content to be patient if no deal arrives before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3. Ebrard also confirmed a “new stage” in relations with India, where talks include tequila, which faces a 150% tariff.

Hurricane Polo hits Baja California Sur, then Sonora

After lingering off Mexico’s Pacific coast for much of a week, Hurricane Polo made landfall in Baja California Sur late Monday near Las Barrancas, in Comondú. It arrived as a Category 2 storm, far weaker than the Category 5 it reached days earlier, when it became one of the most rapidly intensifying storms on record. Before reaching the peninsula, it caused at least four deaths in Jalisco.

Polo dropped 15-30 centimeters of rain on Baja California Sur, but authorities reported no deaths or injuries. “There was more water than wind,” Gov. Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said. The storm then crossed the Gulf of California and lashed the Sonora coast on Tuesday as a Category 1 hurricane, causing flooding, power outages and downed trees in Guaymas and Empalme.

Vice principal killed in Torreón school attack

On Thursday, two 18-year-old twin brothers who were former students attacked the Number 13 Secondary School in Torreón, Coahuila, with machetes and rudimentary explosives. Vice principal Nery Edith Narváez González was killed, and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said four people were injured. Students helped restrain the suspects.

At her Friday mañanera, Sheinbaum announced a working group to demand that social media platforms remove content promoting violence. Luisa María Alcalde, Sheinbaum’s top legal adviser, will lead it, and a decree setting platform obligations is expected to be drafted next week. Authorities say the brothers were inspired by attackers abroad whom they learned about online.

Senate passes dual nationality ban for top offices

The Senate approved a constitutional reform on Tuesday requiring exclusive Mexican nationality for presidential, gubernatorial and Mexico City mayoral aspirants. The vote was 86 to 42, with Morena, the PT and the PVEM in favor. The bill needs ratification by at least 17 state legislatures, and would take effect in 2028 without affecting current officeholders. “The presidents of Mexico can only have one flag,” Sheinbaum said Wednesday.

Ayotzinapa: Authorities present 4 new lines of investigation

Twelve years after 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College were abducted in Iguala, Guerrero, after municipal police stopped their bus on Sept. 26, 2014, federal officials outlined four new lines of investigation on Monday. Sheinbaum had stressed that morning that the case is “not closed” and that the students’ parents had been briefed. The remains of only three students have been identified, and 168 people face judicial proceedings, but no one has been convicted.

The first line stems from analysis of phone records, which identified 17 new suspects and calls between Guerreros Unidos members and staff at funeral homes and the health sector. Investigators say an Iguala funeral parlor owner who also ran forensic services used a student’s phone, prompting searches. In October 2025, authorities found a human femur, a firearm and an unregistered crematorium oven. Searches between March and June 2026 turned up hundreds of bone fragments, dental prostheses and bullet casings, now under expert analysis.

The second line, based on three students’ phones later used by a municipal official, a police officer and people close to an ex-public servant, strengthens the hypothesis that 17 students were taken to the Iguala municipal lockup. The third identified a new suspect who was 14 at the time and whose July 30 statement implicates Guerreros Unidos members. The fourth concerns the concealment of courthouse security video from that night, which led to the arrests of a former judge and inspector and the Aug. 6 arrest of former Guerrero Gov. Ángel Aguirre.

Deputy Interior Minister Arturo Medina said 17 soldiers face prosecution but that the army as an institution is not accused. Tomás Zerón, the former head of the Criminal Investigation Agency, remains at large in Israel.

Oaxaca prosecutors investigate six municipal presidents

After the Sept. 23 arrest of Juchitán Mayor Miguel Sánchez Altamirano over alleged ties to a CJNG-linked group, the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office has opened cases against six other municipal presidents, all tied to Juchitán. Attorney General Bernardo Rodríguez said they come from “different political affiliations.” A warrant was issued for Mariano Rosado, Sánchez’s second-in-command, and Emilio Montero resigned as head of the state’s public education institute. The Isthmus of Tehuantepec has recorded 957 murders since 2022, 70% linked to the “Los Cromos” gang.

Airlines abandon Tulum

Aeroméxico suspended its Tulum flights after Sept. 30, and Volaris then announced it will end service starting Jan. 7, 2027. The airport handled 471,500 travelers from January to June, a 33.2% drop from last year, and beachfront hotel occupancy was below 20% by mid-September. Volaris pointed to rising costs for foreign visitors, including a planned 35% increase in the non-resident fee.

Peso nosedives as growth, jobs and exports impress

Peso returns to 18 to the dollar

The peso weakened to 18 per U.S. dollar on Monday, a 6.2% drop from the month’s strongest close of 16.89 on Sept. 4. The newspaper El Financiero blamed risk aversion, higher oil prices after Trump rejected an Iranian proposal on the Strait of Hormuz, and a tighter U.S. Federal Reserve, which raised its rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4%. The peso ended Friday at 18.16, and Banco Base’s Gabriela Siller said it could end the year near 2025’s close of 18.0080.

The slide came just after the MND Peso Index™ found the peso to be 5.8% overvalued in early September, its highest reading yet, comparing a 16.98 Banxico FIX rate with an MND Peso Rate of 17.96. With the peso now near 18, that gap has largely closed, at least for now.

Economy grows 3.3% in July

Mexico’s economy grew 3.3% year over year in July, the strongest monthly result of 2026, according to INEGI, with services up 4% and the secondary sector 2.4%. Pantheon Economics’ Andrés Abadía said July puts the third quarter in a “much stronger position than expected,” but that one month doesn’t make a sustained recovery.

Employment tops 60 million

Labor Minister Marath Bolaños said Monday that 60.7 million people were employed at the end of August, up 1.2 million from a year earlier. He didn’t mention that 55% of workers are in the informal sector.

Exports surge, led by computers

Exports rose 40.4% annually in August and 29.3% through eight months, reaching a record US $549.4 billion. Non-automotive manufacturing, mainly computer equipment, was up more than 63% in August. Mexico exported nearly $83 billion in servers, 93.9% of them to the U.S. Analysts flagged the dependence and reliance on Asian suppliers, with Taiwan providing about 44% of key inputs.

Looking ahead

Morelos security: Sheinbaum said the federal government will coordinate with Gov. Margarita González Saravia on where support is needed, and Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez has been in touch with the UAEM rector. Cuernavaca Mayor José Luis Urióstegui has warned that security leadership could change if there are no results within two weeks.

Sheinbaum said the federal government will coordinate with Gov. Margarita González Saravia on where support is needed, and Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez has been in touch with the UAEM rector. Cuernavaca Mayor José Luis Urióstegui has warned that security leadership could change if there are no results within two weeks. Social media decree: Security Minister García Harfuch said work on a decree setting obligations for platforms to detect and remove violent content is expected to begin next week.

Security Minister García Harfuch said work on a decree setting obligations for platforms to detect and remove violent content is expected to begin next week. Dual nationality reform: The bill heads to the state legislatures, where Morena holds majorities. Sen. Jasmin Bugarín, who was born in Los Angeles, has pledged to renounce her U.S. citizenship.

The bill heads to the state legislatures, where Morena holds majorities. Sen. Jasmin Bugarín, who was born in Los Angeles, has pledged to renounce her U.S. citizenship. Trade and the peso: Tariff talks continue ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterms. The peso’s gap with the dollar could widen if the Fed raises rates again next month.

World.title: I moved to Mexico City in my 20s. Here’s what I learned
World.content:
If you move to Mexico City in your 20s, I hope it becomes a home and not just a destination.

I came to Mexico at 25 thinking I was moving abroad one more time. I had already lived outside Spain, so I knew what it meant to arrive somewhere new, figure out a city, make friends and eventually find my way around. I thought Mexico City would be another chapter in that story.

A year later, I realized something else happened. I didn’t just move to Mexico; I started building a life here.

When you’re in your 20s, it’s easy to romanticize starting over somewhere else. How many of us, after a mental breakdown, have thought about leaving everything behind? Maybe moving to Paris like Blair, or finding the messy, exciting life Carrie Bradshaw had in New York City in her 30s.

I’m not saying New York or Paris won’t give you what you need to find. They might. But I found something in Mexico City that I wasn’t necessarily looking for: a place where I could become a slightly different version of myself.

Asking better questions in a new city

For me, my 20s have become less about figuring everything out and more about asking better questions. Do I want to become a mother? Will I get married? What do I want my career to look like? What kind of woman do I want to become? What do I want my future family to look like? I don’t have the answers yet. But living abroad has made me more conscious of the questions.

When I told my friends in Europe that I was moving to Mexico, some of them were worried. I wasn’t particularly afraid. My biggest concern was more mundane: I love walking, and I simply wondered whether I would be able to walk as much as I did back home. I quickly found out I could. I walk from our apartment in San Miguel de Chapultepec to Condesa to see friends, or go to a class. I walk through Chapultepec Park almost every day, and sometimes all the way to Polanco, which can take close to an hour.

One of the first things Mexico City taught me was how easily we can misunderstand places we’ve never experienced ourselves.

Before coming to Mexico, I only knew two Mexicans. They had been exchange students in Finland when I was studying there in 2020 and 2021. We weren’t friends. I just remember them being very good at beer pong and drinking rum or gin with water.

Then I arrived. And I started meeting people.

Finding kindness in the unlikeliest moments

Before Mexico, the country that completely changed my understanding of human connection was Cuba. I would need to write another article about everything that island gave me, but I truly thought nothing could surprise me in the same way again. Until Mexico did.

On my third day living in Mexico City, I was waiting in line to pay for a haircut. The woman behind me noticed what I was doing and immediately told me there was a cheaper hairdresser in the shop across the street. This act of kindness was the first one that people have shown me here. They aren’t normally dramatic moments, but they happen very often. Sometimes it is smiling in the street, starting a conversation or simply making an effort when they have no reason to.

At home, you move through your busy day surrounded by people and routines that are familiar. Abroad, you become more aware of your interactions, and they end up becoming part of what makes a place feel like yours.

There was another adjustment I was not expecting. As a European — very active and not particularly patient — I was struck by how slowly life seemed to move here. I learned that “ahorita” doesn’t necessarily mean right now. It can mean soon. It can mean later. Most of the time it’s just a polite way of saying something will happen when it happens. And you’ll get your coffee when you’re meant to get it. If you’re in a hurry, I recommend you insist a couple of times.

How different neighborhoods shape who you are

One of the things that continues to amaze me about Mexico City is how different each neighborhood feels. Polanco and Santa Fe have their own rhythm: business, luxury, restaurants, offices, polished cars and people dressed for work.

Then you go to Condesa or Roma, and suddenly you’re surrounded by leafy streets, cafes, parks and lots of dogs. I spend a lot of time in Parque México with a good friend of mine who has lived here since 2024, and we still find ourselves surprised by what we see: people dancing, doing karate, playing pickleball, learning to skate, practicing hula-hoop, someone selling poems, couples sitting on benches, foreigners taking photographs of a scene that locals barely notice because, to them, it’s simply Tuesday. That is Mexico City.

The Historic Center still leaves me speechless: the old buildings, the ruins, the Zócalo, Alameda Central, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL), the markets and the streets where centuries of history exist on top of each other.

And then there is Coyoacán, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, colorful markets, museums, and streets that feel completely different from the rest of the city.

The most interesting part is not just that these neighborhoods look different. They also make you feel different. You become a different version of yourself depending on where you are in the city. And in your 20s, that gives you something I have learned to appreciate: perspective.

Experiencing Mexican art and architecture

I’ve visited many museums since arriving — some of the famous ones and others that are less known. I don’t want to pretend I can explain Mexican art after a year here. But I can say that I have never experienced history through public art in quite the same way. The murals of Diego Rivera are not simply beautiful paintings. They tell stories about Mexico, its people and its history. Artists like Frida Kahlo transformed personal pain into art and became part of a cultural identity recognized around the world. I was also so impressed by Luis Barragán. Have you seen his house in San Miguel de Chapultepec? It was designed in the late 1940s, and I swear if you discover it today, you’ll want to move in there. Mexico City reminds me that contemporary doesn’t always mean new.

The joys of Mexican food

The same happened with food. Unpopular opinion: I’m not a foodie. I enjoy a latte and a cookie as much as avocado toast or a good meal at a cool restaurant every once in a while. Just give me some food when I’m hungry, and I’ll be happy. But even I have been fascinated by Mexican food. Mexican cuisine was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010, and one of the things I’ve learned is that there is no single thing called “Mexican food.” Ingredients, dishes and traditions change so much from state to state.

Even as a vegetarian, I have found myself trying things I never expected to eat: nopal, huitlacoche and many other ingredients I did not know of before arriving.

And Mexico City is not only Mexican food. You can eat Thai, Italian, Spanish, Chinese … you name it, you’ll find it. I even discovered one of my favorite Lebanese places here in the Historic Center.

Lessons in community through Día de los Muertos

I moved to Mexico City about a year ago, just as the rainy season was ending and Independence Day celebrations were beginning. I was warned before arriving that people knew how to celebrate. “But isn’t that true everywhere?” I thought. Especially coming from Spain, where we’re always down to party. But I understood quickly that celebration here can mean something bigger than drinking late into the night. There is a sense of community, belonging and gathering together.

To this day, experiencing Día de los Muertos in Mexico has been one of the best experiences of my life. We went to the village of Malinalco, less than two hours from Mexico City, to visit family altars. We entered house after house, each one belonging to families that had lost someone that year. Every house was different. Some had large patios and modern buildings; others were old. In all of them, they replicated the profession of the person who had died through objects, decorations and food: a baker, a secretary, a police officer, a chef. The altars were filled with bright orange cempasúchil flowers and candles.

In some of them, we lit our own candles as a sign of respect. Every family gave us something to eat and drink — from tamales and tacos to mezcal, tequila or warm spiced wine. In some of them, you could really feel the presence of the person being remembered. How generous of those families, after losing their loved ones, to celebrate their lives with us, strangers to them. It was so magical. I left with tears in my eyes from the lesson in humanity I had just experienced.

Building a life together while making it your own

I’m not single, and my boyfriend and I moved here together. Some people might think moving with your partner in your 20s means you miss out on the experience. That hasn’t been our case. If anything, moving here has made us more intentional about building a life, both individually and as a couple.

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: 2 Mexico City chefs launched an international ‘Pay What You Can’ model. How did it go?
World.content:
Food is, in many ways, the greatest of social equalizers. Everyone, after all, must sit down to eat at various points in the day, and there’s no escaping the fact that we must all break bread together.

But too often, there’s an exclusivity around who gets to actually sit at the proverbial table. In a bustling metropolis like Mexico City, in particular, many residents are gatekept and unable to enjoy the city’s most sought-after offerings, largely due to massive socioeconomic barriers.

Wealth disparities shape capital dining

The gap between those who can, or can’t, access Mexico City’s jeweled offerings is wider than ever. A 2026 report from Oxfam Mexico revealed just how disparate Mexico has become as a nation, with 1% of the population hoarding 40% of the country’s wealth.

The divide is glaringly obvious in high-end neighborhoods like Mexico City’s Santa Fe. Oscar Lopez of The Guardian wrote about how “unbelievably unequal” certain areas of Mexico City actually are: “The stark contrast in this little enclave of the capital is a microcosm of a problem that has plagued Mexico for decades: rampant income inequality, with a small slice of the population living in opulence while millions of families languish in poverty.”

The irony, of course, is that the essential workers who sustain the infrastructure for opulent lifestyles in Mexico rarely — if ever — get invited to partake in it. That trickles down to something like booking a table at a popular restaurant in CDMX, which only a select few get to enjoy.

Taking that reality into account, Norma Listman and Saqib Keval — the married chef-owners of Masala y Maíz, a prominent Michelin-starred eatery in Mexico City’s historic center that serves a blend of Mexican, Indian and East African dishes — have made efforts to raise awareness around such issues in the food industry, including workers’ rights and dining accessibility for all.

A global movement for humane hospitality

This summer, they initiated a “Paga Lo Que Puedas” or “Pay What You Can” (PWYC) day, effectively opening their doors to every diner, regardless of their tax bracket or bank account. A powerful and unprecedented gesture, it triggered a wave of support among participating restaurants who joined the cause throughout Mexico, and beyond, to galvanize a movement centered on humane hospitality.

“As the city becomes more expensive and more oriented toward tourism and higher-income visitors, there are people who have lived here and built these communities who are increasingly unable to participate in the spaces around them. For us, that contradiction is important,” Listman and Keval told Mexico News Daily. “Restaurants are part of neighborhoods and communities, but they can also become spaces that feel increasingly inaccessible to the people who live there.”

The couple went on to say, “Dining out has become a privilege for many people, and as it becomes more expensive, it can become more segregated by class. That goes against how we understand hospitality and why we entered this industry in the first place. ‘Paga Lo Que Puedas’ was one small way of responding to that reality.”

In Mexico City, more than 20 restaurants — including MUX, Sin Nombre, Baldío, Cicatriz and Fideo Gordo — declared their commitment to “Paga Lo Que Puedas,” which took place Aug. 26. More than 100 dining institutions across 14 countries also joined in.

So how did it fare? Masala y Maíz, along with 12 participating restaurants, shared their experiences with us.

The origins, challenges and joys of a novel model

The concept originally emerged years ago, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Listman and Keval — who initially opened their restaurant as a small brick-and-mortar in San Miguel Chapultepec back in 2017 — were experimenting with ways to attract customers during a challenging time for food businesses to keep their staff employed and to provide the luxury of dining out in their community.

That evolved into a regular practice, in which diners would enjoy a meal and leave whatever they could afford inside an envelope. What began as an in-house tradition ballooned into a bigger idea that would, years later, result in a global effort.

“From the beginning, we were thinking about how we could make the restaurant more accessible while also creating a tangible way to support the people around us and keep our staff working,” they noted. “It started as a small gesture, but it was also an experiment in trust: What happens when we remove the fixed price from the menu and ask people to honestly decide what they are able to pay for their meal? In Mexico City, that question felt particularly relevant because we were already seeing how quickly the cost of living was changing around us.”

Social media deepens urban segregation

In the fall of 2026, those factors had only become more urgent. In analyzing the stratification of diners in Mexico City through the increased use of social media, Guillermo Echauri of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) found that the role and perception of food influencers in Mexico City have only exacerbated the problem of inaccessibility.

He writes that “the attributes, perspectives, and personal experiences of the foodies themselves are integrated into an environment of significant socioeconomic disparities, urban segregation, and ethnic discrimination. This shapes their representation of the culinary landscape in the Mexican capital, as digital dynamics intensify existing inequality.”

In other words, the systemic issues around dining accessibility that Listman and Keval were attuned to nearly a decade ago haven’t disappeared — they’ve arguably worsened with the rise of food influencers and rampant social media usage, among other shifts in the community and global economy at large.

By reviving the PWYC initiative in Mexico City, the founders of Masala y Maíz — and the many restaurateurs who chose to join them — are emphasizing the ongoing need for inclusivity and egalitarianism through local and international gastronomy.

Measuring turnout and financial realities

Despite logistical complications that arose through staffing and clarity around how to accept payments in a PWYC framework (in which some diners paid with non-monetary goods, such as original artwork), a survey of 12 participating restaurants unanimously confirmed a “very positive” experience and that the day “opened doors to new audiences,” with 83% of the restaurants declaring they would “definitely” participate again.

“The response we experienced was largely one of curiosity and solidarity,” Listman and Keval affirmed. “Other chefs and restaurant owners were also thinking about accessibility, rising costs, and what it means to be a restaurant within a community. We did not approach this as a model that every restaurant should adopt. Restaurants have different circumstances and different economic realities, and sustainability for the restaurant and for its workers is important. What we wanted to do was create an invitation to think differently about what hospitality can look like.”

In terms of profitable sales, the results were mixed — although that’s to be expected when the public is invited to pay whatever they wish.

Forty-two percent of the surveyed restaurants reported a “better” day of sales; a combined 33% reported either “much worse” or “about the same.” Conversely, 75% of the food businesses shared that they saw a “much higher” or “higher” turnout than an average day, while 25% believe they saw “about the same” number of diners that they would have during normal hours. In all, it seems that the restaurants saw a boom in diners, but not necessarily in income (in an act of reciprocal care, tips reportedly went up by 42%).

Building connection beyond the dining table

Importantly, 58% of the diners self-identified as first-timers at the surveyed restaurants, indicating demand and engagement from a wider range of customers than usual, and affirming the PWYC blueprint as socially equitable.

“What has stayed with us most is the sense of connection that the initiative created. For us, the success of Paga Lo Que Puedas is not simply measured by how many meals were served or how much money was collected. It is also about what happens when people feel that a restaurant is making room for them,” Listman and Keval said. “We hope that diners experience a sense of belonging and joy, and that they are able to enjoy a meal without the usual anxiety around whether they can afford to be in that space. We also hope the experience encourages people to think about the labor, care and knowledge that goes into a meal, and to recognize the workers who make that experience possible.”

Nourishing a better city

In a city as increasingly divided as Mexico City has become in the past half-decade alone — due to gentrification, mass tourism and other sociopolitical factors — PWYC is a bold, if not necessary, kind of reclamation for the people. However, that responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on small-business owners and their staff to level the playing field (or dining tables, in this case); that work should ultimately be the focus of elected officials and local governments, who should be looking for ways to support not only diners, but those who provide the city’s best dining experiences.

Without them, what would be left to nourish and feed us when we want a transcendent meal or simply a night out? Keeping local culinary arts scenes alive — and attainable for diverse residents — should be every world-class city’s priority. No matter the price.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Does civility in politics still exist? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am currently spending a few days visiting family and friends in the U.S. and, being a month away from the midterms, have had the opportunity to experience firsthand the run-up to the elections in multiple states. As is always the case now, the TV ads and political speeches of the candidates are increasingly over the top.

Do I choose the candidate who wants to turn the U.S. into a communist country? Or the one who wants to further enable a dictatorship? Do I prefer the candidate who wants to put a data center in my backyard? Or the one who wants to increase my energy costs and threaten my water supply with a data center that’s not in my backyard? It’s all so silly, so anxiety-producing, so insulting to our intelligence. In Mexico, where paid political ads on radio and TV are prohibited, it’s refreshing to not be subjected to this every two years.

Mexican politics, of course, are far from perfect, but there have been some examples of real civility demonstrated lately that give many of us some hope and inspiration. And that civility comes from the tone being set from the top by President Sheinbaum. Let me explain.

The word I most often hear to describe President Sheinbaum is “classy.” The way she dresses, the way she smiles, the way she carries herself, and the way she interacts with people are all frequently mentioned. Even those who don’t agree with all of her policies are impressed by that aspect of her.

Being an American, I have found the contrast to my native country and the increasing lack of class in politics in the United States to be maddening. I can understand genuine differences of opinion on important issues and on the general direction of the country, but I cannot get past the lack of class being exhibited by politicians that we see on a daily basis. The name-calling, the put-downs and the unwillingness to acknowledge anything positive from the other side is really depressing to watch. And it’s on both sides of the political aisle. I know I am not alone in often thinking, “We pay these people to represent us, find compromise, and make decisions — why can’t they seem to actually do it anymore?”

Which brings me back to Sheinbaum. There have been three incidents in just these past few weeks that were impressive examples of civility.

1. The U.S. administration has been back at it again, attacking Mexico for supposedly not doing enough to combat the cartels. This is despite nearly daily progress on high-profile arrests, drug and weapons seizures, and a significant reduction in homicides throughout the country. Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State, again hinted that the U.S. could act unilaterally against criminal organizations in Mexico. President Trump, acknowledging progress but not wanting to be outdone, added: “However, Mexico must take additional action against the narco terrorist organizations that dominate vast areas of its territory and continue to threaten the American people,” and arrest “the many corrupt public officials” who have colluded with them.

Sheinbaum responded calmly, saying that Mexico doesn’t need to be judged “from the outside.” She went on to say that she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use and combat drug trafficking. She asked, “Where is the effort being made to stop drug cartels and distributors in the United States? What’s going on with money laundering in the United States?” Fair questions of a government that has no problem frequently questioning her and her administration.

2. Sheinbaum recently completed her second year in office and as a result, just gave her second annual “state of the union” address. She then did something similar to last year, traveling to each of Mexico’s 32 states over a period of several weeks to personally give a “state of the state” address in which she presented, in detail, what the government has accomplished for the people of the state in the past year and what is planned for the following years.

Regardless of which political party is leading the state she visited, or which candidate they voted for, she showed up and presented a business-like progress report for the state. There was no avoiding the states that didn’t vote for her. There was no minimizing the progress in states that don’t support her. But rather a consistent, fact-based, optimistic outlook on what the government is doing to improve things in the state. It’s inspiring to watch, and impressive to see her making the effort to visit every state and make the individual presentations.

3. Sheinbaum’s visits to two states in particular, Jalisco and Nuevo León, most caught my attention. These states have the second and third largest cities in the country after Mexico City, and neither state has a governor of the Morena political party that Sheinbaum is part of. It didn’t matter; Sheinbaum showed up in both states, was warmly greeted by the governors, and spoke about the progress that the federal and state governments have made working together. This was not a post-natural disaster photo op. This was a real effort to present a progress report to the people of these states and present a united front of government.

The governor of Jalisco greeted Sheinbaum along with famous singer Vicente Fernández’s wife (Doña Cuquita). In Nuevo León, she was greeted by Governor Samuel García, his wife and their two daughters. The images of Sheinbaum kissing their youngest daughter with a beaming Governor García looking on would touch even the biggest cynic of politicians.

What we are seeing lately in Mexico is a welcome reminder that politics doesn’t have to be so classless, so off-putting, so negative, so nasty. It hasn’t always been this way in the U.S. — I’m not sure how it got this bad.

I’m not saying things are perfect in Mexico. They are far from it. But seeing politicians of different political parties together, seemingly genuinely acting like polite, kind, classy people is quite inspiring and uplifting. Perhaps that is why a recent poll just put the level of national pride of Mexicans at 90%, a record high.

Let’s hope it continues for the good of the country!

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico’s fastest-growing states aren’t the ones having the most children
World.content:
The 2025 Intercensal Survey by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) has revealed a paradox in Mexico’s new demographic map: The states that have seen the greatest population growth are not those with the highest fertility rates.

Mexico reached a population of 130.9 million in 2025 – the country’s highest population in history. However, the population grew at an average annual rate of just 0.7%, its slowest pace in recent decades, with growth concentrated in states in the north and southeast of the country.

Which states lead population growth?

According to INEGI, Baja California Sur led in population growth with an average annual rate of 3.4%, followed by Quintana Roo at 2.2%. Querétaro recorded 1.7%, while Nuevo León and Coahuila grew by 1.5% annually.

Population growth in Quintana Roo is a result of its population dynamics: For years, the state has recorded growth linked to an influx of people from other states and the expansion of its urban and tourist areas, among other factors.

The same pattern is observed in Baja California Sur. Meanwhile Baja California, Querétaro and Nuevo León are attracting new residents thanks to urbanization, employment and internal migration.

In contrast, Guerrero and Veracruz lost population, shrinking by -0.6% and -0.3%, respectively.

Which states have the highest and lowest fertility rate?

The states topping the growth rankings are not the same ones showing the highest fertility rates. The Intercensal Survey revealed that Chiapas had the highest fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman, followed by Guerrero (1.6) and Durango (1.5).

The contrast is particularly striking in Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo. Despite ranking at the top for population growth between 2020 and 2025, their fertility rates were among the lowest in the country — 1.2 and 1.1 children per woman, respectively.

Mexico City has the second largest population of any entity or state, despite having the lowest fertility rate (0.8). According to the survey, its population stands at 9.1 million, just behind México state, which with 17.5 million inhabitants is the most populous state in the country.

With reports from Uno TV

JUSTICE · HONDURAS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, where the Koriun Inversiones scheme in Choloma promised 5 percent weekly returns and left about 30,000 people affected, La Prensa reported in February 2026.

— What happened On Friday 2 October 2026 an appeals court upheld the indictments of four Koriun defendants, keeping ex-manager Iván Velásquez in preventive prison, the Supreme Court spokesman said.

— The numbers Raids on 23 April 2025 found L358.2 million in cash (about US$13.3 million) at seven sites, El Heraldo reported on 12 September 2026, citing prosecutors.

— What it means for you The case moves on, but investors still have no route back to their money. Funds handed to unauthorised firms carry no legal protection, the regulator has warned.

— Still open No trial date has been reported. The result of a forensic evaluation of Velásquez on 3 September 2026 has not been made public.

A Honduras appeals court has upheld the case against the former manager of Koriun Inversiones, so he stays in preventive prison. Koriun was an unauthorised investment business in Choloma that collapsed after raids in April 2025.

Supreme Court of Justice (CSJ) spokesman Carlos Silva announced the ruling on Friday 2 October 2026. El Mundo reported that the court rejected all defence appeals, and the broadcaster HCH also reported the ruling.

What the Appeals Court Decided

The ruling came from the appeals court for organised crime, environment and corruption cases. It confirmed the “auto de formal procesamiento”, the order that formally opens criminal proceedings against a defendant.

Prosecutors allege that Iván Abad Velásquez Castro committed money laundering, disobedience, illegal possession of firearms and ammunition, and criminal association. He has not been convicted and is presumed innocent.

Silva said the preventive detention therefore continues. He added that no new request to review the measure was pending, after an earlier one was rejected.

Cash found in the 23 April 2025 Koriun raids by location, in million lempiras (total about US$13.3 million at L26.85). Source: El Heraldo, citing the Public Ministry, 12 September 2026.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Three Other Defendants

The court also confirmed the indictments of Marcos Abel Villeda Galdámez and Juan Carlos García Ríos. Both face money laundering and criminal association charges and also remain in preventive prison.

A fourth defendant, Kefi Esmeralda Gavarrete Sánchez, faces the same two charges. She remains free under house arrest and other conditions because she had recently given birth, Silva said.

How the Koriun Case Grew

Koriun promised investors returns of 5 percent a week, La Prensa reported in February 2026. The paper put the number of people affected at about 30,000.

On 23 April 2025 prosecutors raided the Choloma head office, five branches and Velásquez’s home. El Heraldo reported they found L358.2 million in cash (about US$13.3 million), including L125 million (about US$4.7 million) at the house.

La Prensa reported that in May 2025 frozen accounts were released and L69.2 million (about US$2.6 million) ordered returned to investors. A year after the raids, the paper said, most of the money could not be traced.

Velásquez was first sent to preventive detention in May 2025, according to El Heraldo. US$ figures use 26.85 lempiras to the dollar, the rate on 2 October 2026.

Defence Claims and Investor Pressure

On 17 September defence lawyer Omar Dubón told El Mundo that Velásquez had been beaten in the maximum-security unit at Támara prison. He said he would seek house arrest, and the authorities have not publicly confirmed the alleged assault.

Some investors back him. On 25 September a group marched through Choloma demanding his release, HCH reported, saying he had promised to repay them once free.

The regulator has tried to prevent new cases, as covered in Honduras CNBS Warns Public as Investment Fraud Schemes Proliferate. On 25 August the National Banking and Insurance Commission (CNBS) warned that such schemes were spreading.

What Is Not Yet Known

No date for the trial stage has been reported, and the forensic report on Velásquez from 3 September has not been released. It is also unclear whether the defence will file a new request for house arrest.

Above all, investors do not know how much of their money can be recovered. For background on the country, see Honduras Explained 2026: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch.

What was Koriun Inversiones?

A business based in Choloma, northern Honduras, that took money from the public and promised 5 percent weekly returns. It operated without authorisation from the financial regulator, according to El Heraldo.

Has the Koriun ex-manager been convicted?

No. The appeals court only confirmed that the case against him goes forward and that he stays in preventive detention. He is presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

Will Koriun investors get their money back?

That is not yet clear. Part of the frozen funds was ordered returned in May 2025. But La Prensa reported in February 2026 that most of the cash could not be traced.

Sources: El Mundo, 2 October 2026; HCH, 2 October 2026; El Heraldo, 12 September 2026; La Prensa, 15 February 2026; El Mundo, 17 September 2026; HCH, 25 September 2026.

POLITICS · GUATEMALA

Key Facts — The country Guatemala, Central America’s largest economy, is rebuilding worn bridges on its main highways under a 2024 law that allows fast emergency tenders.

— What happened On 3 October 2026 La Hora reported that three bridges were awarded for Q89.8 million (about US$11.8 million) more than the roads directorate’s own April estimate.

— The numbers Awards totalled Q276.9 million (about US$36.2 million) between 25 June and 2 July 2026, per La Hora and Infobae. The internal estimate was Q187.0 million (about US$24.5 million).

— What it means for you The bridges sit on the CA-2 Pacific highway and the CA-14 route to the Verapaces. Any cancellation could delay works that drivers and hauliers rely on.

— Still open The state audit office has issued only a preliminary report. Its final ruling, and whether the contracts stand, were not known as of 3 October.

The Guatemala bridge deals that La Hora calls the “Puentes de Primavera” drew a new allegation on Saturday 3 October. The newspaper reported that the roads directorate’s own engineers priced the three bridges far below the final contract prices.

The government rejects any overpricing and says the contracts cover more than the bridges themselves. The new figures come from unnamed ministry sources and have not been independently confirmed.

What the internal estimate showed

According to La Hora, engineers at the General Directorate of Roads drafted the tender rules in early April 2026. Its estimate for the Mocá, Las Pericas and Santa Bárbara bridges totalled Q187.0 million (about US$24.5 million).

The contracts were later awarded for Q276.9 million, a gap of Q89.8 million or about 48 percent. Mocá shows the widest difference: Q74.7 million estimated against Q130.3 million awarded (about US$9.8 million and US$17.1 million).

Internal estimate (April 2026) versus contract award (25 June to 2 July 2026) for three Guatemalan bridges, in million quetzales; total gap Q89.8 million. Source: La Hora, citing internal CIV sources, 3 Oct 2026.

Rates here use Q7.64 per US dollar, the 2 October close. La Hora earlier estimated possible overpricing of up to Q148.6 million (about US$19.5 million), using a quote from an experienced builder.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Guatemala Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the bid rules allegedly changed

La Hora’s sources say Gilberto Guerra, a former roads director now advising the ministry, told engineers in mid-April to leave costs alone. They also say he objected to tough experience requirements for bidders.

The engineers refused, the sources say, but the rules were changed at the minister’s office between late April and mid-May. Guerra did not answer La Hora’s calls or messages.

The Ministry of Communications, Infrastructure and Housing (CIV) says Guerra plays no role in contracting. A past complaint against him was dismissed, it adds.

The tenders ran under article 95 of the Priority Road Infrastructure Law, passed in November 2024. It allows awards within 15 calendar days.

The government’s defence

On 24 September Minister Norma Zea said the contracts include demolitions, temporary crossings and protection works, state news agency AGN reported. She argued that comparing prices per metre of bridge proves nothing about overpricing.

On 2 September President Bernardo Arévalo pledged to seek concurrent audits of all emergency road contracts, Infobae reported. Zea said the law even allowed a direct award, yet the ministry invited two extra bidders per project.

On 30 September La Hora reported a preliminary audit finding that Zea lacked legal power to choose the bidders. Arévalo questioned how the paper obtained the draft, said the ministry had answered it, and pledged to obey the final report.

The audit office faces its own test, as reported in US Demands Guatemala Comptroller Vote Free of Narcos. For background on the president, see Who Is Bernardo Arévalo, Guatemala’s President in 2026.

What Is Not Yet Known

No second outlet has confirmed the internal estimate or the account of the rule changes. The final report of the audit office, the Contraloría General de Cuentas, has no published date.

La Hora’s sources say the minister wants to drop the Puentes de Primavera contracts and offer cheaper ones. The builders reportedly object. The ministry has not confirmed this. How any change would affect work on the CA-2 and CA-14 is unclear.

Sources: La Hora, Puentes de Primavera sobrevalorados (3 Oct 2026); La Hora, Arévalo on the preliminary audit report (30 Sep 2026); Infobae, concurrent audits for emergency road projects (2 Sep 2026); AGN, CIV explains bridge costs (24 Sep 2026).

World.title: Brazil Election Explained Before Sunday’s Vote
World.content:
An electronic voting machine in training mode ahead of Brazil's first round on 4 October 2026. Photo: Paulo Pinto/Agência Brasil (CC BY 3.0 BR).

ANALYSIS · BRAZIL ELECTION 2026

Key Facts — The vote Brazil elects a president, governors, senators and deputies on Sunday 4 October 2026. Polls are open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time: 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern, 12 noon to 9 p.m. in Lisbon.

— Who President Lula (PT, left), 80, seeks a fourth term. His main rival is Senator Flávio Bolsonaro (PL, right), son of the jailed ex-president. Four other candidates poll in the low single digits.

— Why a runoff is likely A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes to win outright. No major poll puts either man there. The second round is Sunday 25 October.

— The numbers Datafolha (1 October): Lula 45%, Flávio Bolsonaro 40% of valid votes; runoff 48% to 45%. About 158.7 million Brazilians are registered to vote (TSE).

— Why Americans care US tariffs of up to 37.5% hit Brazilian goods. US consulates in Brazil halted in-person services on 2 October. Petrobras and Vale ADRs and the EWZ fund trade on the result.

— The markets Traders on Polymarket and Kalshi give Flávio Bolsonaro about a 60% chance of becoming president, but expect Lula to finish first on Sunday.

— What it means for you Expect a volatile Monday for the real and Brazilian stocks, and three more weeks of uncertainty if the race goes to a runoff. Results go live on our results page from 4 p.m. ET.

Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, votes on Sunday in a first round that polls say neither Lula nor Flávio Bolsonaro will win outright. Voting runs from 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time (8 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Brasília), and the electoral court (TSE) starts publishing results after 5 p.m. Brasília time, which is 4 p.m. on the US East Coast.

The most likely outcome is a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. The latest polls give Lula a lead of a few points in the first round, but they show the runoff as a statistical tie. Most polls are inside their margins of error.

For US readers the stakes are concrete. Brazilian exports already face US tariffs, Washington shut its consular services in Brazil this weekend citing security concerns, and a President Lula or a President Bolsonaro would handle China, trade and the courts very differently. This guide explains the race in about ten minutes. For live numbers, use our Brazil election results page, which shows official TSE figures from 4 p.m. ET.

Why the institutes disagree

Three things explain most of the gap between a 5-point Lula lead and a 1-point Flávio lead. First, the base. Datafolha’s headline is 42% to 38% of all voters, but 45% to 40% of valid votes. Comparing one institute’s total with another’s valid-vote figure creates false differences.

Second, the method. In-person pollsters such as Datafolha and Quaest, telephone pollsters such as Nexus and Ideia, online pollsters such as AtlasIntel, and automated phone surveys such as PoderData reach different kinds of voters. Third, the timing: ten days is a long time in a tight race. Our own coverage found Quaest’s director crediting late gains for Lula to women, low-income voters and Bolsa Família recipients (read the poll comparison).

Polls have missed before. In 2022 Datafolha’s penultimate poll gave Jair Bolsonaro 36% of valid votes in round one. He received 43.20%, against 48.43% for Lula, according to the TSE. Whether the polls err the same way this year is unknown.

How the vote and the count work

Voting is compulsory for Brazilians aged 18 to 69 and optional for 16- and 17-year-olds, people aged 70 and over and those who cannot read. Missing a round without a justification brings a fine of R$3.51 (about US$0.67). In 2022, 79.05% of registered voters turned out; 20.95% stayed away (TSE data).

Everyone votes on electronic machines. There are 563,910 of them this year, and the TSE president said on 29 September that 90% were ready. Each machine prints its own tally at the close, and those tallies are transmitted to the TSE. Phones must be switched off and left outside the booth. Foreign residents cannot vote, apart from Portuguese citizens with equal political rights under the bilateral treaty.

The TSE starts releasing results after the polls close at 5 p.m. Brasília time. In 2022 the court had counted about 97% of the vote by roughly 9:30 p.m. Brasília time (8:30 p.m. ET), and the outcome was clear that night. The full count took until Tuesday.

To win in round one a presidential candidate needs more than half of valid votes. Blank and null ballots do not count in that base. If nobody gets there, the top two meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October. Governors follow the same rule in each state. Senators do not: the two most-voted candidates in each state win, with no second round.

The Senate: why a majority matters

Voters fill 54 of the 81 Senate seats, two per state. Each voter casts two Senate votes. Only the Senate can try and remove Supreme Court justices, and conviction needs two-thirds, or 54 votes. Approving a justice nominated by the president needs an absolute majority of 41, according to O Povo. That is why the right wants a big Senate result: a majority would let it press the Supreme Court. The left wants to block that.

The PL has been the largest Senate party since January, with 15 senators (Agência Senado). Projections published on 3 October by Estadão/Quaest, as reported by O Povo, see it rising to about 25. Even then it would still depend on allies for 54 votes. Datafolha’s last Senate polls show four-way ties in São Paulo and Minas Gerais, clear leaders in Rio (Benedita da Silva, PT, 19%) and the Federal District (Michelle Bolsonaro, PL, 23%) and a two-way tie in Pernambuco (state-by-state numbers).

How strong is the left, how strong is the right

Add up the candidates in the polls and the blocs are almost level. In Datafolha’s valid votes, Lula has 45%. Flávio Bolsonaro, Caiado and Zema, the three right-of-centre names, have 44% together (40%, 3% and 1%). Cury and Renan Santos, who reject both camps, have 7%. In AtlasIntel’s valid votes the picture is the same: Lula 46.2%, the three right-of-centre candidates 45.8%, Cury and Santos 7.4%. The grouping of candidates into camps is our own.

The key battleground is Congress. In the 513-seat Chamber of Deputies the PL is the largest single party with roughly 100 seats, and the federation of the PT with the Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB) and the Greens (PV) has roughly 80. A loose group of centre-right parties, União Brasil, PSD, PP, Republicanos, MDB, Podemos and PSDB, holds the balance. Counts differ by source and date, because deputies switch parties.

That group is the “Centrão”, a shifting set of pragmatic parties that trade support for budget money, committee posts and ministries. It is not one party and it has no single leader. Lula says Congress has “kidnapped” presidential power by controlling budget amendments (our report). Any president will have to deal with it. Our party guide on the live results page explains every party on the ballot, from the left-wing PT to the right-wing PL.

What holds the blocs together is largely personal. Lula’s coalition rests on his name, the Northeast and cash-transfer programmes. The right is held together by the Bolsonaro surname, evangelical and conservative voters and agribusiness. Both have seams. The left is split between PT and PDT candidates in Minas Gerais and Pernambuco. The right is split between the PL, the PSD’s Caiado and the Novo party’s Zema, whose voters could go either way in a runoff.

The mood of Brazilians

Brazilians are divided and tired of the fight. Datafolha found 48% approve of Lula’s work and 50% disapprove (poll of 15 to 17 September, reported by Poder360). On a different scale, 34% rate his government good or great, 23% regular and 42% bad or terrible. His approval is mixed, but it has not collapsed.

Rejection is the sharper number. In BTG/Nexus, 51% said they would never vote for Flávio Bolsonaro and 48% never for Lula. Quaest put rejection at 56% and 54%. The two men are about equally disliked, so each needs to bring out his base and win over the undecided.

Fatigue is a risk. In Quaest the share saying they would vote blank, vote null or stay home rose from 7% to 10% in a week, and O Globo reported that analysts expect more “non-voting” than in 2022. The economy gives Lula something to point to. Unemployment fell to 5.3% in the quarter to August, the lowest for that period since the series began in 2012 (IBGE, 29 September). Inflation was 4.22% in the 12 months to August (IBGE). The central bank cut its Selic rate by a quarter point to 13.75% on 16 September, down from a peak of 15%.

Security worries voters more than the economy in some surveys. A Quaest/Pax poll published on 18 September had 28% naming violence as Brazil’s top problem, ahead of corruption (22%), the economy (19%) and health (15%). The tone of the campaign is rough: on 1 October Lula called Flávio a “mongrel” on a podcast (our report).
