What is at stake

The economy and markets

Brazilian assets rallied into the vote. The Ibovespa rose 2.63% on Friday 2 October to 192,115 points, and the dollar ended the week at about R$5.22 (EODHD). In New York the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) gained 2.8% to US$38.19, Petrobras ADRs (PBR) 3.2% to US$21.65 and Vale ADRs (VALE) 2.3% to US$13.76. Speculators held a net long position of 60,538 real futures contracts on 29 September, up 6,337 in a week (CFTC). We could not confirm what drove the Friday jump; it may reflect positioning before the vote.

The candidates differ on fiscal policy. Lula’s government has already exempted workers earning up to R$5,000 a month (about US$957) from income tax. Flávio Bolsonaro’s SOS Brasil fund would draw on oil concessions, receivables and federal property to pay down debt (details). Markets will watch which one signals more spending restraint.

The United States, China and the world

The US is the central foreign-policy question. Since 22 July Brazilian goods face a 25% US tariff under Section 301, and since 24 July a second 12.5% “forced labour” tariff applies to most goods, so some exports pay up to 37.5%. The Section 301 case covered digital trade and electronic payments, ethanol market access, anti-corruption enforcement, intellectual property and illegal deforestation, according to the US Trade Representative. A US trade court heard a challenge to the 12.5% layer on 30 September (our report).

China is Brazil’s largest export market. In 2025 Brazil sold China about US$100 billion of goods, or 28.7% of its exports, against US$37.7 billion, or 10.8%, to the United States (MDIC). Lula courts both, with BRICS at the centre of his foreign policy. Flávio Bolsonaro says he wants a close US relationship but an “economically pragmatic” China policy, as he told a rally in Natal on 21 September.

The European Union’s interim trade agreement with Mercosur has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026, and Brazil completed its own ratification in March. The European Parliament has not yet given its final consent.

The Amazon, security and the courts

Deforestation alerts in the Amazon fell 36.87% to 2,874 km² between August 2025 and July 2026, the lowest in the series, INPE said on 7 August. Lula’s plan targets zero net deforestation by 2030. Flávio Bolsonaro promises to end illegal deforestation by 2029, and critics say his positions favour agribusiness and mining.

On security, the United States announced in May that it would designate Brazil’s PCC and Comando Vermelho gangs as terrorist groups. Brazil’s foreign ministry warned that this could open the door to military action on Brazilian soil. Lula’s government has called it a threat to sovereignty.

The courts are a campaign issue. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year coup sentence, reportedly at home in Brasília for health reasons, and his lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to suspend it (our report). Both Lula and many Senate candidates support fixed terms for Supreme Court justices, who now serve until 75.

Interference and the fight over the rules

This campaign has been fought in courtrooms as much as on television. What is documented:

Aparecida posts. A false claim that Flávio Bolsonaro wanted to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of her title as Brazil’s patron saint spread across social media. TSE Justice André Mendonça ordered more than a thousand links removed on 25 September, with a daily fine of R$50,000 (about US$9,600) per platform for non-compliance. Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino reversed the order on 27 September, and Justice Luiz Fux restored it the next day. On 30 September the TSE plenary kept the removal of posts stating the claim as fact, while allowing satire and commentary (our report).

Debates and ads. TV Globo cancelled the last presidential debate on 1 October after the TSE barred an empty lectern for Lula, who had decided not to attend, and Flávio Bolsonaro withdrew, accusing the electoral court of censorship (our report). The TSE also suspended a Lula radio ad that linked his rival to a jailed banker, with the judge faulting its framing rather than its facts. Meta blocked Lula’s ad account on 23 September and says it works again.

Rules on artificial intelligence. TSE rules require clear labels on AI-made campaign content and, as we read them, ban new synthetic content using a candidate’s image or voice from 72 hours before the vote until 24 hours after. Platforms must obey takedown orders and block identical reposts.

The US consulates. The US embassy in Brasília and four consulates suspended in-person services on 2 October, citing security concerns, with no reopening date. The Federal Police searched two addresses over an alleged plan against US diplomatic sites. The police and the intelligence agency Abin deny reports of a “coup alert”. Lula’s campaign asked the TSE to add the closure to a foreign-interference case (our report).

What is not established: any proof that a foreign government changed votes, or that the consulate closure was linked to the election. The claims come from the campaigns and political actors, and we label them as such.

Lula or Bolsonaro: what changes for the United States and the world

Forecasting is not our job here. These are the documented positions and stakes under each outcome, not predictions.

If Lula wins a fourth term

Tariffs. Brazil’s government said on 23 July it would use its Reciprocity Law and take the US tariffs to the World Trade Organization. A Lula government would likely continue that track, and it has said it does not want to choose between Washington and Beijing.

China and BRICS. Brazil’s trade with China is large and Lula treats BRICS as central. Expect more of the same: Chinese investment pledges, trade in local currencies and a “multipolar” message.

Amazon and climate. Enforcement would continue and the zero net deforestation target stay in place, though Lula’s government also backs offshore oil exploration at the mouth of the Amazon. Petrobras reported a second oil find there this week (our report).

If Flávio Bolsonaro wins

The United States. He has promised to seek a free-trade deal with Washington and deeper cooperation on security and critical minerals. He met Donald Trump at the White House on 26 May and told the US trade office’s tariff hearing in July that he wanted the tariff cancelled, not postponed, CNN Brasil reported. A deal is not guaranteed: Trump has so far declined to say whether he backs him.

China and BRICS. He criticises what he calls submission to China but has said his policy would be “economically pragmatic”. His written government plan does not mention BRICS.

Courts and platforms. His campaign accuses the electoral court of censorship, and press summaries of his plan say it proposes changes to the Supreme Court and an end to presidential re-election. US tech firms would watch whether Brazil keeps the Supreme Court’s 2025 ruling that makes platforms liable for some illegal content.

Amazon. His plan promises to end illegal deforestation by 2029 and proposes environmental licences that are granted automatically if agencies miss deadlines. Critics worry that this and his support for mining and farming in protected areas would weaken enforcement.

Either way, the EU–Mercosur interim trade agreement stays in force, and Argentina’s Javier Milei has said he hopes “his friend” Flávio wins (report).

Behind the scenes: how hard Washington and Beijing are pushing

Foreign pressure is the most heated claim in the campaign, so we separate what is documented from what is alleged.

Documented The US imposed Section 301 tariffs on Brazil in July (US Trade Representative). Washington sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes under the Magnitsky Act in 2025 and lifted the sanctions in December 2025. Flávio Bolsonaro made six trips to the United States this year, including the White House meeting on 26 May (Itatiaia). Brazil’s Supreme Court convicted his brother Eduardo in June for coercion linked to lobbying Washington for sanctions (Gazeta do Povo). Trump said on 1 and 2 October that he was following the election closely and did not say whether he backs Flávio (G1). US consulates closed to the public on 2 October. Alleged, and by whom Three US Senate Democrats (Shaheen, Kaine and Welch) say the Trump administration promotes “interference and destabilization” in Brazil. Lula’s campaign calls the consulate closure an “anomalous diplomatic gesture”. The State Department says it does not seek to influence foreign elections. Some outlets reported a “coup alert” tied to the closure; the Federal Police and Abin deny it. China Beijing has not publicly endorsed a candidate, and we found no public evidence of Chinese efforts to influence the vote. What is documented is trade and investment: China buys about 29% of Brazil’s exports, and Lula has courted Chinese investment and BRICS. Unknown What the original security threat to US sites was. Whether any foreign actor affected the campaign. How much the Eduardo Bolsonaro lobbying shaped US policy. Whether Washington would change its tariff stance after a Lula or a Bolsonaro win.

The swing factors

Five things can decide a result this close.

Undecided and soft voters. A Meio/Ideia poll found 31.5% of voters could still switch candidates, though 68.5% said their choice was made. BTG/Nexus found only 12% still open (our report). Among the persuadable group, 45.1% said a new proposal could move them and 29.3% a late scandal.

Cury and Santos voters. The two outsiders have about 7% of valid votes combined. Their supporters reject both camps, so they may abstain in a runoff.

Rejection. With both front-runners rejected by about half of voters, the winner may be the one more voters can tolerate.

Southeast versus Northeast. Lula needs a big Northeast turnout to offset losses in the South and the farm belt. Flávio Bolsonaro needs to win or tie São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio.

Turnout. A higher abstention rate than in 2022 (20.95%) would change the arithmetic, and Quaest sees more blank and null voting.

The three weeks that decide everything (4 to 25 October)

If Sunday does not settle it, the runoff campaign runs 21 days. Four things will shape it.

Endorsements. Zema signalled he would back Flávio. Caiado and Renan Santos have refused to choose. Cury first left the door open to Flávio, then said he backs neither. Lula’s allies are seeking the neutrality of the PSD and a bridge to Cury, Diário de Pernambuco reported. These are reported manoeuvres, not signed deals.

Debates. TV Globo’s debate collapsed, so the runoff debates matter more. Band and Estadão have reserved Sunday 11 October at 8 p.m. Brasília time for a debate between the two finalists, and Record has pencilled in the same date at 9 p.m. These dates depend on the first-round result and could change.

Legal surprises. The Federal Police are examining a R$3.1 million (about US$590,000) BRB state-bank loan that helped Flávio Bolsonaro buy a Brasília house in 2021, O Globo and Valor reported. No charge has been filed (our report). Jair Bolsonaro’s lawyers have again asked the Supreme Court to suspend his sentence and annul the conviction; the petition was filed with the court’s president, Edson Fachin.

Policy fights. The Senate opens floor debate on ending the six-days-on, one-day-off work schedule on 6 October, though the vote may wait (our report). The US court ruling on the 12.5% tariff could also arrive at any time.

What it means for you

US investors. Expect a volatile Monday. Brazilian markets reopen on Monday, and US-listed ADRs such as Petrobras (PBR) and Vale (VALE) and the EWZ fund react in New York. Friday’s rally leaves room for a pullback if the result disappoints and for a further gain if it does not. A runoff would extend the uncertainty to 25 October. The real closed at R$5.22 per dollar on Friday.

Expats and travellers. Foreigners cannot vote, but the election shapes the weekend. There is no national alcohol ban, but states and cities can impose their own “dry law”, so check local notices. Party colours worn quietly are allowed, but rallies, loudspeakers and handing out campaign material are banned on election day. US citizens needing consular help should phone the embassy’s duty officer, since in-person visits are suspended.

Companies. The Section 301 tariffs, the pending court case and the EU–Mercosur agreement matter for exporters. A runoff means three more weeks before a policy direction is clear.

What is not known

We do not know how large the abstention will be, or whether late polls on Saturday evening from Quaest and Datafolha show a change. We do not know what the US security threat was, when consulates will reopen, or whether the endorsements will move voters. We cannot say which way the polls’ error, if any, will run.

Brazil’s politics are also a story about balance. A Lula win would test whether a divided Congress lets him govern. A Flávio Bolsonaro win would test whether his coalition holds without his father on the ballot. In both cases, the Senate arithmetic will shape the next four years.

When do polls open and close, and when are results published?

Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time on Sunday 4 October, which is 7 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time. The TSE begins publishing results after 5 p.m. Brasília time (4 p.m. ET). Our results page shows official TSE figures from 4 p.m. ET.

What do prediction markets say about the Brazil election?

On Saturday 3 October, Polymarket gave Flávio Bolsonaro a 60% chance of becoming president and Lula 40.5%; Kalshi priced it at 61 to 40 cents. Both expect Lula to finish first on Sunday, and Polymarket put a first-round win at 5%.

Will there be a runoff?

A runoff is likely. A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes, and no major poll puts Lula or Flávio Bolsonaro above that. In Datafolha’s poll of 1 October, Lula had 45% and Flávio Bolsonaro 40% of valid votes. If nobody passes 50%, the top two meet on Sunday 25 October.

Who is ahead in the polls?

Most national polls put Lula ahead in the first round, by roughly 3 to 5 points among all voters, while a few put Flávio Bolsonaro ahead. The runoff is a statistical tie: Datafolha had 48% to 45% for Lula, AtlasIntel 47.6% to 47.7% for Flávio Bolsonaro, and PoderData 50% each among valid votes.

Can foreigners vote, and what changes for visitors?

Foreign residents cannot vote, apart from Portuguese citizens with equal political rights under the bilateral treaty. Visitors should check local notices on alcohol sales, avoid rallies and the handing out of campaign material, which are banned on election day, and know that US consulates have suspended in-person services since 2 October.

How could the result affect US tariffs and investors?

Brazilian goods face a 25% Section 301 tariff and a 12.5% forced-labour tariff, so some exports pay up to 37.5%. Lula’s government is challenging them at the WTO, while Flávio Bolsonaro has promised to seek a free-trade deal with the United States. The Ibovespa closed at 192,115 on Friday and the real at R$5.22 per dollar, so a volatile Monday is possible.

Why does the Senate result matter?

Voters fill 54 of the 81 Senate seats. Only the Senate can try Supreme Court justices, and conviction needs 54 votes, two-thirds of the chamber. A larger PL bench would raise pressure on the court, but projections suggest the party would still need allies.

World.content:

SECURITY · HAITI

Key Facts — The country Haiti, a Caribbean nation of about 12 million people, has had no elected president since 2021. It plans a national vote on 13 December 2026.

— What happened On Friday 2 October the UN human rights chief said at least 5,700 people were killed or injured by gangs, or in operations against them, from 1 January to 11 September 2026.

— The numbers Over half of those casualties came during security operations. Gangs kidnapped more than 230 people and raped over 1,000 women and girls in the same period (UN rights office, 2 October).

— What it means for you Importers take note: third-country goods for Haiti may not transit the Dominican Republic and must land at Haitian ports or airports (finance ministry circular, 30 September).

— Still open Whether the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, about 1,500 strong according to a UN expert on 2 October, can hold ground before the December vote.

Haiti gang violence killed or injured at least 5,700 people from 1 January to 11 September 2026, the UN human rights office said. Volker Türk, the UN rights chief, gave the figure in Geneva on Friday 2 October.

More than half of those casualties occurred during security operations against the gangs, he said. Türk welcomed the first operations of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, but said it remains far below the strength needed.

What the UN figures show

The 5,700 figure counts both deaths and injuries, caused by gangs or during operations against them. Türk said the real numbers are likely much higher, because data on the violence is incomplete.

Gangs also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped over 1,000 women and girls, his office documented. So-called self-defence groups killed or injured some 280 people this year.

The UN Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), the UN political mission in the country, publishes quarterly detail. It counted 1,642 killed and 745 injured from January to March, then 1,408 killed and 656 injured from April to June.

People killed and injured in Haiti, January to March and April to June 2026; OHCHR counts at least 5,700 killed or injured from 1 January to 11 September. Source: BINUH quarterly reports, 8 May and 25 Aug 2026; OHCHR, 2 Oct 2026.

Last year about 6,000 people were killed and 2,700 injured, the Spanish agency EFE reported in El Nacional, a Santo Domingo daily. According to the same report, Türk said summary executions by specialised police units have fallen by almost half compared with 2025.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Children, displacement and Gros-Morne

Some 30 to 50 percent of gang members are children, Türk said, and their recruitment nearly tripled last year. Close to 1.5 million people are forcibly displaced across the country.

The latest flight came from Gros-Morne, in the Artibonite region, after a gang reprisal on 28 September. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) counted about 5,254 people displaced, Le Nouvelliste reported on 2 October.

The reprisal followed a brief operation by the force, as covered in Haiti Gang Suppression Force Faces UN Renewal Vote After Reprisal Kills at Least 11. The UN rights office count stops at 11 September, so it does not include Gros-Morne. The UN Security Council extended the force’s mandate by six months on 29 September.

The state restates its ban on transit through the Dominican Republic

Haiti’s finance ministry has reminded customs that the state recognises no dry port in the Dominican Republic. Nor does it accept any transit or transshipment there of third-country goods bound for Haiti.

The circular is dated 30 September and signed by Finance Minister Serge Gabriel Collin, Le Nouvelliste reported. Such goods must arrive directly at the country’s seaports or international airports, where customs applies duties and taxes.

Products legally made in the Dominican Republic may still enter through official land crossings. The General Customs Administration (AGD) has been told to tighten border controls.

Officials did not link the circular to security in the parts made public. Separately, UN expert William O’Neill said on Friday that weapons also cross that land border, El Nacional reported.

The oldest school carries on in borrowed rooms

Lycée Alexandre Pétion, founded in 1816 and the country’s oldest school, has lost its downtown Port-au-Prince premises to insecurity. It now works from a national school on Rue Capois, Le Nouvelliste reported on 2 October.

The paper says the lycée has educated at least 46 of the country’s heads of state. It keeps teaching after several moves in three years, a small sign of resilience amid the violence.

For the wider picture, see Haiti Gang Crisis Explained 2026 Gangs and the UN Force.

What Is Not Yet Known

BINUH has not yet published its casualty figures for July to September. It is unclear how far the Gros-Morne violence will lift the full-year count.

It is also unclear how fast the force will grow toward its authorised strength before the 13 December vote. Customs has not said how it will enforce the transit ban at the land border.

Sources: OHCHR, High Commissioner Türk statement on Haiti, 2 Oct 2026 · UN News, World News in Brief, 2 Oct 2026 · BINUH, first-quarter 2026 report, 8 May 2026 · BINUH, second-quarter 2026 report · El Nacional (EFE), 3 Oct 2026 · Le Nouvelliste, dry port ban, 2 Oct 2026 · Le Nouvelliste, transit circular, 2 Oct 2026 · Le Nouvelliste, Gros-Morne displacement, 2 Oct 2026 · Le Nouvelliste, Lycée Alexandre Pétion, 2 Oct 2026

ECONOMY · GUYANA

Key Facts — The country Guyana, on South America’s north coast, has pumped oil since late 2019 and saves its oil income in the Natural Resource Fund (NRF), a sovereign wealth fund.

— What happened Central government net borrowing reached G$105.6 billion (about US$505 million) in January–June 2026, against G$35.9 billion a year earlier, the Finance Ministry’s Mid-Year Report shows.

— The numbers Net foreign borrowing rose from G$19.1 billion to G$71.4 billion, domestic from G$16.8 billion to G$34.3 billion. Public debt stood at US$8.57 billion at end-June 2026.

— What it means for you Debt is moderate, at 28.6 percent of GDP at end-2025 by the ministry’s count. But first-half interest costs rose 53 percent year on year, to about US$66 million.

— Still open The full IMF staff report for 2026 is not yet out. The ministry plans G$503.8 billion of borrowing for the year and expects debt of US$10.33 billion by December.

Guyana borrowing nearly tripled in the first half of 2026, according to the Ministry of Finance’s own Mid-Year Report. Net financing for the central government reached G$105.6 billion (about US$505 million), up from G$35.9 billion (about US$172 million) a year earlier.

Kaieteur News, a Georgetown daily, published a letter on Saturday 3 October by Charles Sugrim warning that oil wealth is at risk. His numbers match the ministry’s tables, though his conclusions are his own.

What the Mid-Year Report shows on Guyana borrowing

Net external borrowing, mostly loans from development banks and foreign governments, rose from G$19.1 billion to G$71.4 billion (about US$341 million). Conversions use G$209 per US dollar, the 2 October close.

Disbursements from abroad reached US$447.5 million, up from US$130.7 million a year earlier. Net domestic borrowing, largely through short-term Treasury bills, doubled from G$16.8 billion to G$34.3 billion (about US$164 million).

Net central government borrowing in the first half of 2025 and 2026, in G$ billion, split into external and domestic financing. Source: Ministry of Finance of Guyana, Mid-Year Report 2026, Sept 2026.

The gap reflects spending running ahead of income. Total central government spending rose 11.5 percent to G$599.8 billion (about US$2.87 billion), while current revenue slipped 0.7 percent.

That revenue figure includes transfers from the oil fund, which fell to G$212.1 billion from G$249.6 billion. Tax and other non-oil revenue actually grew 18.7 percent, to G$279.5 billion.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The case made in Kaieteur News

Sugrim writes that “borrowing tripled in a single year” and blames “runaway public expenditure.” He argues the country risks seeing its oil wealth “pledged away to banks and other creditors.”

He also says state borrowing has fuelled inflation and crowded out private investment. Those wider claims are his opinion and cannot be checked against the ministry’s tables.

Why the official measures still look moderate

Total public and publicly guaranteed debt stood at US$8.57 billion at end-June 2026, up from US$6.81 billion a year earlier. The ministry puts debt at 28.6 percent of GDP at end-2025, with debt service taking about 5.5 percent of revenue.

The oil fund held US$4.29 billion at end-June, after first-half withdrawals of US$1.02 billion. A Rio Times report in August noted that the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) sees Guyana’s debt burden falling.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) held its annual review mission in Guyana from 20 to 31 July. Its concluding statement assessed the risk of debt distress as low, as in 2025.

The statement also urged that a larger share of extra oil revenue be saved if prices stay high. Kaieteur News reported it on 4 August as praise for a “prudent borrowing strategy.”

Where the risk lies

The ministry expects public debt to reach US$10.33 billion by end-2026, a third higher than at end-2025. Its full-year financing plan was revised up to G$503.8 billion (about US$2.41 billion), from G$448.9 billion in the budget.

The first half therefore used about a fifth of planned Guyana borrowing for the year. On the ministry’s own plan, roughly G$398 billion more would be borrowed between July and December.

Foreign-currency debt rose 3.5 points to 38.6 percent of the total, raising exposure to exchange-rate swings. About 84 percent of domestic debt is Treasury bills, which must be rolled over within a year.

How fast withdrawals from the oil fund grow will shape how much of the gap borrowing must fill.

What Is Not Yet Known

The IMF’s full 2026 staff report, with its updated debt analysis, had not appeared on the Fund’s Guyana page by 3 October. It is also unclear how second-half borrowing will split between foreign lenders and local banks.

Oil prices will largely decide how quickly the oil fund grows against new debt. The end-2026 debt figure is a ministry projection, not an outturn.

Sources: Ministry of Finance of Guyana, Mid-Year Report 2026 (Sept 2026); Kaieteur News, letter by Charles Sugrim (3 Oct 2026); IMF staff concluding statement, 2026 Article IV mission (31 Jul 2026, via Caribbean News Global); Kaieteur News on the IMF statement (4 Aug 2026); Guyana Chronicle (2 Aug 2026); IMF, 2025 Article IV press release (7 May 2025).

CARIBBEAN · GRENADA

Key Facts — The country Grenada is a three-island state in the eastern Caribbean. Carriacou and Petite Martinique are its two smaller sister islands, north of the main island.

— What happened The government said on 3 October 2026 that two new 100,000-imperial-gallon water tanks, at Mt Royal and Belair on Carriacou, had been commissioned under the G-CREWS climate project.

— The numbers The Green Climate Fund has paid out US$40.04 million in grants to the project since 2020, its project page shows. Co-financing brings the total to about US$47.7 million.

— What it means for you Carriacou should be better protected against dry taps in droughts and storms. Two clinics there also gained water cisterns, the ministry said.

— Still open The ceremony date, the cost of the Carriacou works and the timeline for a further desalination plant were not given. The project’s listed end date, 25 November 2025, has passed.

Grenada has commissioned new water infrastructure on Carriacou, the larger of its two sister islands. The works were built under G-CREWS, a climate project paid for mainly by the Green Climate Fund (GCF).

The Ministry of Carriacou and Petite Martinique Affairs announced the commissioning on Saturday 3 October 2026, via NOW Grenada. Its centrepiece is two storage tanks of 100,000 imperial gallons each, at Mt Royal and Belair.

What was commissioned on Carriacou

The ceremony was held on the grounds of the Princess Royal Hospital in Belair, the ministry said. Each tank holds about 455,000 litres, stored for dry spells and storms.

Tevin Andrews, the minister for Carriacou and Petite Martinique affairs and local government, recalled the 2010 drought that hit the islands hard. He said the tanks leave the sister islands far better prepared for natural disasters.

Health Minister Phillip Telesford said new cisterns now serve the Windward Medical Station and the L’Esterre Medical Centre. They are meant to keep both clinics running safely all year.

Todd LaBarrie, acting manager of the state water utility Nawasa, said a further desalination plant is being set up on the island. Such a plant turns seawater into drinking water.

Project development specialist Natasha Joseph said 18 farmers on the two islands received irrigation kits, shade houses and water systems. That support came through the project’s Challenge Fund for Agriculture, run by the Grenada Development Bank.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who pays for the project

G-CREWS stands for Climate-Resilient Water Sector in Grenada. Germany’s development agency GIZ runs it with Grenada’s government, the National Water and Sewerage Authority (Nawasa) and the Grenada Development Bank.

The GCF project page shows US$40.04 million in grants, fully paid out in four tranches between 2020 and 2024. Co-financing of US$7.68 million, including from Germany’s International Climate Initiative, brings the total to about US$47.7 million.

Green Climate Fund grant tranches paid to G-CREWS, US$ million: 4.54 (Feb 2020), 17.02 (Nov 2021), 10.50 (Dec 2023), 7.99 (Oct 2024). Source: Green Climate Fund, project FP059, accessed 3 Oct 2026.

The GCF board approved the project on 1 March 2018, and implementation began in November 2019. The fund expects about 107,000 people to become more resilient to climate shocks as a result.

Why water infrastructure matters on small islands

Grenada relies heavily on surface water and rainwater catchment, the GCF notes. Rising temperatures, erratic rain and saltwater seeping into groundwater are making shortages worse.

Storage is the first line of defence when rain fails or a hurricane cuts supply. The wider project also funds new wells, rainwater harvesting, renewable-powered pumping and a climate-linked water tariff.

Progress, and what is behind schedule

The project’s 2025 annual report to the GCF, submitted in July 2026, records real gains. A new water resources law was gazetted in February 2025, and more than 50 local professionals were trained in climate-resilient plumbing.

The same report shows the heavy water infrastructure lagging. By the end of 2025, only two of eight planned hurricane-proof storage tanks had been commissioned.

The Seven Sisters transfer line, meant to serve 11,400 residents in south-eastern Grenada, was 62 percent complete at that point. The GCF page still lists 25 November 2025 as the implementation end date.

The commissioning lands as Grenada heads to a general election. The Supervisor of Elections said the election writ was received on 2 October.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ministry gave neither the ceremony date nor the cost of the Carriacou works, and its account is not independently confirmed. It is also unclear whether the two tanks count among the eight in the GCF plan.

No timeline or budget was given for the further desalination plant. The GCF has not published a revised end date for the project.

Election background is in Grenada Parliament to Dissolve, Election Date Due Sunday (2 October). Country context is in Grenada Explained 2026, the Spice Island at a Glance.

Sources: Ministry of Carriacou and Petite Martinique Affairs release, via NOW Grenada, 3 October 2026; Green Climate Fund, project FP059 (G-CREWS), accessed 3 October 2026; GIZ, 2025 Annual Performance Report for FP059, submitted 17 July 2026; Supervisor of Elections notice, via NOW Grenada, 3 October 2026.

SOCIETY · SURINAME

Key Facts — The country Suriname, a former Dutch colony on South America’s north coast. Most people live on the coast, while the forested interior is reached by river, dirt road or small plane.

— What happened On 3 October 2026 the Suriname Herald reported that Social Affairs Minister Diana Pokie wants her ministry to clear interior benefit backlogs, some owed since 2024, before the year ends.

— Who is involved Recipients in Sipaliwini, Brokopondo and Upper Suriname waiting for household, disability and child payments. Nearly 200,000 people are registered for state support, Pokie said in September 2026.

— What it means for you Interior payouts still depend on cash trips that need extra money from the Finance Ministry. Pokie says all benefits should move to bank transfers in 2027.

— Still open No payment dates, total amount or number of affected households has been published. An outside audit of the recipient register is still under way.

Suriname’s Ministry of Social Affairs and Housing wants to clear its benefit backlogs in the interior before the end of 2026. Families in Sipaliwini, Brokopondo and Upper Suriname are still waiting for payments owed from 2024 and 2025.

Minister Diana Pokie set out the plan in remarks reported by the Suriname Herald on Saturday 3 October. She said payments on the coast are now largely up to date, but parts of the interior remain well behind.

What the minister said

The arrears cover several programmes, including support for poor households, payments to people with disabilities and the general child allowance. Pokie said the overdue child money is not the regular allowance, without giving more detail.

Much of the preparatory work is done, she said. What is missing is money for new trips into the interior. The ministry has raised this with the Ministry of Finance and Planning.

A push to clear much of the backlog during the holiday period did not fully succeed. Interior residents staying in Paramaribo, the capital, at the time could collect their payments at the ministry instead.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Suriname Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the benefit backlogs built up

Pokie blamed part of the problem on the previous government, which held office from 2020 to 2025. She said it sent payment teams into the interior only twice in five years, which built up a large backlog.

Payments in remote villages have so far been made in cash. The minister said this invited fraud and kept the paperwork heavily manual and poorly kept.

The recipient register is also out of date, as the ministry still works from 2023 data. An outside, independent institute has been hired to check and update it.

The frustration is not new. On 4 July the news site Waterkant reported a complaint from Brokopondo recipients. They said other districts had been paid while Brokopondo and Sipaliwini were still waiting.

The move away from cash

“Next year there should no longer be payments in cash,” Pokie said. The ministry is close to paying benefits by bank transfer, which she called safer, more transparent and more efficient.

That could end the costly river and air trips that have held payments back. The open question is how villagers without nearby bank branches will reach their money.

Pressure on the wider system

The interior is not the only problem, as other programmes also have arrears. The ministry is investigating what happened to money set aside for them in the 2024 budget.

According to Pokie, those funds were never actually released. Demand is also growing: registered recipients are nearing 200,000, about a quarter of the population, she told Radio ABC in September.

In June the Suriname Herald put the child allowance at SRD 250 (about US$6.62) per child. The conversion uses 37.75 Surinamese dollars per US dollar, as of 2 October.

The arrears come as the government tightens public finances, as set out in Suriname President Simons Uses Annual Address to Set 2027 Deficit at 4% of GDP. For wider context, see Suriname Explained 2026: The Oil Hope, the Dutch Legacy, the Economy and What to Watch.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ministry has not said how many households the benefit backlogs affect, how much is owed, or when the next payment trips will leave. Those trips still depend on the Finance Ministry releasing extra money.

It is unclear when the register audit will finish or when bank transfers will start. The fate of the 2024 budget funds has not been explained, and these claims come from the minister alone.

Sources: Suriname Herald, remarks by Social Affairs Minister Diana Pokie, 3 October 2026; Suriname Herald, 10 September 2026 (citing Pokie’s Radio ABC interview); Suriname Herald, 25 June 2026; Waterkant, 4 July 2026.

World.content:

ECONOMY · GUYANA

Key Facts — The country Guyana is spending its oil revenue on mega projects in power, roads and bridges. Chinese state firms and US-linked contractors are bidding against each other for the largest contracts.

— What happened Kaieteur News reported on 3 October 2026 that Juan Pablo Segura, the senior US diplomat for the Western Hemisphere, warned that some foreign investments come with “a hidden price tag”.

— The numbers For a gas storage facility, Lindsayca bid US$493.4 million and China CAM Engineering US$28 million, according to tender board figures Kaieteur News reported on 26 September 2026.

— What it means for you Which bids win will shape how soon daily power cuts ease and what electricity costs. Officials target first turbine power at the delayed Wales gas plant around 4 December 2026, a date Kaieteur sources doubt.

— Still open Whether the rival bids cover the same work, who wins the storage and Amaila hydropower contracts, and whether US financing offers carry conditions on contractor choice.

Guyana’s mega projects have become an open contest between the United States and China. A senior US diplomat has warned against Chinese state builders, and Beijing’s embassy has called such criticism a smear.

Kaieteur News, a Georgetown daily, reported the latest US warning on 3 October 2026. It comes as Guyana weighs Chinese and US-linked bids for a gas facility and a hydropower dam.

A warning about a hidden price tag

Juan Pablo Segura is the US Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs, the State Department’s top official for the region. In a post on X, reposted by the US Embassy, he wrote that some foreign investments hide their true cost.

“Lower upfront costs mask higher lifecycle expenses and long-term risk,” he wrote, according to Kaieteur News. Without naming China, he linked “state-owned companies” to unsustainable debt, shoddy workmanship, corruption and delays.

Kaieteur did not date the post, and its wording could not be confirmed. In late August, Segura had singled out a Chinese-built airport project in Guyana for years of delays and cost overruns.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Latin America Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Two bids, one wide gap

The sharpest numbers come from a gas storage tender at Wales, west of Georgetown. It would serve the gas-to-energy plant being built there.

Lindsayca, the contractor building that plant, submitted two bids: US$537.1 million and US$493.4 million. Kaieteur News reported the figures on 26 September, citing the National Procurement and Tender Administration Board (NPTAB), the state tender board.

Financial proposals for the Wales natural gas liquids storage and offloading facility, in US$ million. Source: NPTAB bid figures as reported by Kaieteur News, 26 September 2026.

China CAM Engineering offered US$28 million, about 6 percent of Lindsayca’s lower bid. Whether the three offers cover the same scope of work has not been published.

Citing unnamed sources, Kaieteur News also reported that the tender’s short deadline favoured the incumbent. That claim is not confirmed, and no award has been reported.

A delayed US-financed plant and a Chinese-built bridge

Lindsayca won the US$759 million contract for the Wales plant in 2022, with first power promised for the end of 2024. After a US$97 million settlement, the first turbine now targets about 4 December 2026, as reported in Guyana Gas-to-Energy Plant Aims to Fire First Turbine Around 4 December, Adding 57 MW of 300 MW. Kaieteur sources say test firing may slip to January 2027.

The US Export-Import Bank (EXIM), Washington’s export credit agency, approved a US$527 million loan for that plant. On 22 September, Kaieteur News quoted a US official saying EXIM could lend up to US$550 million for a second phase.

The newspaper contrasts it with the new Demerara River Bridge, built and financed by China Railway Construction Corporation. It says the bridge came about three months late, at no added cost.

Beijing pushes back as Georgetown weighs its options

On 1 September the Chinese Embassy in Guyana called Segura’s earlier remarks “malicious smears” against normal trade ties, Kaieteur News and News Source Guyana reported. It cited the bridge and six regional hospitals as Chinese contributions.

The next test is the Amaila Falls hydropower project, a dam of at least 165 megawatts first proposed in 2011. Five bids were opened on 8 May: three Chinese, one from a US-led group and one from an Indian-led venture.

Sinohydro offered the lowest disclosed price at US$416.9 million, while the US-led group with GE Vernova bid US$800.1 million, Kaieteur News reported. President Irfaan Ali said in late September that the bids are under evaluation.

Ali said the winner must accept terms that “make economic sense”. Smaller Caribbean states face the same pull, as shown in Antigua and Barbuda Won’t Pick China or US, Says Browne.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not known whether the gas storage bids are comparable in scope, or when the tender board will award that contract. The exact date of Segura’s latest post is also unclear.

The government has not said whether US financing offers depend on choosing US-linked contractors. For now, Guyana still awards major work to both Chinese and US-linked firms.

Sources: Kaieteur News, 3 October 2026, 26 September 2026 (NPTAB bid figures), 27 September 2026, 22 September 2026, 1 September 2026 and 9 May 2026; News Source Guyana, 1 September 2026.
