World.title: Nearly 500,000 people protest in Madrid over Spain's housing crisis
World.content:
Demonstrators are marching in several Spanish cities on Saturday, a day after parliament voted down two government decrees aimed at giving tenants stronger protection.

 

In Madrid, according to the organisers, around 500,000 people took part in the demonstrations, while the authorities put the number at around 70,000. Activists have been camped for about a week in Puerta del Sol, one of the capital's main tourist squares.

Participants could be seen carrying placards reading "General strike" and chanting slogans such as "Down with rentierism".

The protest remained peaceful, under a visible police presence. The president of the employers' confederation CEOE, Antonio Garamendi, says he respects the protests but warns that he will take action if a general strike is called, as he considers it "illegal".

The Tenants' Union, which is coordinating the protests, says in a statement, "There is an irreparable disconnect between what the people want and what the parties vote for."

The Tenants' Union is demanding a 50% cut in rents, open-ended contracts and the expropriation of homes from vulture funds. Its spokesperson, Valeria Racu, says there is still no date for the general strike, which is being negotiated with other organisations and which they want to be "historic".

Tensions in Valencia and protests across the rest of the country

In Valencia, protesters marched towards the Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, where the Valencia Real Estate Summit 2026 property investment conference is taking place, with former Citizens leader Albert Rivera among the speakers.

Some protesters removed barriers and the police cordon and threw objects at officers. Police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas. Several people managed to reach the upper part of the building. The march had been called by four organisations, including the Tenants' Union and the Housing Union.

There were also demonstrations in many other cities. In San Sebastian, the protest entered its second consecutive day, called by the LAB union with the backing of the Tenants' Union. In Cádiz, where according to organisers the average rent is about 900 euros and buying a home reaches 200,000, the march ended at City Hall with the reading of a manifesto.

There were also marches in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, with further rallies in Lanzarote, Fuerteventura and Tenerife. In Barcelona, Luana Rocha, a member of the camp, told 'TVE' that the intention is to stay indefinitely, "We are heading towards a general strike". Teruel will join in on Sunday with a demonstration at 18:30 starting from Plaza del Torico.

Sánchez begins a period of reflection as parties trade blame

On Friday, Congress rejected the government's two housing decrees, with votes against from PP, Vox and UPN and Junts refusing to support them. The first falls by 172 votes in favour to 178 against, and the second by 166 in favour to 184 against.

Sánchez ended his speech with a warning, "History will judge you sooner than you think and more harshly than you imagine". He now enters a period of reflection over whether to call early elections, a decision that rests solely with him. The opposition is again calling for elections, and some PSOE leaders and ministers now think so too, according to the original report.

Junts urges the PSOE to sit down and negotiate. Its spokesperson, Míriam Nogueras, described the decrees as "a poorly drafted law", and its secretary general, Jordi Turull, argues that they would have "discouraged" property sales. The PSOE replies that the texts already include Junts' proposals, "What more do they want?"

Vice-President Yolanda Díaz says that responsibility for evictions “has three names”: Feijóo, Abascal and Nogueras. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, for his part, pledges to look for a legal formula so that there is no further term without a budget.

Meanwhile, the camp in Sol reaches its seventh night, with around 2,000 people.

The protests begun after the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was carried out on a stretcher and is now recovering in hospital.

Housing campaigners say an investment company has bought the property where she lived for around seven decades and sought to raise her rent by 275 percent. After the backlash, the new owners have agreed to let her return at a low rent.

World.title: IEA says 325 million barrels of emergency oil released, with 75 million still to come
World.content:
The International Energy Agency said Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from the 400 million barrels promised in March.

 

The update came a day after G7 leaders, in a statement issued by French President Emmanuel Macron's office, agreed in coordination with the IEA to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil, following US pressure on Europe to tap its reserves and ease supply concerns caused by the US-Iran war.

The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that.

The IEA statement said "around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on 11 March have so far been released, representing over 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged in the action".

The pledge made in March was offered up by the IEA's 32 member countries, a group that includes all the G7 nations: of Britain, Canada, Italy, Germany, the United States and Japan.

On Friday, the G7 countries agreed that over the next four months 100 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products, "including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days".

They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between the two countries, heading off a threat previously raised by Washington, which Donald Trump later said would not be imposed.

Trump's administration has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in America and elsewhere.

The war in the Middle East has squeezed diesel supplies, with Iran restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.

The market has also been hit by Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, as Kyiv hits back against Moscow's own attacks.

World.title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer
World.content:
Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation.

A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPTcreator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough."

David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax."

OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access.

How US, China could end the AI race To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did David Robinson write?

In an op-ed for The Atlantic, Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over."

He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."

Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility."

"An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."

The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up.

"As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added.

Activists have staged protests calling on AI labs to slow development Image: Karl Mondon/AFP

ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe

OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."

In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity.

Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals.

This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google.

The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable.

He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI.

A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society.

World.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
World.content:
For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.

On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.

These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.

Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

Pakistani security officials inspect a mosque destroyed in an attack in the border town of Kohat, September 2026 Image: Hussain Ali/Anadolu/picture alliance

TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.

Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."

This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.

Difficult borders

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.

So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.

"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.

Pakistan exerts pressure

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

A Taliban soldier with an anti-aircraft gun on the border with Pakistan in April 2026 Image: AFP

Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."

Significant escalation

This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.

Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.

Militants kill dozens of security officers in Pakistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times , Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.

The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.

"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.

In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.

This story was originally published in German.

World.title: Tennessee's prison chief resigns after botched execution of murderer Christa Pike
World.content:
Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike. He is set to leave his post this month.

The head of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong, the state governor said Saturday.

Witnesses said Pike was still breathing and moaning after two doses of the anesthetic pentobarbital failed to kill her during Wednesday's procedure.

The attempt was halted and she was transferred to hospital in critical condition.

It was the second time this year that an execution in the southern state had to be halted.

What do we know about the resignation?

Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that prison commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post sometime this month.

Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."

In the same statement, Strada acknowledged that: "Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."

Frank Strada took on the role in January 2023 [FILE: August 2026] Image: Mark Humphrey/AP Photo/picture alliance

He said the department had carried out its responsibilities in accordance with established protocol, but called the review "entirely appropriate and necessary."

The state has halted further executions until the review has been completed.

Strada took on the role in January 2023. Nearly two years later, he announced that Tennessee would, from then on, only use pentobarbital for lethal injections of death-row inmates.

What went wrong?

Tennessee authorities have yet to explain why Pike survived.

Her attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

Pike's lawyers said Friday that she is unconsciousand on a ventilator in hospital.

While they welcomed Strada's departure, her legal team said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”

"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said.

"We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system," it added.

Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state since 1820.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, aged 20, for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convinced was trying to steal her boyfriend.

Slemmer, who was 19, was tortured and killed in a remote area near the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

World.title: Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains
World.content:
According to an exit poll by public broadcaster LSM, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centerist party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote.

The party of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs took a comfortable lead in parliamentary elections on Saturday, exit polls showed.

Kulbergs' centerist, pro-Ukraine party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote, according to an exit poll by public proadcaster LSM.

"It's remarkably ‌good. ​I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga.

The exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.

Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.

Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

Estonia and Latvia: Life on NATO's eastern edge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Natalie Muller

World.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
World.content:
As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.

Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.

In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.

Russia targets Kyiv bridge network To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Zelenskyy say?

In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."

Second Kyiv bridge struck

This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.

In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.

"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.

The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

Cars were stuck in traffic jams on Friday after Russian attacks on the Southern Bridge Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv

Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."

In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.

Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.

Putin on a war footing: escalation on all fronts? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine

Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.

"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."

"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.

The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.

Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.

Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.

World.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
World.content:
The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.

The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England.

He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.

The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.

Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.

He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.

The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.

One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.

The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.

Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance

Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.

Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.

The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.

Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.

UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.

Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.

The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.

Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.

Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
World.content:
Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.

They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

Protesters demanded affordable housing Image: Javier Soriano/AFP

"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.

Protests in dozens of cities

Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.

Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.

In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.

Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

Protesters filled the streets of the Spanish capital Image: Juan Barbosa/REUTERS

What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.

This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.

"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

Demonstrators held signs calling for 'a right to a roof' among other slogans Image: Javier Soriano/AFP

Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decion.

Sahcnez's office declined to comment on the reports.

World.title: Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
World.content:
A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed by North Macedonia.

The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.

Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.

But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.

Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."

The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.

They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.

Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.

Through the ages in Sofia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'

"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.

Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.

"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."

Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."

In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.

Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."

Greece: How the Jewish cemetery in Thessaloniki disappeared To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?

However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.

"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.

"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.

Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.

"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."

World.title: Decenas de miles de personas se manifiestan por la vivienda en Madrid en medio de la incertidumbre electoral
World.content:
Decenas de miles de personas, unas 70.000, según la Delegación de Gobierno, se han manifestado este sábado por el centro de la capital española en un frente común contra todos los sectores que dificultan el acceso a la vivienda y propician los desahucios, incluyendo entre los culpables a la clase política y los fondos buitre internacionales, presentados como “los verdaderos invasores”. “Derecho a techo”; “Hace falta ya una huelga general”; “Fuera rentistas de nuestros barrios”; o “Esto es lucha de clases, no podemos hacer las paces” fueron algunos de los lemas más coreados. La multitud ha puesto en evidencia que la izquierda está activada en la calle, indignada con la reciente expulsión de su casa de una anciana de 87 años, Mari Carmen Abascal, y con los partidos que han tumbado esta semana los decretos que habrían ayudado a evitar desahucios similares, pero también molesta con la legislación y las administraciones que los han permitido, incluyendo al Ejecutivo central.

La manifestación llegó a la plaza de Cibeles cerca de las dos de la tarde después de una marcha que salió desde cuatro puntos distintos de la capital y a la que, pese a la llovizna, fueron uniéndose durante el recorrido, grupos de distintas edades. Los convocantes, el Sindicato de Inquilinas, organización que ha liderado las protestas desde el desahucio de Maricarmen, insisten en que es necesario convocar “pronto” una huelga general para elevar la magnitud y la trascendencia de su protesta. Valeria Racu, la portavoz del sindicato, adelantó que está en conversaciones con los sindicatos laborales tradicionales, CC OO y UGT, principalmente, y explicó que fijarán conjuntamente una fecha definitiva. Racu separa la fecha de una huelga general de un posible adelanto de los comicios generales para finales de noviembre, es decir, la movilización en la calle del cálculo electoral. “Este es un aviso a navegantes. La protesta seguirá gobierne quien gobierne”, insistió. El sindicato de Inquilinas cargó contra el Ejecutivo —“Ocho días de apoyo popular han hecho más que ocho años de Gobierno progresista”— y contra “las derechas arrodilladas ante los fondos buitre”.

Manifestantes de vivienda, este domingo en la plaza de Cibeles de Madrid. Jaime Villanueva

Los manifestantes celebraron su fuerza al reunirse en la plaza de Cibeles las cuatro columnas que habían partido desde distintos puntos de la capital. Allí, frente a la sede del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, agitaron una vez más sus llaves a mientras reivindicaban el derecho a una vivienda digna y repartían sus críticas al alcalde, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, la presidenta madrileña, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, y el Gobierno de coalición.

El papel que jugará a partir de ahora el Sindicato de Inquilinas entra en otra fase, al señalar que abandonan la acampada en la Puerta del Sol que se inició hace una semana, pero no la movilización en la calle hasta que se satisfagan sus demandas. Su propósito es trasladar a partir de ahora la protesta “a los barrios” y a otras ciudades. En Bilbao, Valencia y Canarias y otro medio centenar de ciudades se repitieron manifestaciones similares a las de la capital.

La de este sábado ha sido la segunda manifestación masiva por la vivienda en apenas siete días. La semana pasada miles de personas ―25.000, según Delegación de Gobierno― marcharon por las calles de Madrid para defender a Mari Carmen, pero el foco se ha ampliado desde entonces a la convocatoria de una huelga general. Se trata de un llamado atípico organizado por un sindicato que no es ninguno de los tradicionales y que no apela a los obreros, a las fábricas ni a los funcionarios, sino a los inquilinos.

Si Pedro Sánchez estaba esperando a medir hasta dónde llega la movilización de la izquierda para decidir si adelanta o no las elecciones, la manifestación de este sábado le ofreció una imagen poderosa: decenas de miles de personas expresando su rechazo a un eventual Gobierno de PP y Vox, el escenario que pronostican las encuestas. Pero la protesta también dejó patente, a través de cánticos, lemas y pancartas —“¿Dónde está el Gobierno progresista?”; “Rentista culpable, Gobierno responsable”; “Ministra rentista, estás en nuestra lista”…—, el profundo descontento con el propio Ejecutivo de Pedro Sánchez y con los decretos de última hora para tratar de evitar nuevos desahucios como el de Mari Carmen, el detonante de la movilización ciudadana que continúa ingresada en el hospital desde su desahucio.

“El adelanto electoral no es la solución”, opinaba Clara, que ha acudido a la manifestación con sus padres y su hijo. “Esto debería haberse resuelto mucho antes de los decretos”, añadía. Sandra, madrileña que tuvo que mudarse a Toledo ante la incapacidad de pagar un alquiler en Madrid, aseguraba que la próxima vez que acuda a las urnas, haya adelanto o no, votará con “más miedo” que ilusión.

Desde la tarima era fácil detectar las distintas sensibilidades movilizadas. “Estamos aquí a pesar de la puñalada trapera que nos dieron ayer”, resumía el sindicato que engloba a las mujeres trabajadoras del hogar. “Somos invisibles y se ejerce el racismo contra nosotras, pero aquí estamos a pesar de la puñalada trapera”, insistió su portavoz. “Vamos a la huelga el 14 de octubre”, añadió el colectivo de educadoras infantiles que se han sumado desde el principio a la causa.

La manifestación a su paso por la Gran Vía madrileña, este sábado. Santi Burgos

A pie de calle, Javier Moya, de 58 años, celador sanitario que salió desde el hospital de La Princesa, insistió en la opción la huelga general “si no hay más remedio”. “Estoy a favor de que siga y crezca. Si no hay más remedio que la huelga general, pues habrá que hacerla”, expone. Carmen, de 27 años, y David, de 30, inquilinos del barrio de Salamanca, también se unieron en Diego de León a la protesta. “Esto no solo perjudica a las nuevas generaciones. Existe un clamor social que la clase política está ignorando”, señaló Carmen.

La manifestación fue también el epílogo de diez días que han cambiado el discurso público. Comenzó el pasado 23 de septiembre cuando Mari Carmen fue desahuciada de su casa y salió en camilla en dirección al hospital. Su caso movilizó a cientos de activistas que llevan tiempo reclamando una intervención del mercado de la vivienda y protestando discretamente cada semana contra los desahucios. Pero el de Mari Carmen dio un paso más y activó a miles de personas que salieron a la calle por primera vez el pasado sábado. Esa misma tarde, muchos de ellos protestaron contra Ayuso frente al ático de lujo adquirido por la Comunidad de Madrid, ahora en venta. Al día siguiente, Mari Carmen envió desde el hospital su primer vídeo. Un día después, las protestas llegaron a las calles de Madrid y apareció la primera tienda de campaña en la Puerta del Sol, que desde entonces se ha convertido en el epicentro de las reivindicaciones por la vivienda.

World.title: Mijas para una escapada otoñal: tres municipios en uno en el corazón de la Costa del Sol
World.content:
Arropado por la sierra, el mirador Juan Antonio Gómez Alarcón es uno de los mejores lugares para entender Mijas (Málaga, 95.104 habitantes), municipio dividido en tres variados núcleos a lo largo de sus casi 150 kilómetros cuadrados. A los pies de esta atalaya se despliega el casco antiguo, su origen. En la panorámica es fácil reconocer la torre y muralla de su vieja fortaleza, la iglesia o su singular y ovalada plaza de toros. Unos kilómetros más al sur, al fondo, se ve cómo el Mediterráneo baña las playas de La Cala de Mijas, segundo núcleo de la localidad. El tercero es Las Lagunas, que acoge a la mayoría de la población y queda a mitad de camino. Las vistas demuestran que este es un territorio repleto de contrastes: la sierra, el campo y lo rural frente a lo urbano, el asfalto y el aroma a salitre. El mar pone límites a la estampa, que desde la balconada está plagada de pequeñas terrazas que asoman desde casitas blancas y encaladas. Puro tipismo andaluz.

Antes de dejarse caer por sus callejuelas, es buena idea conocer su entorno natural. A pesar de ser pasto de las llamas en numerosas ocasiones, muchos de sus pinares aún muestran un intenso color verde y se pueden conocer en bicicleta o a pie. A pocos metros del mirador —donde hay espacio para dejar el coche— parten varias rutas que se adentran en los bosques. Un panel informativo muestra media docena de ellas. Hay una, extensa, que llega hasta Benalmádena, 17 kilómetros después. Son seis horas estimadas de paseo por Sierra Blanca entre suelos de arenisca y mármoles dolomíticos. También se puede andar hasta Ojén, a 50 kilómetros, pero hay otras opciones mucho más humildes y asumibles para cualquiera. Entre ellas, un sendero que incluye bancos para descansar y las etapas de un Vía Crucis que acaba en la ermita del Calvario en apenas unos minutos. “Desde ahí se puede subir al Puerto del Pino en un recorrido muy bonito donde suelen verse ejemplares de cabra montés, águilas, culebras o lagartos”, señala Huan Porrah, miembro del grupo montañero Ahexo p’arriba y que conoce esta montaña al detalle. “Y se puede completar en un paseo circular o desviarse hacia la Cruz de la Misión y la vieja cantera de mármol hasta caer al barrio de Santana”, recomienda. Allí, el bar El Niño es el lugar favorito de los locales para desayunar.

Las vistas desde el mirador del Parque La Muralla, situado en Mijas Pueblo. Nacho Sánchez

Un laberinto de callejones cae desde la parte más alta hacia el centro histórico de Mijas. Son calles estrechas, con fachadas repletas de macetas de tiestos azules y residentes que comparten territorio con pisos turísticos. Hay que bajar con pausa, sin prisa, para disfrutar del silencio que, poco a poco, va dando paso al bullicio de la plaza de la Libertad. El restaurante Meguiñez y el Café Bar Porras —frente a la ermita de San Sebastián— ejercen allí de punto de atracción para numerosos turistas. Desde las terrazas, cerveza en mano, muchos prestan atención al singular tráfico de la zona: igual pasa el camión del butano o la limpieza que un tuktuk, un coche de caballos o un burro taxi. En este lugar se mezclan los acentos extranjeros —sobre todo, del Reino Unido— con señoras que arrastran su carrito de la compra y las historias que los mayores cuentan, a la sombra, en los bancos frente al Museo Histórico-Etnológico. Su exposición de objetos y artesanías tradicionales refleja mejor el mundo que ellos conocen frente al actual, marcado por el turismo de masas, en el que sobreviven.

Terrazas y un 'tuktuk' frente a la ermita de San Sebastián, un templo histórico de fachadas blancas ubicado en la plaza de la Libertad de Mijas. Nacho Sánchez

Hacia la plaza de la Constitución, las tiendas de souvenirs se multiplican. Ofrecen gorras, imanes, bolsos de cuero, carteras de corcho, bolsas de tela, cuencos de cerámica, camisetas, cinturones, peluches, trajes de gitana, toros al estilo trencadís, tazas con frases, delantales con imágenes de bailaoras flamencas. Todo el imaginario andaluz resumido en un puñado de artículos que hacen las delicias de los visitantes, como las postales —todas con imágenes antiguas, ya casi de coleccionista— a 18 céntimos cada una. Merece la pena adentrarse en el pasaje Trocha de los Pescadores y subir la Cuesta de la Villa, que asciende hasta un promontorio donde se ubica una vieja torre y parte de la muralla, restos de la antigua fortaleza que protegía a la ciudad. Convertida hoy en una balconada con vistas al litoral, el recinto incluye la iglesia de la Inmaculada Concepción, el auditorio municipal y una curiosa plaza de toros. Levantada en el año 1900, es de forma elíptica. En el ruedo, Macareno —nombre con el que han bautizado la escultura de un morlaco— protagoniza multitud de fotografías de recuerdo. Más abajo, la calle Muros devuelve al jaleo turístico camino de la plaza Virgen de la Peña, cerca de la ermita que lleva el mismo nombre y el Museo del Arte en Miniatura. La parada de burro taxi, más abajo, está cerca ya de la oficina de turismo. Un enorme aparcamiento municipal permite dejar el coche por un euro al día.

Exterior de la singular plaza de toros de Mijas. Nacho Sánchez

De Casa Navarra a la playa

La carretera que baja desde ahí hacia el mar entre curvas desemboca en Fuengirola. Antes, un viejo caserío sirve carne a la brasa, además de buen pescado. Es el restaurante Casa Navarra, fundado hace casi cuatro décadas por Carlos Herrero y María Mercedes Lacunza, navarros que llegaron hasta la zona en su viaje de novios y les gustó tanto que dejaron lo que hacían en su tierra para bajar al sur y lanzarse en la hostelería. “Primero abrieron en Fuengirola, pero tras una inundación durante una riada, decidieron subirlo hasta aquí para olvidarse de agua para siempre”, cuenta Leire Herrero, quien ahora regenta junto a su hermano Asier el negocio. Cuentan que el chuletón es lo que más se vende, pero también las alcachofas con almejas, las anchoas con piparras o los pimientos del piquillo.

Para llegar desde allí hasta la costa mijeña existe la opción de hacerlo por una estrecha carretera que atraviesa Las Lagunas, zona residencial donde vive la mayoría de vecinos que se despliega en las cercanías del viejo hipódromo y de varios de los 12 campos de golf que tiene el municipio, el que más, tras Marbella, en toda la Costa del Sol. Eso sí, la forma más directa de llegar al tercer núcleo de Mijas es tomar la autovía A-7 en dirección a Marbella. El camino es corto. En apenas 10 minutos y tras una pronunciada curva, aparece el desvío, anunciado por unas letras al más puro estilo de Hollywood sobre la ladera.

Desde la carretera no se intuye, pero La Cala de Mijas sorprende por sus casitas blancas, que comparten callejero con estudios de tatuaje, barberías, agencias inmobiliarias, tiendas de regalos y el cuartel de la Guardia Civil. Desperdigado aquí y allá hay un puñado —grande— de restaurantes internacionales con propuestas procedentes de Tailandia, China, Corea o la India, además de algún pub irlandés. Destaca, en un rinconcito, la venta La Butibamba, cuyas raíces profundizan en 200 años de la Costa del Sol y donde se sirve un legendario bocata de lomo, amén de multitud de platos a la vez sencillos y deliciosos, como los dos huevos fritos con ajos y chorizo de Ronda. Cuentan en esta casa que por sus salones pasaron personajes como Ernest Hemingway o Camarón de la Isla.

Chiringuito El Trópico, ubicado en el paseo marítimo de La Cala de Mijas. Nacho Sánchez

Más cerca del mar llama la atención el edificio blanco y verde que acoge el Hogar del Jubilado, en primera línea y con precios asequibles para los veteranos extranjeros. Fritura mixta, berenjenas fritas, boquerones en vinagre o lubina a la espalda andan por el menú, que también ofrece platos de espaguetis. La cocina abre de 9.00 a 17.00 de martes a domingo.

La torre vigía de La Cala de Mijas (también conocida como el Torreón). Nacho Sánchez

A esta playa se la conoce como la del Torreón, porque la vieja torre, construida en el siglo XVIII y aún en pie, fue levantada para colocar dos cañones que sirvieran para proteger la costa de invasores. Quizá por eso hay un parque infantil con forma de barco pirata que da la bienvenida al pequeño paseo marítimo. Este cuenta con lo que se espera de un lugar así, y que el fotógrafo inglés Martín Parr inmortalizó en 2021: chiringuitos, hamacas, sombrillas y mucha arena para disfrutar de un buen baño, muy tranquilo en la temporada otoñal a pesar del calor. La senda litoral, con algunos tramos aún en construcción, ofrece seis kilómetros para que, a pie o en bici, se pueda recorrer toda la costa mijeña, que incluye alguna zona naturista como Playa Marina.

World.title: Fries with that? Homes near Amsterdam TikTok queue sell for less
World.content:
Homes near Fabel Friet, an Amsterdam chip shop whose TikTok-fuelled queues have become one of the city’s more unlikely tourist attractions, sell for less than comparable homes just streets away, according to a TU Delft study.

The research, reported by local broadcaster AT5, came out this week at the same time as the city council and the shop’s owners faced off in court over the queue and how to deal with public nuisance caused by it.

PhD researcher Rosa van der Drift compared the sale prices of 6,233 Amsterdam homes between 2015 and 2023, taking account of factors such as size and condition. Homes within 500 metres of the shop sold for 4.88% less on average, or about €41,000.

Within 70 metres, the gap widened to 11.4%. The study does not establish any correlation with causation.

Old licence

The court case was made by a group of residents against the city council, not the business. They argue the council did not properly weigh their interests when it granted Fabel Friet an operating licence, and want the licence withdrawn or its conditions tightened.

In 2024, a judge suspended a council rule limiting the queue to 10 people after Fabel Friet called it unworkable.

On Tuesday, one resident told the court there were people eating chips outside “every day, from 11 in the morning until 9 in the evening”, AT5 reported. The residents’ lawyer said a serious accident on the crowded bridge was only a matter of time.

The owners told the court their crowd managers keep the queue safe, the street is cleaned 4 times a day and crowds are down 23% since they opened other branches. For a while they hired a falcon 3 times a week to scare off the gulls, but stopped when residents began using it as evidence against them.

A representative of mayor Femke Halsema acknowledged that the old licence had not been effective enough, and said stricter conditions had been added to the current one about 6 months ago. “It is complicated,” the representative said, according to AT5. “You are so successful, is that not allowed?”

The judge urged both sides to find common ground, reminding the residents of the Dutch saying that a good neighbour is better than a distant friend. She will rule within 6 weeks, but only on the old licence, because objections to the current licence have yet to be decided.

World.title: Cabinet backtracks on box 3 tax plans for small savings
World.content:
The cabinet has promised to rewrite part of its new tax plan for savings and investments, just two days after announcing it, so that fewer people with modest savings are impacted.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen, of the right-wing liberal VVD, made the commitment in parliament on Thursday after MPs from both opposition and coalition parties attacked the plan.

“I have discussed this with the prime minister and with the coalition,” the Financieel Dagblad reported him as saying. “We are prepared to make changes. There will be a proposal to spare small savers.”

Under the plan presented on Tuesday, people would pay 36% tax on returns above €1,000 a year from 2028, down from €1,800 in the earlier version of the reform. Heinen also said he still believed the plan would exempt couples with up to €100,000 in savings.

No funding yet

The minister said he did not yet know how the cabinet would make up the shortfall. Small savers were the main source of funding for the box 3 overhaul, which reports say could cost up to €20 billion.

“We don’t have many levers to pull,” Heinen said. “And every choice you make is enormously complicated.”

The cabinet will send the bill to the Council of State, the government’s senior advisory body on legislation, without an alternative source of funding. Heinen said he would come up with proposals by October 12, when MPs debate the cabinet’s annual package of tax changes.

He also said he would look again at a temporary measure for next year, which would cut the tax-free allowance from €59,357 to €30,846 per person and raise the tax rate. You can find out more about how the changes would affect you in our box 3 explainer.

World.title: Dutch royal house earned nearly half a billion from slavery
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch royal family, the House of Orange-Nassau, earned an estimated €576 million from slavery, mostly in the former Dutch East Indies, according to a new investigation into the monarchy.

The research was commissioned by king Willem-Alexander, who granted access to the royal archives and funded the inquiry.

“All stadtholders, kings, and queens, at least up to and including Wilhelmina, were convinced of the legitimacy of colonialism and its importance for the Netherlands,” lead researcher Gert Oostindie said during a ceremony on Friday to present the findings.

The 2,000 page report has been published into five books and was presented to the king. Willem-Alexander described the conclusions as “heartbreaking and confronting” during the gathering at the Academy Building in Leiden.

“I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future to the best of my ability,” he said.

According to the research, the royals earned very little from the transatlantic slave trade, not because they were opposed but because they were unsuccessful.

Oostindie’s work found that while monarchs voiced support for the institution, few had a direct impact on policy.

Only King William I, who was in power from 1813 to 1840, had a direct hand in colonial slavery. Prior to that, leaders left it to the States General, the country’s early administrative assembly, or to the powerful Dutch East India Company (VOC).

After the reign of William I, monarchs were forced to share power with an increasingly important parliament, which made most of the policy decisions.

Willem-Alexander asked Oostindie, a former professor of colonial history, to conduct the investigation in 2022. Sixty researchers were involved in the nearly four year project.

In 2023, the king formally apologised for the Netherlands’ slave trading history during an annual commemoration for the abolition of the practice.

The monarch also stopped using a ceremonial golden coach which has repeatedly come under fire for a painted panel that depicts scenes of colonialism.

Research by the home affairs ministry in 2023 came to a similar conclusion. That study, carried out following a 2021 parliamentary motion, involved some 30 academics and historians and was published as the book Staat en slavernij (State and slavery).

World.title: Rivers too low for depth checks, leaving ships to risk stranding
World.content:
Rivers in the east of the Netherlands have fallen so low that the authorities can no longer measure whether ships can pass safely, leaving skippers to decide for themselves whether or not to sail and risk getting stranded.

Rijkswaterstaat, the transport ministry department that manages the waterways, told broadcaster NOS its survey boats can no longer reach the shallowest stretches of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal.

In certain places the channel is less than 125cm deep, leaving only three agency boats that are shallow enough, but they are also needed in other regions.

Without them, Rijkswaterstaat cannot publish its daily shipping readings of the depths, which barge operators use to avoid getting stranded. Commercial firms collect and sell similar data, but not every skipper has or can pay for a subscription.

Transport under pressure

“This is very worrying,” Fiona Oomen, of inland shipping association Koninklijke Binnenvaart Nederland, told NOS. “All transport is under pressure, on the roads and on the waterways. What if the water drops even further? Where is everything supposed to go?”

The flow of the Rhine at Lobith, where the river enters the Netherlands, is now around 545 cubic metres per second. That is well below the record low of 614 set in August.

Last weekend a Dutch cruise ship carrying 140 passengers became stuck at Cologne as the Rhine dropped to new lows in Germany.

On the IJssel, a one-way system imposed last week has forced some vessels to take a detour of up to 300km.

Freight carried on Dutch waterways fell by 19% in August, according to CBS figures, with cross-border traffic with Germany worst hit.

The infrastructure ministry lifted the national water shortage in early September, but warned that river levels could stay low until the end of the year. The cabinet has ruled out compensation for businesses hit by the drought.

Rain needed

Rijkswaterstaat could not say how long the situation would last. “We need rain in the catchment area,” a spokesman told NOS, adding that it would have to fall mainly outside the Netherlands. Current forecasts suggest the flow will not get worse, but will not improve much either.

He warned that a different problem would follow. “When it’s over, we get the next problem,” he said. “Then we’ll have high water again.” The North Sea is currently exceptionally warm, which could mean a very wet autumn.

New numbers from the Dutch statistics agency CBS show the inflation rate rose slightly in August.

The preliminary estimate from the Central Agency for Statistics shows a 0.1% rise from August, putting September’s inflation rate at 3.4%.

The final numbers will be released on October 13.

Fuel and energy prices account for most of the increase. The cost of petrol and gas for heating is was up 13.9% in September over the same month the year before.

Grocery prices, however, have dropped slightly for the second month in a row. Food staples were down 1.3% over the year before, after dropping 0.5% in August.

World.title: The Netherlands had its first TV broadcast 75 years ago
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Seventy-five years ago today, the Dutch had their first opportunity to watch a television broadcast: a performance of the play De Toverspiegel, live from a studio in Bussum.

The Royal Family watched the 90-minute production from the Soestdijk Palace.

Concerns about television’s corrupting influence on society and a focus on post-war reconstruction meant that the Netherlands entered the television era only in 1951, later than the United Kingdom or the United States.

The BBC had begun broadcasting in 1936.

The country had around 500 television sets at the time. Radio was the much more widely consumed medium, with around 250,000 devices in homes across the Netherlands.

A television set cost 785 guilders, about a third of the average annual salary, putting the luxury good far out of reach for most of the country.

Media historian Huub Wijfjes told the NOS that initial television broadcasts simply copied whatever was on the radio. “TV took a dominant position and reached its peak in the 60s, 70s, and 80s. The medium displaced radio,” he said.

By 1956, there were 75,000 television sets in the country.

On the website for the Netherlands Institute for Sound and Vision, you can watch the early broadcasts.

World.title: Israeli group disrupts Delft screening of Gaza documentary Naza
World.content:
A premiere screening of the documentary Naza, which investigates the killing of civilians by the Israeli military in Gaza, was interrupted in a Delft cinema on Thursday afternoon by a woman taking a microphone and addressing the audience about the October 7 massacres.

She stood in front of the screen midway through the film and began describing how her family members were murdered during the Hamas attacks that sparked the Gaza war in 2023.

The crowd booed her off stage, the microphone was disabled, some shouted “shame on you”, though some applauded her. The woman’s name is Sabine Taasa, a French-Israeli citizen from a town near the Gaza strip and who lost her husband and a son during the attacks.

An Israeli activist group Ad Kan accompanied Taasa to the screening. The group describes itself as former army and intelligence officers who infiltrate and obstruct what they say are anti-Israeli and anti-Semitic activities in foreign countries.

Another member tried to project footage from the October 7 attacks in the cinema while Taasa spoke, according to broadcaster NOS.

Naza, which has been lauded by critics, consists of anonymous interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military services. They describe how they attacked Gaza, how AI systems were used to select targets, and the policies toward collateral damage and loss of innocent life.

Some describe killing hundreds of civilians at a time to target single military figures; others describe using surveillance techniques to wait for militants to be at home with their families before striking – a tactic known as “where’s daddy”.

Israeli officials have condemned the film, with prime minister Netanyahu pledging to strip the film makers of their citizenship. Other military figures have disputed the claims made in the film and branded it propaganda.

Dutch-Israeli relations have been strained recently over the decision to ban imports of goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestinian territories. Dutch diplomats have had their status stripped in response.

The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule. The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020. However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040. “This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.” Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱 To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️ ✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych; ✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026 Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors. The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway. The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030 In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025 Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned. Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation. Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year. Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government. That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications. The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026 The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU. Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity.
