World.title: Weekly review of prices of Azeri Light, Dated Brent, and Urals
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 3. This week (September 28–October 2), average prices for Azeri Light (CIF), Azeri Light (FOB Ceyhan), Dated Brent, and Urals crude decreased.

According to Trend’s calculations, based on data from oil market participants, the average price of Azeri Light (CIF) crude, produced at the “Azeri-Chirag-Guneshli” field in Azerbaijan, increased by $0.67, or 0.6%, compared to the previous week, reaching $121.75 per barrel.

Based on the information, the highest price for this grade of crude oil during the week was $124.76 per barrel, and the lowest was $118.22.

The average price of Azeri Light crude on a FOB basis at the Turkish port of Ceyhan was $114.30 per barrel, which is $0.08, or 0.1%, lower than the previous week’s figure. During the week, the maximum price was $117.33 per barrel, and the minimum was $111.45.

The average price of Urals crude oil increased by $1.2, or 1.5%, compared to the previous week, reaching $84.22 per barrel. During the week, the highest price was $87.22, and the lowest was $80.89.

Dated Brent crude averaged $123.52 per barrel, up $2.87, or 2.4%, from the previous week. During the week, the price reached a high of $127.11 per barrel and a low of $119.09.

World.title: Call for witnesses after ball bearings used to smash windows at government buildings
World.content:
ACT Policing is calling for witnesses to come forward after ball bearings were used to damage windows at two government buildings on Thursday night.

Police said on Friday morning that detectives were investigating after windows were damaged at a building near the Housing ACT Central Access Point at Emu Bank in Belconnen.

Staff inside the building were temporarily locked down and then sent home for the day, while the Housing ACT office was closed on Friday.

On Sunday, police issued a media release asking for information relating to the damage.

Police said ball bearings were used to damage windows at the Housing ACT building in Belconnen. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

ACT Policing said between 7pm and 9:30pm on Thursday, October 1, "two incidents of criminal damage occurred at buildings on Emu Bank and Benjamin Way".

"At both locations, ball bearings are believed to have been used to impact shopfront windows," it said.

"No one was harmed by these incidents."

Anyone who saw any persons or vehicles in the vicinity is being asked to come forward.

Anyone who can assist police should provide their contact details to Crime Stoppers via the Crime Stoppers ACT website, quoting 8516326.

World.title: A doctor said Tim was incapable of love. His mum knew otherwise
World.content:
When Judy Sharp was told by doctors that her three-year-old son Tim would be "unfeeling and incapable of love", she refused to accept those limitations.

In the years after his autism diagnosis, Tim began using drawings to communicate with his mum, sharing his feelings, sense of humour and love for her.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Judy and Tim's words.

'What's wrong with your son?'

Judy: When Tim was born in 1988, it was the best day of my life, my heart was ready to burst.

It was the same day the queen was opening the new Parliament House in Canberra, so I thought this is a very special day.

Judy says there were early signs of autism when Tim was just a baby. (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

It wasn't easy after he was born, the first thing I noticed was he didn't sleep.

He was distressed all the time, constant crying and unsettled. As he got older, he had to keep moving, he couldn't stay in the same room as people, and he only ate a few foods.

These were unusual things to me that I didn't understand.

Tim almost looked like he was in pain, you could see the fear in his eyes.

The most common thing that was said to me at the time was, "What's wrong with your son?"

The doctors kept saying, "wait till he's three, to see a specialist".

So, the appointment was made for the day after his third birthday and that was the worst day ever.

Don't tell me that boy doesn't love me

Judy: They sent us to a doctor who was supposed to be the best specialist.

He diagnosed Tim with autism and just wrote him off.

He told me all the things that Tim would never do, that he would be unfeeling and incapable of love.

I had a physical reaction, not only mental and emotional, but it was like someone was sucking the life out of me.

The worst thing anyone can do is take away all your hope and that's what he did.

Judy with Tim and her youngest son Sam (middle). (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

So, by the time I got out of that doctor's office and to the car, I was hysterical.

I'm putting Tim into his little car seat and he's patting me on the back and wiping away my tears.

And I wanted to march back in there and say, "You tell me that boy doesn't love me."

This was perfect love and I knew that little boy loved me.

And I was going to keep on loving him no matter what anyway.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

The birth of Laser Beak Man

Judy: One of the things the specialist said to me was that Tim would not speak.

But when he was five, he started to draw.

So, by accident, we started to draw to communicate between the two of us.

And it turned out that Tim had this natural ability for drawing, we thought, "he's got talent".

So, every day, the house was covered in pens, papers, I never put them away.

Tim's Laser Beak Man character has taken him and his mum across the world. (Supplied: Brisbane festival)

Then he did start speaking. And when he was 11, he started walking around the house saying, "When I grew up, I'm going to be Laser Beak Man" — a superhero he had created.

Tim injected his own personality and his own sense of humour into Laser Beak Man.

He's not a classic superhero; he's one defined by Tim in a different way and he's got a very unique way of looking at life.

And Laser Beak Man has taken us on a journey that no-one ever could have imagined; from New York, London, the Sydney Opera House, TV, theatre, movies, you name it.

We've travelled the world with Laser Beak Man and met so many people and Tim's had so many opportunities and things that we never thought would have been possible in any way, shape or form.

Tim: [Drawing] makes me happy and I relax doing it. I can have fun with it. I can use my big imagination.

[Mum and I] made the Laser Beak Man theatre show come true and went to New York with it. He's a superhero and he's really awesome.

One of Tim's drawings of Laser Beak Man represents love. (Supplied: Tim Sharp)

Love is everything, I feel it in everything

Tim: I love that Mum is a good friend and a good mother to me.

She takes care of me.

She is a kind mum.

She sits with me and we don't even talk sometimes, we like being together.

She likes me just the way I am. She makes me feel peaceful and special.

I tell her I love her all the time. I like to help her and make her happy, I like to buy her some flowers and Maltesers.

Love is everything. I feel it in everything. You can see it and hear it. It makes life better and happy.

Tim says love makes "life better and happy". (Supplied: Judy Sharp)

Judy: Tim and I spend most of our time together and I find that a very, very easy thing to do, to be with him.

He's patient and he's kind.

I love that he thinks another way because it makes me think other ways.

I love his natural ability to want to connect with people.

And it's really inspiring to watch him do that in his own way without trying to be like anyone else.

And he will frequently tell me that he loves me.

At the end of the day, he'll say to me, "I've had a really good day with you, Mum. We're a great team."

You don't even get that in a marriage.

The best thing you can do in life is just follow Tim's example; be brave, be yourself and show the world who you really are.

World.title: On duty just after 6pm, these paramedics' shift is about to go bad
World.content:
Abbey Studley sits in the passenger seat of a kitted-out SUV as her colleague, Dave O'Toole, runs through potential scenarios with the intel they have on their comms screen.

It's a little after 6pm on a Tuesday night and the Alice Springs intensive care paramedics have just begun their shift.

They've received a simple call to assist a person experiencing a medical issue, but a recent spate of violence against frontline workers in the Central Australian town means the St John Ambulance crews never know what they will face when they're called out.

Abbey Studley calls the police after a violent incident in which her colleagues were punched and spat on. (ABC News: Emma Haskin)

Earlier this week, they invited the ABC to ride along with paramedics — and although everything is calm when they pick up their first patient, things change en route to the hospital.

By the time they arrive at the ambulance bay at Alice Springs Hospital, the patient has become aggressive and attacks the paramedics, punching and spitting at them as they try to provide care.

It's the 100th attack on Alice Springs ambulance staff for 2026, according to St John data, with the majority being physical assaults.

With just three 24-hour crews and one intensive care unit staffed by 45 paramedics, there aren't many local St John staff members who haven't experienced violence.

Abbey calls the police and the patient is arrested and taken to the watch house.

"It makes me particularly disappointed and I'm angry that another one of my staff have been victims of violence," Abbey says.

Paramedics in Alice Springs have been subject to 100 assaults so far this year. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

" There's never an excuse for violence … and what we've seen tonight is another example of our staff being victims of violence for no reason. "

NT paramedics assaulted, lacking resources The ABC rode along with St John Ambulance NT paramedics to hear the impact under-resourcing is having on the workforce, including stories of staff being assaulted on the job.

The flow-on effects from occupational violence will mean people will be waiting longer for an ambulance.

"We've now got three staff delivering statements to police currently, and as you can see behind me all three of our Alice Springs resources are currently at hospital handing over patients or providing statements to police," Abbey says.

Abbey is no stranger to violence on the job. Two years ago, she was brutally attacked in the line of duty.

'I thought I was going to die'

The attack occurred shortly before midnight in October 2024, just as Abbey finished her shift, when a man pulled her from her fast-response vehicle.

"I thought I was going to die," she says.

Abbey says she had time to activate a duress alarm before the perpetrator dragged her down the street by her arm.

Abbey Studley suffered a traumatic brain injury and blindness in one eye following an attack while she was at work. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Much of that night is a blur due to the level of violence she experienced.

"I've psychologically blocked a lot of that out and it's hard now for me to recall exactly what transpired," Abbey says.

"I think in the police report, I said I got over 20 punches to the head.

"I have blindness in my right eye and I have limited feeling in my left arm."

She also sustained permanent injuries, including a traumatic brain injury.

As a result, she spent two months in an acquired brain injury unit in Melbourne, and many more months seeking treatment to recover.

Abbey Studley and her colleagues never know what will happen on the job. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I was told by a number of specialists and doctors that I would never return to this career and that made me really devastated and really sad," she says.

But 16 months later, Abbey returned to the community and the job she loves.

"I feel so lucky and privileged to come to work every day and proud to wear this St John uniform and provide life-saving critical care and really high-level compassionate care to the community," she says.

No one has ever been charged with Abbey's assault.

"I think what's tough is knowing that there's still somebody that could be in the community or in the wider community who could perpetrate that level of violence again," she says.

Abbey Studley with colleagues Benson Chan and Gareth Aescht in the midst of a busy night on the job. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Following the assault on her colleagues on Tuesday, Abbey says her team will take their time to regroup and debrief.

"They'll be given time to stand down and recoup, maybe have a cup of tea or a coffee and a break and a little check-in with each other," she says.

"It's up to them whether or not they would like to keep working and that's obviously very individual.

"Look, they're upset. This is a significant number of assaults now in this region since the start of this year."

Searching for solutions

Body-worn cameras and OC spray have been floated as measures to curb violence against paramedics across the Northern Territory.

Last month, Alice Springs Member for Braitling Joshua Burgoyne revealed the NT government had been discussing the two measures with St John management.

According to St John Ambulance data, police have been called to assist their workers on 43 occasions so far this year. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

St John NT chief executive Abigail Trewin says although body-worn cameras pose some privacy challenges, the service is talking to staff about "who and where and how we would roll something like this out".

She says they will also consult with staff about OC spray, although it came with potential problems.

"We work in effectively a tin box — you're transporting a patient," she says.

"It's not a lot of space, so discharging OC spray in that environment is probably not very sensible."

NT Health Minister Steve Edgington says while no paramedics have approached him requesting OC spray for protection in their workplace, the government will consider it.

"If that's something that St John believes will assist them in delivering their services and protecting and providing evidence of any assaults or threatening behaviour against them again, we will work with St John to look at what their needs are," he says.

"They need to be protected. They need to be supported.

"When they go to work they're there to help people. They shouldn't be threatened."

A community partnership

Last month, St John NT joined forces with Tangentyere Council, which manages Aboriginal town camps in Alice Springs.

Ms Trewin says the partnership aims to create "safer, more positive interactions" between paramedics and Aboriginal patients in the town.

"Providing the best emergency healthcare is more than clinical skills," she says.

"It is also about trust, communication and understanding the communities we serve."

She hopes the partnership will eventually lead to Indigenous liaison officers working with the ambulance service, although that will rely on funding.

Alice Springs paramedics hope a new partnership with Tangentyere Council will help strengthen relationships in the community. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Tangentyere Council chief executive Walter Shaw says he hopes the memorandum of understanding will result in a safer work environment for Alice Springs paramedics.

"We need to ensure that we put out a social safety net for our St John's Ambulance Service and also the residents of town camps in Alice Springs," he says.

NT paramedics could carry pepper spray for safety, minister says The NT government has floated the idea of paramedics carrying pepper spray as they continue to face high rates of assault on the job.

"I'd like to see young Aboriginal paramedics working within St John's itself."

For Abbey, the partnership is some of the best preventative work she's ever seen.

"It's about two-way learning, it's about sharing knowledge and it's about becoming part of the community," she says.

Despite all that she's experienced on the job, she remains steadfast in her love of her work.

"It's a real privilege to wear this uniform and it's a real privilege to serve this community," she says.

"We're really grateful for community members for protecting us and keeping us safe whenever they can."

World.title: Houthis target Saudi oil facility as hostilities escalate in Yemen
World.content:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say a targeted attack on a Saudi Arabian oil company facility near the capital Riyadh is retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen.

The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait in a lightning offensive last month.

Houthi-affiliated channel Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting "Saudi aggression" against the Yemeni capital.

Houthis say they targeted a Saudi oil facility, south of Riyadh. (AP)

Two correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles at the city.

In Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones.

They said the attack sparked fires at the targeted sites.

Al-Masirah also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen's north-western governorate of Saada, one of the group's strongholds.

Hunger warning

After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of north-west Yemen, including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east, a region that is larger but much less populated.

A big, expensive, global excursion into hell What so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions.

Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.

The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a decade-old practice.

Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.

Since then, fighting has intensified, with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Houthi fighters took over the Red Sea port of Sanaa in Yemen. (AP)

They have also struck multiple Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and Riyadh, while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.

Battle for Taiz

Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.

The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources said 26 troops had died.

The Houthis leave Trump in a bind The Houthis have moved on strategic islands in the Red Sea and are now putting one of the richest and most powerful nations in the Middle East in a tricky spot.

The Houthis said on Friday Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the previous 24 hours.

Saudi authorities reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemeni border.

Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.

Iraq ships crude through Hormuz

Meanwhile, Iraq's state-owned Oil Tanker Company transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude aboard a large crude carrier through the Strait of Hormuz, in what its director general described on Saturday as the company's first such operation in decades.

A week of Houthi attacks threatens oil and markets The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made their biggest land grab in years, reigniting Yemen's 12-year long civil war and pushing up global fuel prices.

The announcement means the company is transporting the crude through the strait rather than delivering it at the port of Basra, giving state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility in how and where it sells the crude.

The company's director general, Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar, said in a statement that the Oil Tanker Company was working to buy specialised crude oil tankers to expand its fleet.

Iraq has previously secured Iranian permission for Iraqi oil tankers to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively closed during its conflict with the US.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Two helicopter rescues in Tasmania after separate bushwalker mishaps
World.content:
Two separate rescues involving Tasmania's rescue helicopter has prompted police to urge bushwalkers to carry communications devices when out and about.

A 62-year-old man from New South Wales has had what police described as a "lucky" escape from a cliff fall in southern Tasmania.

The man was walking alone on a track at Dennes Point on North Bruny Island on Saturday morning when he fell over and slipped about 10 metres down a steep hill towards the water.

Police said the man, who was not injured in the incident, contacted emergency services by mobile phone about 10:30am, with police attending the scene shortly afterwards.

A specialist police roping team was sent to the scene in the Westpac Rescue Helicopter, with the man rescued about 1pm.

Senior Constable Callum Herbert, from Search and Rescue, said the man had slipped about 10 metres down an unstable slope at the edge of a coastal track.

"He luckily stopped himself at the top of a further 40-metre cliff," Senior Constable Herbert said.

"A sensible decision was made to contact emergency services as in this case an attempt to self-rescue may have resulted in him falling further and could have had a catastrophic outcome.

"I remind all walkers to carry a charged mobile phone with them, no matter if the walk is only a short distance and also to remain vigilant around coastal areas, as the ground can be unstable due to loose vegetation and gravel."

Walkers activate beacon for rescue

In a separate incident on Saturday, a 44-year-old man was rescued from the Tyndall Range on Tasmania's west coast after becoming ill while bushwalking.

Police said the man was part of a group of three on a day walk from an overnight campsite when he became unable to continue.

Going hiking? You should take a locator beacon — here's how to use it When you go hiking, experts say a personal locator beacon should be a non-negotiable. So how do they work, and where do you get one?

The group activated a personal locator beacon (PLB) and contacted emergency services via satellite communications about 3pm.

Police said the Westpac Rescue Helicopter located the group and transported the man to the Royal Hobart Hospital for assessment last night.

The group was equipped for their overnight camping trip, with "appropriate supplies and communication equipment including their PLB which ensured a quick response from emergency services," police said.

Inspector Steve Jones said it was a "timely reminder for bushwalkers in remote areas to carry sufficient food, water, communication equipment and emergency shelter for unexpected delays".

World.title: 'Forgotten' outback town faces scorching summer without a pool
World.content:
As the weather turns, residents of inland Australia will begin flocking to their local pool for the start of the swimming season.

But with a scorching summer looming, residents of Walgett in western New South Wales will not be taking part in the seasonal ritual.

The town's pool will remain closed this season after it was deemed unsafe and beyond repair.

Walgett Shire Council says building a new pool is simply beyond the capacity of a small rural council to fund alone. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)

It leaves few options for cooling off for Walgett parents like Katrina Marshall and her two boys aged 17 and 14.

"Our rivers stink so it's not like the kids can even go down there and enjoy themselves," she said.

" It's going to be a very boring summer. "

Ms Marshall said the closure was a reminder of the disadvantage felt in parts of regional NSW.

"We're always forgotten. We're a little town in the middle of nowhere. We don't exist in Sydney unless kids are stealing cop cars," she said.

Walgett children swimming in the local pool in 2023. (ABC Western Plains: Emily Middleton)

A pool ready to retire

The Walgett Memorial Swimming Pool was first opened to the public in the early 60s.

Sixty years on and the pool is showing its age.

In 2023, council voted to decommission the pool before patching it up to reopen in late 2024.

It closed again in April, before the end of last season, after council deemed it unsafe.

Walgett Shire Council Mayor Jasen Ramien said the council did not want to close the pool this season, but it had no choice.

"The decision to close the Walgett pool was one of the hardest decisions this council has had to make," he said.

" We didn't want to close it, but the reality was the pool had reached a point where it was no longer safe. "

The council will focus on building a replacement pool instead of investing up to $1 million in short-term repairs that were not guaranteed to last, according to a NSW Public Works inspection.

In a letter to NSW Premier Chris Minns, Cr Ramien described the pool as the backbone of the community.

"It is one of the few places in our town that offers relief from the heat, but also relief from boredom, disengagement and isolation," he wrote.

"In a community like ours, that matters more than words can properly capture."

Fixing Australia's aging pools could cost $8 billion. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The council has requested up to $420,000 from the state government to provide a free daily bus service from Walgett to the Collarenebri Swimming Pool.

The towns are about 75 kilometres apart, with a bus service going once a day in each direction.

Former Olympic swim coach's warning

Former Olympic swim coach Laurie Lawrence is worried the bush faces a generation of kids who cannot swim due to aging pool infrastructure.

"It could be a generation, particularly in the country areas where kids, because they have a lack of pools, don't get to enjoy the water, don't get to stay safe," he said.

"We all deserve an opportunity to learn to swim, the whole country."

Laurie Lawrence says everyone in Australia should have an opportunity to learn to swim. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

Many council-run pools were built in the 60s during the golden era of swimming.

But with a life span of 50 years, most are nearing or have passed their use-by date.

"You can't have the country people being disadvantaged over the city people," Mr Lawrence said.

The National Drowning Report 2026 by Royal Lifesaving Australia found drowning rates were double for those from the most disadvantaged areas and nearly triple for regional residents and nearly quadruple for remote residents compared to major cities.

Walgett Memorial Pool remains closed until funding is found to build a new one. (ABC Western Plains: Zaarkacha Marlan)

The member for Barwon, Roy Butler, has called on the state government to audit pools across the state.

"In New South Wales, 54 per cent of public pools are in regional communities," he said.

"I've spoken to the minister for local government, and the minister for sport about doing an audit of those pools, and I've also taken it up with Royal Life Saving Australia … to get them to pull together a report that prioritises pools so then government can prioritise allocation of funds," he said.

In a written response, a spokesperson for the NSW Minister for Sport Steven Kamper said, "The NSW Government supports sports facilities by providing grant funding and working in partnership with local government, State Sporting Organisations, clubs and associations."

In 2022, the State of Aquatic Facility Infrastructure in Australia report, commissioned by Royal Life Saving Australia, found 500 pools nationally would need replacing, or require "significant repairs" to the pool shell within the next 10 years, at a cost of $8 billion.

Vital blue spaces

Public policy researcher Ian McShane has been following the deterioration and closure of public pools for over 15 years.

He said losing a pool resulted in losing a vital part of a town's social fabric.

"It would be a loss of an important recreational function," said Dr McShane, from the Centre for Urban Research at RMIT, said.

" Local public pools are one place where anybody, regardless of who you are and your social status, can mix. "

Dr McShane said the loss of a pool would mean people might look elsewhere to settle down.

"It can be a tipping point," he said.

"Families would be reluctant to move to areas that don't have good social infrastructure."

Losing a public pool could make people think twice about settling down and raising a family in the area. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Dr McShane said he wants to see pools classed as critical infrastructure, alongside roads and energy networks.

"I think the three levels of government should get together and agree that these are important community places and closing them can really have a significant personal and social impact on communities, particularly small communities."

World.title: 'Really unfair': Victim-survivor's almost two-year wait for her own records
World.content:
For years, Sam Morgan kept the memories of the abuse she allegedly experienced while in foster care and at a Tasmanian government school buried.

When she was ready to seek justice, Ms Morgan made a Right to Information (RTI) request to have her foster care and school records, held by the state's education department, sent to her lawyer so she could start a civil court claim against the state.

It took 23 months for the documents to arrive.

"When it drags on for two years … the anxiety just becomes horrific," she said.

Ms Morgan alleges she was physically abused by a foster carer when she was aged 12 or 13, and sexually abused by a foster carer when she was a teenager. She also alleges she was physically abused at a Tasmanian government high school.

The abuse allegedly happened in the 1980s.

Ms Morgan said she was out having a coffee with her daughter when she found out the files had finally been received by her lawyer.

"It was a big surprise but a huge relief. I cried when I got home because it was just a relief," she said.

Her lawyer, Azita Arian, an associate in the abuse law team at Maurice Blackburn, said Ms Morgan was not the only person whose civil court abuse case had been held up because of delays in obtaining records.

"These are people who were abused in state care and they shouldn't have to wait almost two years to access their records," Ms Arian said.

Azita Arian says the RTI delays are limiting the choices victim-survivors have when it comes to pursuing justice. (Supplied: Maurice Blackburn)

She said the records were important because they helped establish when and where people were placed and could help identify foster carers and workers who are relevant to the claim.

She said, in some cases, the files may also document any disclosures of abuse.

Delays reducing choice

Ms Arian said the delays were reducing the choices victim-survivors had when seeking justice.

One of the options they have is the National Redress Scheme (NRS), which does not require the same level of documentation and evidence as a civil court claim, but compensation payments under the scheme are capped at $150,000.

Ms Arian said Ms Morgan had applied to the NRS and was offered a payment of $100,000.

After receiving advice that accepting the payment would essentially bar her from pursuing a civil claim, Ms Morgan has not accepted the offer.

Ms Arian said she had many clients also facing long waits for their records who could not afford to wait.

"Survivors are effectively tunnelled towards redress by default," she said.

Ms Morgan said the delays seemed "to just be really unfair".

"It's almost like the government does it to get people to pull out."

Delays in obtaining her records have delayed Sam Morgan's case against the state of Tasmania. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Ombudsman 'aware of the backlog'

Tasmania's ombudsman has also noted concerns about the delays with RTI applications to the education department.

In an email sent to Ms Morgan's lawyers in May, an officer from Ombudsman Tasmania said their office was "aware of the backlog of requests with the Department for Education, Children and Young People (the department) and concerned by the situation".

"Ombudsman Tasmania staff have been regularly meeting with the department to discuss concerns about the backlog," the officer wrote.

They said the department's "backlog reduction strategies" had "not yet achieved significant progress and the situation is being actively monitored".

The officer also said they were "aware of some applications such as those of your client that have been waiting 18 plus months".

Sam Morgan alleges she was physically abused while a high school student in Tasmania. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Department 'committed to reducing the wait time'

A spokesperson for the Department for Education, Children and Young People said the department was "committed to reducing the wait time to fulfil RTI requests".

"Changes implemented this year, including additional and more senior resources, are expected to further address processing timeframes," they said.

"We will continue to actively engage with applicants or their advocates to identify and prioritise the critical information they need."

Justice Minister Guy Barnett, who has overall responsibility for Tasmania's RTI laws, was also contacted for comment.

Tasmania's child sexual abuse commission of inquiry made recommendations to improve access to records, which are still "in progress" according to the government's latest report on implementation. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

An independent review of Tasmania's Right to Information framework last year found there had been a "rapid growth in volume of applications for access to personal information".

The authors, RTI expert Rick Snell and human rights lawyer Tim McCormack, wrote in their report that they considered the formal RTI application process was "ill-suited for handling requests to access personal information".

They recommended a new system that would protect privacy while letting individuals access their own information.

The Commission of Inquiry into the Tasmanian Government's Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in Institutional Settings also made recommendations aimed at streamlining the process for victim-survivors.

These recommendations were listed as being "in progress" in the government's most recent progress report.

Ms Morgan said she was fortunate to be able to wait the 23 months it took for her records to come through, but it was only the start of the process.

World.title: Workplace dismissal lawsuit rocks top levels of cancer charity
World.content:
A research boss at Queensland's peak cancer charity has alleged its chief executive bullied her, and their workplace relationship became so dysfunctional she was told to not contact him directly, according to a lawsuit.

The lawsuit filed by Sandi Hayes, former director of research at the Cancer Council Queensland, marks the latest upheaval for a charity supporting thousands of patients and raising tens of millions of dollars annually.

Cancer Council Queensland is defending the lawsuit and said an investigation found no wrongdoing by chief executive Matt Gardiner. The defence filings allege Dr Hayes had been hostile and disrespectful in a top-level meeting, and was sacked after her and Mr Gardiner's office vibe deteriorated to the point psychological health was at risk.

Cancer Council helps sufferers through counselling, accommodation, a wig-service and research into areas such as early cancer detection. (Supplied)

Started in 1961, the charity helps cancer patients through counselling, accommodation, a wig service and research into areas such as early cancer detection.

It had in 2025 posted a worsening financial situation, high staff turnover and internal gripes.

While latest accounts are yet to be released, the council has now proclaimed financial performance had surged, and it was providing more services and record research investment.

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail or Signal account.

Wrongful dismissal lawsuit

Mr Gardiner declined interview requests but told the ABC in a statement: "Cancer Council Queensland is becoming increasingly effective, increasingly influential and increasingly capable of creating a future where fewer Queenslanders experience cancer."

Mr Gardiner, who started in February last year, also said: "For more than a year, a small group of former employees have pursued a campaign of damaging rumours, misinformation and unsupported allegations."

The Courier-Mail in October last year first detailed a spate of staff departures and concerns, including one employee in a widespread email complaining of a "shift away from emotional, psychosocial and financial support — the very services that have defined [the organisation's] compassion and impact".

Matt Gardiner is the chief executive of Cancer Council Queensland. (Supplied)

The ABC can reveal further upheaval since.

Among that is Dr Hayes claiming she was wrongfully dismissed in an ongoing Federal Circuit Court lawsuit filed against the council, Mr Gardiner and recently appointed chairman Todd Everitt.

Her filings said she had allegedly levelled complaints against Mr Gardiner, including to board members at the Brisbane Club or over a Microsoft Teams chat.

Former Cancer Council Queensland director of research Sandi Hayes. (Supplied)

That included discussing in April last year Mr Gardiner's communication and alleging "integrity and trust issues including equity issues" about his "relationship" with another person at the organisation.

But the joint defence claimed Dr Hayes's concerns then were about the chief executive's work-style and technical understanding of research, and Dr Hayes's gripes were not a complaint under workplace laws.

Both sides' filings detailed versions of clashes such as an argument during budget planning, or about executive titles.

At one stage, Dr Hayes said a staffer sought approval to opt out of a "Pride Month" computer-screen display due to his strong Christian beliefs. Mr Gardiner rejected the request and, according to the defence, said: "Some people will need to think about whether their personal values align with the organisation's values."

Bullying allegations

Dr Hayes's lawsuit also detailed facing several accusations against herself as matters progressed, such as about her conduct at an August meeting with nine organisation executives.

The defence filings alleged an internal investigation determined Dr Hayes had been hostile and disrespectful then, particularly toward the chief executive, while also criticising "two discreet comments" Mr Gardiner had made.

By October last year, Dr Hayes, who at one stage took temporary leave, had alleged bullying and inappropriate behaviour from the chief executive and the other person at the organisation, her lawsuit claimed.

Dr Hayes has taken action in an ongoing Federal Circuit Court lawsuit. (ABC News: Millie Roberts, Patrick Thomas)

That same month, Dr Hayes was told communications between herself and Mr Gardiner must temporarily be emailed via the human resources chief.

The defence filing stated this was based on Dr Hayes's medical advice, Mr Gardiner had received the same instructions and the no-contact directive would uphold both executives' "psychosocial safety".

Court documents also said a commissioned investigation into Mr Gardiner and the other person at the organisation "did not substantiate" allegations raised. Dr Hayes's lawyers could not obtain a copy of it.

Despite mediation attempts, Dr Hayes was ultimately fired this February. The defence filings alleged this was because Dr Hayes could not work with Mr Gardiner without "giving rise to a health and safety risk".

The organisation and Dr Hayes declined to comment on the lawsuit.

Service questions

The spat contrasts with the council's uplifting public presence; its Facebook page profiles people walking or dancing around athletic tracks for its Relay for Life charity event. Volunteers sell yellow daffodils in another fundraising effort.

The organisation told the ABC service levels had risen: providing 26,575 bed nights last year at accommodation centres, up 8.6 per cent, and financial counselling services for 287 people, up 23 per cent.

It added psychological counselling sessions had been decentralised to reach more people.

The charity told the ABC service levels had risen. (ABC News)

The council also said a recent staff engagement result — which consolidates 12 answers — lifted to a "good" 4.1 out of 5.

But one source with knowledge of the organisation said an internal review in February this year indicated staff satisfaction levels had dropped.

That same month, an employee allegedly emailed others describing trying to alleviate pressure on its psychological counselling service, saying some waiting periods were up eight weeks.

The organisation did not dispute either account.

Cancer costs calculated A report investigating the financial and legal impact of cancer in Victoria has found both patients and carers have significant out-of-pocket costs.

At a town hall meeting last December, then chairman Robert Gregg told that meeting the organisation had needed reform. "Things had to change," he said.

He also argued Mr Gardiner had copped blame for changes previously in train. "Matt's a victim of the journey," he said.

The council said staff turnover had been at 42 per cent in the 2025 financial year, improving to 31 per cent last financial year when it employed 185. That is above typical non-profit organisation turnover rates reported by overseas employment and service agencies of between 19 per cent and 21 per cent.

Cancer Council Queensland lost $4.1 million in financial year 2025, with fundraising slightly down while administration, support services and research expenses rose.

The organisation, above a picture of smiling volunteers holding small teddy bears, in August reported its "strongest" operating result in five years. It has not yet released accounts but said last financial year's profit was $3.24 million.

World.title: ‘Concerning’: Accused flydubai hijacker’s Victorian links under investigation
World.content:
NationalVictoriaAviation ‘Concerning’: Accused flydubai hijacker’s Victorian links under investigation Ashleigh McMillan October 4, 2026 — 10:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ASIO and federal police are investigating the Victorian connections of the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack the aircraft using an axe while flying to Israel. The co-pilot of the aircraft, identified by media as Omani nation Hammam al-Hammami, allegedly brandished an axe towards the lead pilot in a horrifying mid-air clash aboard flydubai’s Flight FZ1073. Loading The attempted attack came close to killing all 174 passengers and crew, according to witness accounts, and was only prevented because passengers seized al-Hammami while two off-duty pilots stabilised the Boeing 737, landing at a regional airport in Saudi Arabia. According to a now-deleted LinkedIn profile publicised by American newsagencies ABC News and CNN, al-Hammami had posted that he studied engineering at a Victorian university.



The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed that the Victorian joint counterterrorism team, which includes ASIO and Victoria Police, were investigating al-Hammami’s links to Australia. Related Article Aviation Flydubai co-pilot allegedly wielded axe in attempted terrorist attack An AFP spokeswoman said a further update would be provided at an appropriate time. A source with knowledge of the inquiry, not authorised to speak on the record, said the suspect was granted a visa to study in Australia in 2014, and was in Melbourne from 2015 to 2017 before leaving. His visa expired in 2019. There was no inference that the visa should not have been granted, the source said. The university al-Hammami included on his LinkedIn profile has been approached for comment.



When asked about the investigation on Sunday morning, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he had not been briefed on al-Hammami’s potential connections to Victoria. “It’s concerning, and I will follow that up as a matter of priority,” he said. “I met with the prime minister last week, and will always continue to work with our law enforcement agencies to keep Victoria safe.” The lead prosecutor in the United Arab Emirates investigation in to the incident, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, confirmed the co-pilot had allegedly attacked the lead pilot inside the ​cockpit with a crash axe that was fitted on board. A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes. “Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted ⁠to carry out a terrorist attack,” the prosecutor general said in a statement carried by the UAE’s state news agency. World.title: Tennessee’s prisons chief to resign after failed execution of Christa Pike
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty Tennessee’s prisons chief to resign after failed execution of Christa Pike Ed White October 4, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Detroit: The head of Tennessee’s prison system was resigning, Governor Bill Lee announced on Saturday (US time), the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator in hospital. Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, would step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership. It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada has stepped down. AP Photo/George Walker IV The governor also announced that former US attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously conducted a review in 2022 after Lee called off a different execution. He found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.



Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review was conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Strada defends execution protocol There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed on Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.



The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believed the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol”. Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said, “it does nothing to help Christa now”. Loading “What happened to her on Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.” Second failed execution since May



Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. Pike was extraordinarily co-operative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. Christa Pike, then aged 19, cries after being sentenced to death in 1996. WBIR-TV via AP In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again. Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.



Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute Some Arizona executions also had problems Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona, when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break. Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.



That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand – at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness. Related Article Updated

Death penalty Christa Pike ‘on a ventilator and unconscious’ after failed execution Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row. World.title: Sydney’s most profitable pokie venues tap millions in discounts under Labor’s nightlife reforms
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWNight-time economy Sydney’s most profitable pokie venues tap millions in discounts under Labor’s nightlife reforms Kayla Olaya October 4, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At 8.30pm on a Thursday at one of the state’s most profitable gaming venues, country artist Craig Woodward sings covers on a stage in the corner of the members’ lounge before dozens of seated audience members. The artists’ stage at Campbelltown Catholic Club is about the size of six gaming machines. The venue has 445. Arts, Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham told the Herald in a September interview: “My view is pokies did kill pub rock.” Matt Willis It’s one of the hundreds of Sydney pokie clubs, hotels and pubs tapping millions in discounts on liquor licensing fees and receiving extra trading hours in exchange for offering live music under Labor’s so-called vibrancy reforms. Critics argue the Minns government is backing powerful commercial interests over the grassroots arts and cultural sectors, following a scathing April assessment that found the push to revive Sydney’s night-time reputation came at a direct cost to those sectors.



Billed as reversing the damage done to the city’s nightlife and live music scene following the 2014 lockout laws, the $150 million reforms, since being enacted in 2023, have cut red tape and enabled councils to designate nightlife areas. But its keystone is the business incentives. Live music and gaming venues can secure an 80 per cent discount on annual liquor licence fees in return for putting on live acts and two extra hours of liquor trading on gig nights, which has led Labor to claim it has quadrupled the number of gigs in the state since the reforms were introduced. Labor has spent $7.3 million since 2021 subsidising the liquor licence fees discount for venues, it revealed in its latest budget estimates response. Flavio Brancaleone Clubs, hotels, small bars, on-premises and wholesale licence holders can become live music venues so long as they host 10 gigs a month, while regional venues must hold 104 annually. Metropolitan venues must have a dedicated live music performance space, while all venues are required to record each gig hosted. Brainchild of Arts, Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham, who in a September interview with this masthead said, “my view is pokies did kill pub rock”, the incentives came under fire in a June live music parliamentary inquiry.



Musician Adam Ventoura said he’d often sing covers shoved into the back corner of “pokies pubs” for $300 because the gigs are guaranteed to pay. “I’ve actually ... played in these places. You’re put in the corner, nobody really cares, and you’re just there … [to] pick up a guitar, and we go and sing for our supper. We prefer to sing our own songs because we have been making our own songs forever, but we’ll go sing Brown-Eyed Girl for somebody because they are paying the money,” Ventoura told the inquiry. Labor has spent $7.3 million since 2021 subsidising the liquor licence fees discount for venues, it revealed in its latest budget estimates response. Under the 2026 Annual Liquor Licence Fee program, it has spent $2.6 million. Data from budget estimates reveal 59 per cent of the 645 venues accessing the live music incentive had gaming machines as of April this year. Hotels comprise the largest share, with 304 venues using the scheme, while 79 clubs do. Under the 2026 Annual Liquor Licence Fee program, hotels saved more than $1.5 million in fees as of April. For clubs, it was nearly $400,000.



Graham’s office said the $7.3 million was foregone revenue from Liquor and Gaming NSW licence fees. Campbelltown Catholic Club’s chief executive Michael Lavorato said the venue had provided free entertainment for decades. The crowd at DJ Buse Sagaga’s performance at an SES Radio event at Disco Pantera in Circular Quay. Audrey Richardson “Ensuring the local community enjoys a vibrant and thriving night-time economy is a fundamental part of the role our club plays,” Lavorato said. “We welcome any government initiatives that help to bolster that effort.” Wentworthville Leagues Club, Canterbury League Club, Dooleys Lidcombe Catholic Club and Dee Why RSL are among the wealthiest clubs accessing the reforms. Meanwhile, live music hubs, including Mary’s Underground and the Divine Playhouse in the CBD, Blah Bar in Lismore, Newtown’s Moshpit and Marrickville’s Lazy Thinking have shut this year.



NSW Greens arts, music and night-time economy spokesperson Cate Faehrmann said the foregone licence fees were another “kick in the guts for struggling arts organisations who have either already closed their doors, or are close to it because the government says there’s not enough money in the budget to support them”. Darlinghurst’s Australian Design Centre – the state’s only dedicated craft and design hub – was forced to shut weeks shy of its 62nd birthday after losing federal funding in 2025 and failing to secure state support to bridge its annual shortfall. A DJ at the Lord Gladstone in Chippendale. Audrey Richardson “Labor likes to talk a big game when it comes to its vibrancy reforms, but the numbers show that most of the venues benefiting from them are wealthy clubs and pubs with poker machines,” Faehrmann said. “It’s outrageous that the government is handing public money to some of the wealthiest gambling venues in the state while independent music and cultural venues fight for survival.”



Graham acknowledged the city had experienced a spate of live music venue closures, adding that without the vibrancy reforms, “there would be less jobs for musicians, less music for fans”. Related Article Live music Teen punks rally to stop beloved Sydney band venue being demolished for a footpath Hotels and clubs overwhelmingly comprise the majority of venues that receive the live music incentive and trade past midnight. Only 16 of 461 venues that trade past midnight are small bars, which don’t allow pokies. After 3am, only one small bar using the incentives trades, but 204 hotels and 83 clubs do. After 5am, it’s 82 clubs and 88 hotels. A spokeswoman for Clubs NSW said club venues had long supported live music, particularly in suburban and regional communities.



“Independent research by Urbis estimates that NSW clubs support approximately 106,100 community and live entertainment activities each year, providing performers with opportunities and communities with accessible local entertainment,” she said. Last month, the government passed a separate new contemporary music bill that also incentivises venues to prioritise local, live music in response to this masthead’s reporting of musicians playing at pokies pubs. Now, venues that regularly host original live music will be tiered as “dedicated”, “significant” or “live music”. “Dedicated” and “significant” venues will be eligible for programs, extended trading hours or government grants. “Live music” venues will still be able to access the vibrancy reforms. “The problem was you couldn’t tell the difference between a pokie venue and a music venue or a venue that was just selling alcohol. They were all treated the same when liquor and gaming looked at it,” Graham said. “The lockouts killed a wave of electronic music coming through small clubs, and now we’re using the liquor and planning system, and now the music bill, to turn that around and actually reward music venues.”

World.title: 30 years ago, Kerry Packer told me you could buy a title. Here’s the proof he was wrong
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion 30 years ago, Kerry Packer told me you could buy a title. Here’s the proof he was wrong Brad Fittler League columnist October 4, 2026 — 9:00am

October 4, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first time I met Kerry Packer was midway through 1995, smack bang in the middle of the Super League war at his office in the middle of the city. Phil Gould was coaching at the Roosters at this point and I was weighing up whether to join him at the club or link with Manly. Kerry was selling the red, white and blue to me and asked me a question I often come back to more than three decades later. “So, Fittler, how do you think you win a grand final?”



I immediately drew on what I knew – the premiership Gus had steered Penrith to in 1991 when I was just 19 and part of a crew of local juniors that included Greg Alexander, Mark Geyer, Brad Izzard and John Cartwright. Along with the born-and-bred westies, we had Steve Carter who had played juniors and went to school in the area after growing up on the Central Coast, winger Paul Smith came to us the same way and our club icon Royce Simmons from Gooloogong in country NSW. Rooster booster: Brad Fittler in his first season with the club in 1996. Tim Clayton “Kerry,” I said (or I might have called him Mr Packer given I was still only 23), “you’ve got to grow your premiership side from within.” He then gave a very Kerry Packer response.



“You can also buy one.” It’s interesting to think back over that conversation around both the way the Roosters have ebbed and flowed with their approach to juniors and development, and rugby league in general. Benaiah Ioelu, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong have come through the Roosters ranks together. James Brickwood Nick Politis, Trent Robinson and the Tricolours have focused heavily on pathway investment and their Roosters Academy since touring Barcelona’s world-famous facilities in 2020. Siua Wong, Salesi Foketi, Rob Toia and Benaiah Ioelu have all come through that Academy, with plenty more first-graders on their way in the future.



Billy Smith, Victor Radley and Hugo Savala are local juniors while the Butcher brothers jumped across Anzac Parade as teenagers. Daniel Tupou, Sam Walker, Naufahu Whyte and Lindsay Collins are all representative stars who haven’t played at any other club, and Mark Nawaqanitawase was a calculated signing gamble from rugby where the Roosters have struck gold. Make them an offer they can’t refuse: The Kerry Packer premiership mantra. Fairfax Media Daly Cherry-Evans, Reece Robson, Spencer Leniu and to a lesser extent, James Tedesco and Angus Crichton – they fit Kerry Packer’s bill of the marquee superstar. And make no mistake, when Nick Politis sets his sights on a player he loves and wants, he will sign him. Newcastle’s own transformation and prioritisation of their juniors throughout the Hunter and right up the NSW North Coast is a great example of “bred not bought” philosophy that goes a lot further in modern rugby league.



Penrith are the greatest example of all of course, their juniors are so prolific you can find their players right across the NRL. Related Article NRL grand final ‘If he wants you, that’s it’: Nick Politis and the secret to his success at the Roosters The Roosters have had a reputation at different times as a transit lounge, and there’s been times when that’s been deserved, when the club has lost its way from the values it was built on. But when you think about the calibre of players that have left in the past few years – Joey Manu, Joseph Suaalii, Jared Waerea-Hargreaves, Luke Keary, Siosiua Taukeiaho, Sitili Tupouniua – and how they have replaced them, the club’s culture speaks for itself. The Roosters foundations have endured since 1908 and ever since I walked through the club’s doors almost 90 years later, the mentality Phil Gould always drilled into us as players was that we had to be fittest players in the competition and its hardest workers.



We always knew we lived in a glamorous, beautiful part of town. How could you not? Bondi Beach is the best place in the world to live. But we knew that was an absolute privilege too, and it had to be balanced with hard work. Guys like Luke Ricketson and Anthony Minichiello, among so many others, they knew this and they lived it. That’s where the Roosters have found such a rich vein of success, and you can see it in the way Trent Robinson’s side plays too. The Dolphins went with them in the grand final qualifier for 20 physical minutes before the Roosters’ physicality and defence prevailed. The Tricolours can win a grand final with their contact, aggression and physicality.



But this is where they can drive their fans up the wall too. Because they fly into tackles and contact, they can overdo things. Their enforcers can give away cheap penalties and give the opposition a chance. At the same time, when I think about Kerry Packer’s question all those years ago – how do you win a grand final? – I do think of moments and motivation. Local junior Billy Smith knows what a win will do for the Roosters community. Getty Images For the Roosters, the horrific events at Bondi Beach last year haven’t been forgotten – the club and players have always been embedded in the eastern suburbs community. And when a game is there to be won or lost in a single second or two, it’s funny how a grand final can swing.



The most famous single moment from a decider that I played in was Scott Sattler’s immortal chase of Todd Byrne in 2003. But a happier one for the Roosters and I, even if it left me seeing stars at the time, was when Warriors prop Richard Villasanti smashed me halfway into Mad Monday with 20 minutes to play a year earlier. We held a narrow 12-8 lead at that point and the game was in the balance. Until Villasanti came hunting me and hit me in the head after I had a kick charged down. I was bloodied and bandaged up. Poor old Richard was just bashed up by my forwards for his sins.

World.title: P-plater in horror Newcastle Knights car crash previously lost his licence
World.content:
The 18-year-old P-plate driver who ploughed into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters on Saturday and injured 10 people, some critically, previously had his driving licence suspended. Court records show Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe was suspended in February and appealed against the suspension in April, but was unsuccessful. Loading Samarasinghe was arrested at the crash site and taken for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. He was later charged with three counts each of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and causing bodily harm by misconduct in charge of a motor vehicle. His licence has again been suspended. Samarasinghe was refused bail and will face court on Sunday.



Of the 10 people injured as they lined a Newcastle street to wave off the Knights to the NRL grand final, the most serious is a five-year-old girl who was in a serious but stable condition in John Hunter Hospital on Sunday morning. A 67-year-old patient is also in a serious but stable condition, and four others, including a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old girl, were stable. Four of those injured were discharged on Saturday, including three men in their 20s and a 63-year-old woman. The crash scene. TNV One of the injured, Chris Clancy, said the car appeared to speed up as it went through a roundabout, and then lost control on the wet road. “No-one had time to move,” he said. “I thought I was going to die, it happened so fast.” Fans at the crash site rushed to provide first aid as emergency crews rushed to the scene and word of the collision spread through the tens of thousands of excited fans waiting for a glimpse of their team. The team’s bus, which had not yet departed when the crash occurred, was rerouted, and players were informed.



“They were shocked, it was a very sombre bus ride,” said one of those aboard. “Our fans mean everything to us. For that to happen; horrible.” The car that Samarasinghe was allegedly driving has been seized to undergo forensic examination. The two male passengers in the vehicle at the time of the crash, aged 18 and 19, were both uninjured. Scenes at Wallsend, Newcastle, after a car crashed into a crowd of Knights supporters. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said officers were investigating reports the P-plater had been “driving erratically” before he lost control of the vehicle. Footage posted to social media depicted the BMW with personalised number plates careering around the roundabout moments before the crash, as shocked onlookers were heard screaming.



Onlookers expressed anger towards the occupants of the car after the crash, police said. “We had to get the three of them out of there because the crowd did turn on them,” Waddell said. Witness Dean Liddell said he could hear the vehicle coming towards the crowd and then “all hell broke loose”. “I watched the little girl get dragged underneath the car. Seeing the whole scene unfold, it took me 10 minutes until I could say anything to anyone,” Liddell said. He said the crowd grabbed the driver from the wreck and a scuffle began before police intervened. “If the copper wasn’t there, the driver would have had massive injuries as well,” he said.



The accident came after a joyous week in Newcastle, where the city threw its support behind a team that has not won a premiership for 25 years. The Knights had been expected to be inspired by the joy of their supporters during the grand final, but will now also feel the weight of the tragedy when they take the field. Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on social media that players’ “hearts are with everyone affected” by the crash. “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” Longtime league watchers say no other grand final has been played under such a shadow. “It’s heartbreaking for the whole rugby league community, not just in Newcastle,” said Brad Fittler, a former Roosters captain and a member of the league hall of fame. “We’ve never seen anything like this ahead of a grand final and it puts everything in perspective.” Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’Landys said he was deeply saddened by the crash. When asked whether it would affect plans for Sunday night’s game, he said “we’re just concerned about the victims at the moment.”



Paramedics prepare to transport the injured by helicopter. Sitthixay Ditthavong Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris said on Nine’s Today program on Sunday morning that the community had rallied behind the victims of the crash, and staff at the John Hunter Hospital had come in to work on their days off given the number of injuries. “The community has gone through the complete and utter full gamut of emotions over the past seven days,” Morris said. “To what happen last Sunday [and] the complete and utter highs. It’s been nothing but a joyous, fun week. “And then yesterday we had our hearts ripped out.”



The crash scene. TNV The injured Clancy said a police vehicle was stationed near the crash site and responded quickly. He said the car came at the group of supporters too fast for them to jump out of the way. He was hit by the front of the vehicle. Fans urged the Knights to press forward and do their best on Sunday night. “It will be tough for them, but do what they’ve always done and do it for the town,” said Clancy. “I believe they can win. Regardless of whether they win or lose, they’ve done the town proud.” Loading

NationalVictoriaAviation ‘Concerning’: Accused flydubai hijacker’s Victorian links under investigation Ashleigh McMillan October 4, 2026 — 10:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

ASIO and federal police are investigating the Victorian connections of the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack the aircraft using an axe while flying to Israel. The co-pilot of the aircraft, identified by media as Omani nation Hammam al-Hammami, allegedly brandished an axe towards the lead pilot in a horrifying mid-air clash aboard flydubai’s Flight FZ1073. Loading The attempted attack came close to killing all 174 passengers and crew, according to witness accounts, and was only prevented because passengers seized al-Hammami while two off-duty pilots stabilised the Boeing 737, landing at a regional airport in Saudi Arabia. According to a now-deleted LinkedIn profile publicised by American newsagencies ABC News and CNN, al-Hammami had posted that he studied engineering at a Victorian university.



The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed that the Victorian joint counterterrorism team, which includes ASIO and Victoria Police, were investigating al-Hammami’s links to Australia. Related Article Aviation Flydubai co-pilot allegedly wielded axe in attempted terrorist attack An AFP spokeswoman said a further update would be provided at an appropriate time. A source with knowledge of the inquiry, not authorised to speak on the record, said the suspect was granted a visa to study in Australia in 2014, and was in Melbourne from 2015 to 2017 before leaving. His visa expired in 2019. There was no inference that the visa should not have been granted, the source said. The university al-Hammami included on his LinkedIn profile has been approached for comment.



When asked about the investigation on Sunday morning, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he had not been briefed on al-Hammami’s potential connections to Victoria. “It’s concerning, and I will follow that up as a matter of priority,” he said. “I met with the prime minister last week, and will always continue to work with our law enforcement agencies to keep Victoria safe.” The lead prosecutor in the United Arab Emirates investigation in to the incident, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, confirmed the co-pilot had allegedly attacked the lead pilot inside the ​cockpit with a crash axe that was fitted on board. A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes. “Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted ⁠to carry out a terrorist attack,” the prosecutor general said in a statement carried by the UAE’s state news agency. World.title: Tennessee’s prisons chief to resign after failed execution of Christa Pike
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty Tennessee’s prisons chief to resign after failed execution of Christa Pike Ed White October 4, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Detroit: The head of Tennessee’s prison system was resigning, Governor Bill Lee announced on Saturday (US time), the first major staff shake-up since Christa Pike’s failed execution left her unconscious and on a ventilator in hospital. Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, would step down this month, Lee said. Some of the governor’s fellow Republicans and other elected officials had been urging a change in leadership. It was the second time since May that Tennessee has not been able to execute a prisoner who was seemingly moments away from death. Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner Frank Strada has stepped down. AP Photo/George Walker IV The governor also announced that former US attorney Ed Stanton would lead a review of what happened in Pike’s death chamber. Stanton previously conducted a review in 2022 after Lee called off a different execution. He found in that case that Tennessee had not complied with its own lethal injection process.



Strada said in a statement that resigning was “in the best interest of Tennesseans” while Stanton’s review was conducted. The state failed to execute Pike despite administering two doses of a lethal drug, pentobarbital. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty ‘There is no precedent’: Tennessee fails to execute woman after two doses of lethal injection Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Strada defends execution protocol There was no immediate response from Pike’s lawyers for an update on her condition at a hospital. They had disclosed on Friday that she was on a ventilator and unconscious in the hours following the execution attempt and that hospital staff were trying to clear the two doses of pentobarbital.



The shocking failure has left both sides of the death penalty debate demanding answers. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted any new executions. Strada said he believed the state “carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol”. Pike’s legal team welcomed Strada’s departure but said, “it does nothing to help Christa now”. Loading “What happened to her on Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” the four-lawyer team said. “We hope the governor’s call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system.” Second failed execution since May



Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. Pike was extraordinarily co-operative with the execution team, even instructing them to “please try here, please try here” as they tried to insert lines, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. Christa Pike, then aged 19, cries after being sentenced to death in 1996. WBIR-TV via AP In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Tony Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm but couldn’t get a secondary IV line. The governor ordered officials to wait at least a year before trying to execute him again. Strada took over the Correction Department in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of the Arizona Department of Corrections. In late 2024, he announced that Tennessee was changing its lethal injection protocol and would use only pentobarbital.



Four people have been executed in Tennessee since 2025, according to the Correction Department. Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute Some Arizona executions also had problems Court filings show that Strada’s job included overseeing executions in Arizona, when they resumed in 2022 following an eight-year break. Clarence Dixon was the first that year. The medical team had trouble finding a vein to administer the lethal drugs and finally made an incision in his groin area. The process took about 25 minutes.



That same year in Arizona, medical staff preparing Frank Atwood for execution initially could not locate a vein in his right arm but inserted the IV in his right hand – at Atwood’s suggestion, said Henry Brean, an Arizona Daily Star reporter who was a witness. Related Article Updated

Death penalty Christa Pike ‘on a ventilator and unconscious’ after failed execution Strada announced Murray Hooper’s execution by lethal injection, the third in 2022. There was an unsuccessful attempt to insert an IV line in his right arm. The IV in Hooper’s leg was inserted into his femoral artery. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee, his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known,” said Kit Thomas, an attorney who has represented people on Tennessee’s death row.
