World.title: Sydney’s most profitable pokie venues tap millions in discounts under Labor’s nightlife reforms
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWNight-time economy Sydney’s most profitable pokie venues tap millions in discounts under Labor’s nightlife reforms Kayla Olaya October 4, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At 8.30pm on a Thursday at one of the state’s most profitable gaming venues, country artist Craig Woodward sings covers on a stage in the corner of the members’ lounge before dozens of seated audience members. The artists’ stage at Campbelltown Catholic Club is about the size of six gaming machines. The venue has 445. Arts, Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham told the Herald in a September interview: “My view is pokies did kill pub rock.” Matt Willis It’s one of the hundreds of Sydney pokie clubs, hotels and pubs tapping millions in discounts on liquor licensing fees and receiving extra trading hours in exchange for offering live music under Labor’s so-called vibrancy reforms. Critics argue the Minns government is backing powerful commercial interests over the grassroots arts and cultural sectors, following a scathing April assessment that found the push to revive Sydney’s night-time reputation came at a direct cost to those sectors.



Billed as reversing the damage done to the city’s nightlife and live music scene following the 2014 lockout laws, the $150 million reforms, since being enacted in 2023, have cut red tape and enabled councils to designate nightlife areas. But its keystone is the business incentives. Live music and gaming venues can secure an 80 per cent discount on annual liquor licence fees in return for putting on live acts and two extra hours of liquor trading on gig nights, which has led Labor to claim it has quadrupled the number of gigs in the state since the reforms were introduced. Labor has spent $7.3 million since 2021 subsidising the liquor licence fees discount for venues, it revealed in its latest budget estimates response. Flavio Brancaleone Clubs, hotels, small bars, on-premises and wholesale licence holders can become live music venues so long as they host 10 gigs a month, while regional venues must hold 104 annually. Metropolitan venues must have a dedicated live music performance space, while all venues are required to record each gig hosted. Brainchild of Arts, Music and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham, who in a September interview with this masthead said, “my view is pokies did kill pub rock”, the incentives came under fire in a June live music parliamentary inquiry.



Musician Adam Ventoura said he’d often sing covers shoved into the back corner of “pokies pubs” for $300 because the gigs are guaranteed to pay. “I’ve actually ... played in these places. You’re put in the corner, nobody really cares, and you’re just there … [to] pick up a guitar, and we go and sing for our supper. We prefer to sing our own songs because we have been making our own songs forever, but we’ll go sing Brown-Eyed Girl for somebody because they are paying the money,” Ventoura told the inquiry. Labor has spent $7.3 million since 2021 subsidising the liquor licence fees discount for venues, it revealed in its latest budget estimates response. Under the 2026 Annual Liquor Licence Fee program, it has spent $2.6 million. Data from budget estimates reveal 59 per cent of the 645 venues accessing the live music incentive had gaming machines as of April this year. Hotels comprise the largest share, with 304 venues using the scheme, while 79 clubs do. Under the 2026 Annual Liquor Licence Fee program, hotels saved more than $1.5 million in fees as of April. For clubs, it was nearly $400,000.



Graham’s office said the $7.3 million was foregone revenue from Liquor and Gaming NSW licence fees. Campbelltown Catholic Club’s chief executive Michael Lavorato said the venue had provided free entertainment for decades. The crowd at DJ Buse Sagaga’s performance at an SES Radio event at Disco Pantera in Circular Quay. Audrey Richardson “Ensuring the local community enjoys a vibrant and thriving night-time economy is a fundamental part of the role our club plays,” Lavorato said. “We welcome any government initiatives that help to bolster that effort.” Wentworthville Leagues Club, Canterbury League Club, Dooleys Lidcombe Catholic Club and Dee Why RSL are among the wealthiest clubs accessing the reforms. Meanwhile, live music hubs, including Mary’s Underground and the Divine Playhouse in the CBD, Blah Bar in Lismore, Newtown’s Moshpit and Marrickville’s Lazy Thinking have shut this year.



NSW Greens arts, music and night-time economy spokesperson Cate Faehrmann said the foregone licence fees were another “kick in the guts for struggling arts organisations who have either already closed their doors, or are close to it because the government says there’s not enough money in the budget to support them”. Darlinghurst’s Australian Design Centre – the state’s only dedicated craft and design hub – was forced to shut weeks shy of its 62nd birthday after losing federal funding in 2025 and failing to secure state support to bridge its annual shortfall. A DJ at the Lord Gladstone in Chippendale. Audrey Richardson “Labor likes to talk a big game when it comes to its vibrancy reforms, but the numbers show that most of the venues benefiting from them are wealthy clubs and pubs with poker machines,” Faehrmann said. “It’s outrageous that the government is handing public money to some of the wealthiest gambling venues in the state while independent music and cultural venues fight for survival.”



Graham acknowledged the city had experienced a spate of live music venue closures, adding that without the vibrancy reforms, “there would be less jobs for musicians, less music for fans”. Related Article Live music Teen punks rally to stop beloved Sydney band venue being demolished for a footpath Hotels and clubs overwhelmingly comprise the majority of venues that receive the live music incentive and trade past midnight. Only 16 of 461 venues that trade past midnight are small bars, which don’t allow pokies. After 3am, only one small bar using the incentives trades, but 204 hotels and 83 clubs do. After 5am, it’s 82 clubs and 88 hotels. A spokeswoman for Clubs NSW said club venues had long supported live music, particularly in suburban and regional communities.



“Independent research by Urbis estimates that NSW clubs support approximately 106,100 community and live entertainment activities each year, providing performers with opportunities and communities with accessible local entertainment,” she said. Last month, the government passed a separate new contemporary music bill that also incentivises venues to prioritise local, live music in response to this masthead’s reporting of musicians playing at pokies pubs. Now, venues that regularly host original live music will be tiered as “dedicated”, “significant” or “live music”. “Dedicated” and “significant” venues will be eligible for programs, extended trading hours or government grants. “Live music” venues will still be able to access the vibrancy reforms. “The problem was you couldn’t tell the difference between a pokie venue and a music venue or a venue that was just selling alcohol. They were all treated the same when liquor and gaming looked at it,” Graham said. “The lockouts killed a wave of electronic music coming through small clubs, and now we’re using the liquor and planning system, and now the music bill, to turn that around and actually reward music venues.”

World.title: 30 years ago, Kerry Packer told me you could buy a title. Here’s the proof he was wrong
World.content:
SportNRLNRL grand final Opinion 30 years ago, Kerry Packer told me you could buy a title. Here’s the proof he was wrong Brad Fittler League columnist October 4, 2026 — 9:00am

October 4, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The first time I met Kerry Packer was midway through 1995, smack bang in the middle of the Super League war at his office in the middle of the city. Phil Gould was coaching at the Roosters at this point and I was weighing up whether to join him at the club or link with Manly. Kerry was selling the red, white and blue to me and asked me a question I often come back to more than three decades later. “So, Fittler, how do you think you win a grand final?”



I immediately drew on what I knew – the premiership Gus had steered Penrith to in 1991 when I was just 19 and part of a crew of local juniors that included Greg Alexander, Mark Geyer, Brad Izzard and John Cartwright. Along with the born-and-bred westies, we had Steve Carter who had played juniors and went to school in the area after growing up on the Central Coast, winger Paul Smith came to us the same way and our club icon Royce Simmons from Gooloogong in country NSW. Rooster booster: Brad Fittler in his first season with the club in 1996. Tim Clayton “Kerry,” I said (or I might have called him Mr Packer given I was still only 23), “you’ve got to grow your premiership side from within.” He then gave a very Kerry Packer response.



“You can also buy one.” It’s interesting to think back over that conversation around both the way the Roosters have ebbed and flowed with their approach to juniors and development, and rugby league in general. Benaiah Ioelu, Robert Toia, Salesi Foketi and Siua Wong have come through the Roosters ranks together. James Brickwood Nick Politis, Trent Robinson and the Tricolours have focused heavily on pathway investment and their Roosters Academy since touring Barcelona’s world-famous facilities in 2020. Siua Wong, Salesi Foketi, Rob Toia and Benaiah Ioelu have all come through that Academy, with plenty more first-graders on their way in the future.



Billy Smith, Victor Radley and Hugo Savala are local juniors while the Butcher brothers jumped across Anzac Parade as teenagers. Daniel Tupou, Sam Walker, Naufahu Whyte and Lindsay Collins are all representative stars who haven’t played at any other club, and Mark Nawaqanitawase was a calculated signing gamble from rugby where the Roosters have struck gold. Make them an offer they can’t refuse: The Kerry Packer premiership mantra. Fairfax Media Daly Cherry-Evans, Reece Robson, Spencer Leniu and to a lesser extent, James Tedesco and Angus Crichton – they fit Kerry Packer’s bill of the marquee superstar. And make no mistake, when Nick Politis sets his sights on a player he loves and wants, he will sign him. Newcastle’s own transformation and prioritisation of their juniors throughout the Hunter and right up the NSW North Coast is a great example of “bred not bought” philosophy that goes a lot further in modern rugby league.



Penrith are the greatest example of all of course, their juniors are so prolific you can find their players right across the NRL. Related Article NRL grand final ‘If he wants you, that’s it’: Nick Politis and the secret to his success at the Roosters The Roosters have had a reputation at different times as a transit lounge, and there’s been times when that’s been deserved, when the club has lost its way from the values it was built on. But when you think about the calibre of players that have left in the past few years – Joey Manu, Joseph Suaalii, Jared Waerea-Hargreaves, Luke Keary, Siosiua Taukeiaho, Sitili Tupouniua – and how they have replaced them, the club’s culture speaks for itself. The Roosters foundations have endured since 1908 and ever since I walked through the club’s doors almost 90 years later, the mentality Phil Gould always drilled into us as players was that we had to be fittest players in the competition and its hardest workers.



We always knew we lived in a glamorous, beautiful part of town. How could you not? Bondi Beach is the best place in the world to live. But we knew that was an absolute privilege too, and it had to be balanced with hard work. Guys like Luke Ricketson and Anthony Minichiello, among so many others, they knew this and they lived it. That’s where the Roosters have found such a rich vein of success, and you can see it in the way Trent Robinson’s side plays too. The Dolphins went with them in the grand final qualifier for 20 physical minutes before the Roosters’ physicality and defence prevailed. The Tricolours can win a grand final with their contact, aggression and physicality.



But this is where they can drive their fans up the wall too. Because they fly into tackles and contact, they can overdo things. Their enforcers can give away cheap penalties and give the opposition a chance. At the same time, when I think about Kerry Packer’s question all those years ago – how do you win a grand final? – I do think of moments and motivation. Local junior Billy Smith knows what a win will do for the Roosters community. Getty Images For the Roosters, the horrific events at Bondi Beach last year haven’t been forgotten – the club and players have always been embedded in the eastern suburbs community. And when a game is there to be won or lost in a single second or two, it’s funny how a grand final can swing.



The most famous single moment from a decider that I played in was Scott Sattler’s immortal chase of Todd Byrne in 2003. But a happier one for the Roosters and I, even if it left me seeing stars at the time, was when Warriors prop Richard Villasanti smashed me halfway into Mad Monday with 20 minutes to play a year earlier. We held a narrow 12-8 lead at that point and the game was in the balance. Until Villasanti came hunting me and hit me in the head after I had a kick charged down. I was bloodied and bandaged up. Poor old Richard was just bashed up by my forwards for his sins.

World.title: P-plater in horror Newcastle Knights car crash previously lost his licence
World.content:
The 18-year-old P-plate driver who ploughed into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters on Saturday and injured 10 people, some critically, previously had his driving licence suspended. Court records show Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe was suspended in February and appealed against the suspension in April, but was unsuccessful. Loading Samarasinghe was arrested at the crash site and taken for mandatory drug and alcohol testing. He was later charged with three counts each of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and causing bodily harm by misconduct in charge of a motor vehicle. His licence has again been suspended. Samarasinghe was refused bail and will face court on Sunday.



Of the 10 people injured as they lined a Newcastle street to wave off the Knights to the NRL grand final, the most serious is a five-year-old girl who was in a serious but stable condition in John Hunter Hospital on Sunday morning. A 67-year-old patient is also in a serious but stable condition, and four others, including a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old girl, were stable. Four of those injured were discharged on Saturday, including three men in their 20s and a 63-year-old woman. The crash scene. TNV One of the injured, Chris Clancy, said the car appeared to speed up as it went through a roundabout, and then lost control on the wet road. “No-one had time to move,” he said. “I thought I was going to die, it happened so fast.” Fans at the crash site rushed to provide first aid as emergency crews rushed to the scene and word of the collision spread through the tens of thousands of excited fans waiting for a glimpse of their team. The team’s bus, which had not yet departed when the crash occurred, was rerouted, and players were informed.



“They were shocked, it was a very sombre bus ride,” said one of those aboard. “Our fans mean everything to us. For that to happen; horrible.” The car that Samarasinghe was allegedly driving has been seized to undergo forensic examination. The two male passengers in the vehicle at the time of the crash, aged 18 and 19, were both uninjured. Scenes at Wallsend, Newcastle, after a car crashed into a crowd of Knights supporters. NSW Police Assistant Commissioner David Waddell said officers were investigating reports the P-plater had been “driving erratically” before he lost control of the vehicle. Footage posted to social media depicted the BMW with personalised number plates careering around the roundabout moments before the crash, as shocked onlookers were heard screaming.



Onlookers expressed anger towards the occupants of the car after the crash, police said. “We had to get the three of them out of there because the crowd did turn on them,” Waddell said. Witness Dean Liddell said he could hear the vehicle coming towards the crowd and then “all hell broke loose”. “I watched the little girl get dragged underneath the car. Seeing the whole scene unfold, it took me 10 minutes until I could say anything to anyone,” Liddell said. He said the crowd grabbed the driver from the wreck and a scuffle began before police intervened. “If the copper wasn’t there, the driver would have had massive injuries as well,” he said.



The accident came after a joyous week in Newcastle, where the city threw its support behind a team that has not won a premiership for 25 years. The Knights had been expected to be inspired by the joy of their supporters during the grand final, but will now also feel the weight of the tragedy when they take the field. Newcastle Knights captain Kalyn Ponga said on social media that players’ “hearts are with everyone affected” by the crash. “We’re thinking of you, your families and everyone in our Newcastle community.” Longtime league watchers say no other grand final has been played under such a shadow. “It’s heartbreaking for the whole rugby league community, not just in Newcastle,” said Brad Fittler, a former Roosters captain and a member of the league hall of fame. “We’ve never seen anything like this ahead of a grand final and it puts everything in perspective.” Australian Rugby League Commission executive chairman Peter V’Landys said he was deeply saddened by the crash. When asked whether it would affect plans for Sunday night’s game, he said “we’re just concerned about the victims at the moment.”



Paramedics prepare to transport the injured by helicopter. Sitthixay Ditthavong Newcastle Lord Mayor Gavin Morris said on Nine’s Today program on Sunday morning that the community had rallied behind the victims of the crash, and staff at the John Hunter Hospital had come in to work on their days off given the number of injuries. “The community has gone through the complete and utter full gamut of emotions over the past seven days,” Morris said. “To what happen last Sunday [and] the complete and utter highs. It’s been nothing but a joyous, fun week. “And then yesterday we had our hearts ripped out.”



The crash scene. TNV The injured Clancy said a police vehicle was stationed near the crash site and responded quickly. He said the car came at the group of supporters too fast for them to jump out of the way. He was hit by the front of the vehicle. Fans urged the Knights to press forward and do their best on Sunday night. “It will be tough for them, but do what they’ve always done and do it for the town,” said Clancy. “I believe they can win. Regardless of whether they win or lose, they’ve done the town proud.” Loading

World.title: National promises $1.75b to build Mill Road as part of  Roads of National Significance
World.content:
National is promising to start construction on Mill Road, one of its Roads of National Significance, if it leads the next government.

It will allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin in late 2028, and look to progress route protection on Stages Two and Three by allocating $100 million.

National's Transport Spokesperson Chris Bishop said "after years of debate and discussion about Mill Road, National in government is getting on with it."

Mill Road was one of the projects relegated to the slow lane in July as part of a "phased approach" to the Roads of National Significance (RONS) delivery, after questions over cost and implementation saw the government "recalibrate people's expectations".

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406182202112

Making the announcement on Auckland's Redoubt Road alongside the National leader Christopher Luxon on Sunday, Bishop said Mill Road was an important Road of National Significance that is part of the Government's Major Transport Projects Pipeline, included in the Auckland City Deal as well as NZTA's Auckland Strategic Motorway Plan.

Stage One was between Manukau and Alfriston, while Stages Two and Three were between Alfriston and Drury.

Bishop said South Auckland was one of the fastest growing parts of the country.

"Drury is at the centre of that growth, but the roading network hasn't kept up."

He said people travelling between Drury, Papakura and Manukau are funnelled onto an "already congested Southern Motorway," while roads like Redoubt Road and the existing Mill Road were built for a "semi-rural community, not tens of thousands of new households."

Bishop said Mill Road would "change that", and once completed, would be a new four-lane, 21.5km corridor running alongside State Highway 1 from Manukau to Drury, "crushing congestion, improving safety, and unlocking land for the homes and jobs the region needs."

The New Zealand Transport Agency estimated Stage One of Mill Road would reduce congestion by 30 percent on that corridor, Bishop added, as well as cut journey times by 25 percent and result in the reduction of more 60 percent of deaths and serious injuries.

Bishop said National would allocate $1.75 billion in Budget 2028 so construction can begin "in the late-2028 construction season."

Currently, NZTA was completing the design work and taking the project through the fast-track process to secure the consents it needs, he explained.

"The commitment to Mill Road builds on the strong progress National has made on transport across Auckland over the last three years.

World.title: Man charged after air-gun shooting in Hamilton
World.content:
An 18-year-old man is facing charges of wounding with reckless disregard, unlawful possession of ammunition and possession of an offensive weapon after a person was shot with an air gun in Hamilton on Saturday.

Police received reports of an air gun being fired at a member of the public at a bus stop on Masters Avenue, near Hillcrest Park, just before 3pm.

The person suffered moderate injuries and required medical treatment.

About 1am on Sunday, firearms, ammunition and other weapons were discovered at a Hamilton property visited by the Armed Offenders Squad, CIB and frontline staff.

Police are working with community members who may have witnessed the incident, and want to thank members of the public who helped with inquiries, Senior Sergeant Mark Pettigrew said.

World.title: Election signage deliberately set on fire, National MP Carlos Cheung says
World.content:
National's Mt Roskill MP says his election signage has been deliberately set on fire, after already being vandalised.

"This is not harmless behaviour. It is dangerous, reckless and completely unacceptable," Cheung wrote on social media, sharing a picture of the signage on fire.

"Deliberately setting fire to signage can put people, property and the wider community at serious risk.

"You may disagree with our views. You may disagree with our candidates. But there is absolutely no place for vandalism, intimidation or criminal behaviour in our democracy," he said.

The incident had been reported to police, Cheung added. His team would assist authorities in any way possible with their investigation, he said.

"And let me be clear: this behaviour will not stop people from voting. If anything, it will strengthen the resolve of our supporters to come out, participate and stand up against this kind of behaviour.

World.title: Tribunal allows deportation appeal by Samoan man convicted of child sex abuse
World.content:
This story discusses graphic details of sexual offending and may be upsetting for some readers.

A Samoan man who sexually abused a child over several years has avoided deportation after a tribunal ruled that removing him from New Zealand would be unjustly harsh and likely to end his marriage.

The man, in his mid-20s, became liable for deportation after pleading guilty to representative charges of performing an indecent act on a child under 12 and performing an indecent act on a young person under 16.

In 2023, he was sentenced to 10 months' home detention and 12 months' supervision for the offending, which occurred between 2018 and 2021.

Despite finding the man's offending was serious and involved a breach of trust against a vulnerable child, the Immigration and Protection Tribunal allowed his appeal against deportation, concluding there were exceptional humanitarian circumstances in his case.

Those circumstances included his decade-long residence in New Zealand, the fact he had spent all of his adult life here, and the likely impact deportation would have on his marriage to a New Zealand citizen.

Marriage and rehabilitation

The man arrived in New Zealand as a teenager. He attended school in Auckland before finding work with a company where he remains employed.

The tribunal heard evidence that he struggled to adjust after arriving in New Zealand. English was not his first language and he had little exposure to life outside his conservative Samoan upbringing.

According to the tribunal's recent decision, the man met his wife in 2019. Their relationship developed and they married in 2021, soon after the offending came to light and before criminal charges were filed.

His wife told the tribunal she had been devastated, angry and confused after learning what he had done, but ultimately chose to support him through his rehabilitation.

The tribunal accepted their relationship was genuine and noted the length of time the couple had been together.

The man's employer, pastor and relatives, all of whom supported his appeal, also gave evidence.

His employer described him as one of the company's most respected staff members and said he had grown into a skilled and valued employee with strong prospects for advancement.

The tribunal heard that the man completed an intensive treatment programme through Safe, a specialist provider for people who have engaged in harmful sexual behaviour.

A counsellor reported the man showed genuine remorse, developed insight into his offending and demonstrated a strong commitment to rehabilitation.

The tribunal also considered sentencing remarks from the District Court, which identified several aggravating features of the offending, including the victim's age, the breach of trust, the length of time the abuse continued and the harm caused to the child.

Why the appeal succeeded

The sentencing judge adopted a starting point of three years' imprisonment before reducing the sentence for factors including the guilty pleas, remorse, rehabilitation prospects and the man's youth at the time of offending.

The man's risk to the public was considered sufficiently low that the judge did not put him on the child sex offender register.

In allowing the appeal, the tribunal found that while the offending was inherently serious, deportation would "most likely end a loving and stable marriage between two young people".

The tribunal accepted that the wife had no practical connection to living in Samoa and would face significant hardship if she relocated there.

It also found the man's ties to New Zealand were particularly strong because he arrived as a teenager and had spent all his adult life in the country.

The decision concluded there were exceptional humanitarian circumstances, that deportation would be unjust or unduly harsh, and that allowing him to remain would not be contrary to the public interest.

The tribunal relied in part on assessments indicating the man presented a low risk of reoffending and noted he had not come to police attention again since the abuse was revealed in 2021.

As a result, the appeal was allowed and his deportation liability was suspended for three years. The suspension was subject to a condition that he not commit further qualifying sexual offences during that period.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Two men jump into river after failing to stop for police
World.content:
Police in the Ōpōtiki area in the Bay of Plenty are appealing for sightings of two men who who failed to stop for officers before jumping in a river.

Duty Inspector Phil Edwards said about 3.45am on Sunday a vehicle ran a red light in Wainui.

"Road spikes were successfully deployed about 10km from Ōpōtiki shortly after 4am, before the vehicle came to a stop down Snell Road, by the Otara River," he said.

"The two occupants have then got out of the vehicle and jumped into the water."

A search and rescue operation was launched, with assistance from the Harbourmaster, Coastguard Ōpōtiki, and a rescue helicopter, but the two men have not been found.

"Police Search and Rescue staff are continuing the search this morning, and are appealing to the public for help," Edwards said.

"If you are one of these males, you know who they are, or you have any other information which may help us locate them, please get in touch. We're also after information about any suspicious behaviour in the area."

Edwards said the priority at this time was ensuring the men were safe.

Urgent information could be passed on via 111, referencing job number P067829874.

Two people in the car had serious injuries, while another had critical injuries, police said.

World.title: Job seeker calls for ban on 'ghost' interviews that harvest data for AI
World.content:
Sitting across from the AI interview agent, Charlie Maclean tried to put her best foot forward, but it was awkward.

"It had specific questions," she said, but it was nothing like connecting with a potential employer face-to-face.

"It would sort of pick up on a key word or something that you've said, [like] 'Hey, that's good experience in project management - tell us more about it'."

Answers were timed, Maclean told RNZ, leaving little room to consider a response.

"You're not really able to take a second to think mid-sentence because it will just assume that you're finished and then cut you off and on to the next bit."

It was a jarring experience, which became more strange after the initially very eager company ghosted her.

Do you know more? Email: mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

Maclean is now sounding the alarm about companies that post prolifically on sites such as LinkedIn, advertising remote roles with attractive salaries.

Charlie Maclean fears she unwittingly handed over her data to a company that used it to train AI. Supplied

After some digging online, she fears the company that sent an AI agent to interview her was simply after her personal data to train artificial intelligence - a potential scam or so-called "ghost" job, a scenario where a company advertises for a role it has no intention of filling.

The experience has prompted Maclean to launch a petition to Parliament explicitly banning such job s.

'Data is king'

Senior lecturer in organisational psychology at Victoria University Ben Walker doesn't have "case-closed" evidence of phantom job listings but feels there is enough online commentary to suggest advertised roles by certain companies were spurious.

Companies under fire in online message threads for suspected data harvesting have not responded to RNZ's requests for comment.

While recruiters RNZ contacted had not come across ghost jobs in New Zealand, they had heard of such practices.

One recruiter, with almost 20 years experience, said companies posting fake jobs to harvest candidate data was a new con for the industry and had been a topic of discussion among colleagues overseas.

Chief executive of Tribe Group recruitment agency Bruce Pilbrow found the scenario plausible, and said it would be an effective way to gather core information.

"There's a lot happening in the AI space and the online space in the sense of harvesting information," he said. "Data is king."

Andrew Lensen, senior lecturer in artificial intelligence at Victoria University. Supplied

Fake job listing or not, Victoria University senior lecturer in artificial intelligence Andrew Lensen said there was growing concern about where personal information ended up.

CVs and cover letters contained potentially valuable data, he said, including a person's name, educational background and even an address.

"It's your career history, it's what you've learned, the skills you have, and we often don't think about it that carefully but that is a lot of information.

"If it is going into any sort of database or system that could be used for things like AI in the future, then I think people are quite rightfully getting more and more concerned about how the data is being used and where it's going."

Rapid recruitment a red flag

In her months-long search for work, Maclean said she came across a handful of companies on LinkedIn - a professional networking platform - advertising remote jobs with inflated salaries that seemed to "go nowhere".

According to Walker, an intense recruitment drive could be a red flag.

"Where it's a company that you've never heard of suddenly doing those sorts of things, it potentially raises a few question marks and alarm bells about whether the jobs are legitimate or whether they may be a cover or some means to another end."

As a global platform, LinkedIn differed greatly from job sites such as SEEK and Trade Me, he said, and in his opinion it had undergone a transformation in recent years: "People talk about the slopification of LinkedIn."

In response to questions from RNZ, a LinkedIn spokesperson said the company was investing in free verifications for jobs, recruiters and company pages, and that every job must be authentic and accurately represented.

Neither SEEK nor Trade Me considered ghost jobs to be a material issue on their sites, citing the financial commitment to advertise a role, verification processes, and the ability for job seekers to report suspect listings.

A petition and a warning

Maclean has since found work but the process was demoralising to the point that she almost forgot what she was good at.

"Jobs that I was really keen on I even took to sending people cupcakes with a little QR code in the icing, literally just to cut through the noise to get a phone call."

The exhausting process, in addition to her experience with the suspect company, has prompted a petition to Parliament to see ghost jobs explicitly banned, in line with crackdowns overseas.

"It's incredibly difficult out there.

World.title: Up There Cazaly singer vowed to make AFL grand final after horrific fall
World.content:
He is a name synonymous with the AFL grand final.

While teams change, pre-game acts change and even the rules themselves change, Mike Brady's performance of unofficial AFL anthem Up There Cazaly has been a fixture of the big day for decades.

Last weekend's grand final was no different — but that was not always a given.

In January, the 78-year-old suffered a horrific fall during a routine evening walk near his Great Ocean Road home.

Mike Brady performed on ABC's Countdown program in 1979 to promote his Up There Cazaly single. (ABC News)

"I fell and landed on my ample backside," he said, laughing.

But the injury was no laughing matter.

Brady described the horror of having to twist his ankle back into place before dragging himself to a nearby fire station, "leaving a trail of blood and mud".

Brady would later learn he had fractured his leg, ankle and foot in 12 places.

With his doctor telling him not to push himself and that it was unlikely he would be able to walk anytime soon, his grand final call-up nine months later was all but certainly out of the picture.

When the AFL asked if he would still be up to performing, he vowed to be there even if he had to crawl on stage.

"I said, 'Try and stop me,'" he said.

"Because I love it. It's a part of me."

'The place was closing in on me'

Mike Brady performed during the 2022 AFL grand final match between Geelong and Sydney. (Getty Images: Dylan Burns)

A self-described "outdoors person" who relishes being active, Brady is the first to admit that even he doubted he would make it during parts of the nine-month journey that followed.

"I wasn't doing well," he said.

"I was waking up and felt like the place was closing in on me.

" I was put in a palliative care place, and that was tough because I felt like I shouldn't be there. "

After five months in hospital, he was able to return home with the help of a wheelchair.

He slowly transitioned to crutches, and now mostly gets around using a walking stick.

But Brady defied all expectations and ditched the walking stick to walk out on stage on September 26.

Mike Brady was interviewed about his famed football anthem in 2002. (ABC News)

The 100,000-strong crowd gave him the strength not just to walk, he said, but to fly.

"At the beginning of the song, I'm singing it kind of normally, but then I thought, 'I've got this, I'm going to be able to sing it!'

"I sang harder than I've ever sung before.

"One hundred thousand people reacted, and the roar — I've never heard anything like it.

"It was fantastic. I felt absolutely vindicated for pushing myself so hard."

Musician vows to perform for years to come

Mike Brady performed at the 1979 VFL grand final. (Supplied)

Brady says he is not one to dwell on the past and spent much of his recovery writing new poetry and music.

But many hours alone with his thoughts left him to reminisce on a career he never expected.

As an English immigrant, Brady moved to Melbourne at the age of 11.

The musician and jingle-maker had never even been to a full AFL game when he was asked to create a tune to market the Victorian Football League.

"What an honour," he said.

He went on to pen what would become a footy phenomenon.

Recalling the day he first performed Up There Cazaly at the 1979 VFL grand final, introduced by his friend John Farnham, Brady said it was the first time he felt truly at home in the country he had lived in for nearly two decades.

"I really felt like I belonged in Australia," he said.

"I'd never felt that before. But hearing men and women in the crowd shouting, 'Good on ya, Mike', I really felt the warmth."

Mike Brady says the 1979 VFL grand final, which featured Carlton legend Alex Jesaulenko (pictured), was a key moment in his Up Their Cazaly journey. (Getty Images)

Even 48 years later, the feeling remains every time the words "up there cazaly" leave his mouth.

"I often say the smile on my face when I sing it is actually me chuckling at the irony," he said.

"I love the irony of being a Pommy immigrant that was taken to heart by so many Australian people, and if that's not a great honour, I don't know what is."

While the honour of performing the track has been handed to other performers over the years, he wants to perform for the next two years, taking it to the song's 50-year anniversary and his own 80th birthday.

"I just hope the crowd is as kind to me as they have been for all those 48 years," he said.

In fact, Brady was more determined than ever to take to the stage this year, fearing the AFL might not ask him back if he did not.

If the crowd's reaction was anything to go by, it was an unlikely fear.

World.title: Aussie duo and new world number one fall at China Open
World.content:
Australian women's involvement at the China Open is down to just one singles player after Kimberly Birrell and Storm Hunter were both second-round casualties.

World number 41 Birrell suffered a 6-4, 6-4 loss to Czech Marie Bouzkova at the WTA 1000 event in Beijing on Saturday night.

Birrell, 28, who won the Korea Open last Sunday with a win over compatriot Maya Joint in the final, raced out to a 3-1 first-set lead before dropping serve twice to lose it in 42 minutes.

Down 3-0 in the second, Birrell lifted and won the next four games but was broken twice more to see her involvement in the Chinese capital come to a premature end.

For Bouzkova, the 28-year-old 18th seed, a meeting with China's Zheng Qinwen awaits.

The 2024 Olympic champion was leading Anna Kalinskaya 6-7 (4/7), 6-4, 3-0 when the Russian retired.

Earlier, Queensland veteran and former doubles world number one Storm Hunter was beaten 6-2, 6-2 by Maria Sakkari in just 73 minutes.

The 182nd-ranked Hunter failed to join 20-year-old fellow Aussie Taylah Preston in round three, losing serve six times in her latest hardcourt tournament clash in Asia.

Next up for Sakkari, the Greek 25th seed and former world number three, is Elina Svitolina.

The sixth-seeded Ukrainian came from a set down to eliminate Czech Katerina Siniakova, 1-6, 6-4, 6-2.

Shock of the day came with newly crowned world number one Elena Rybakina crashing out ‌3-6, 6-4, 6-3 to unseeded Alina Charaeva in the second round.

It couldn't have been a worse start to her reign as the number one as Rybakina lost in her first match since defeating four-times major winner Aryna Sabalenka to capture the US Open title last month.

Charaeva, a 24-year-old Russian-born Armenian ranked 118th ​in the world, etched her name into the record books by becoming the lowest-ranked competitor since the introduction of the WTA rankings in 1975 to rally from a set down to defeat a world number one.

Elsewhere, there were wins for third seed Coco Gauff, eighth seed Iga Swiatek, 21st seed Ann Li and 24th seed Jelena Ostapenko.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL and NRLW grand final day has arrived. Here's what you need to know
World.content:
The final day of the NRL and NRLW seasons is here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held today.

In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.

In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.

Here's everything you need to know about NRL and NRLW grand finals day.

What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.

Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.

NRL grand final

7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

7pm ACDT: South Australia

6:30pm: Queensland

6pm: Northern Territory

4:30pm: Western Australia

NRLW grand final

4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania

3:30pm ACDT: South Australia

3pm: Queensland

2:30pm: Northern Territory

1pm: Western Australia

How can you watch and listen to the grand final?

The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.

To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.

Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?

The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.

Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.

Who is playing in the NRL grand final?

The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.

The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.

The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.

Who is playing in the NRLW grand final?

The Sydney Roosters are undefeated in 2026, winning all 11 matches in the home-and-away season, then defeating the Canberra Raiders in last week's preliminary final.

It mirrors Sydney's fantastic NRLW season in 2025, where they were undefeated until losing in last year's decider to the Brisbane Broncos.

The Broncos finished third on the table, with a record of 8–3 in the home-and-away season. The Broncos suffered a three-game losing run in the middle of the season, but have won their past five matches, including last weekend's preliminary final against the Gold Coast Titans.

What pre-match entertainment is taking place at the NRL grand final?

After talks between the NRL and Australian artist Tones And I, the grand final appeared set to take place without any pre-match entertainment.

However, on Friday it was revealed that an all-star ensemble of Australian musicians, led by Amy Shark, will lead a tribute to recently retired player Jai Arrow, who was diagnosed with MND earlier this year.

Shark will be joined by members from Newcastle favourites and Better hit-makers The Screaming Jets, plus rock groups Grinspoon, and Teen Jesus and the Jean Teasers.

Electronic duo Peking Duk revealed on Instagram on Sunday morning that despite rumours to the contrary, they would not be part of the performance.

Shark previously performed at the 2020 NRL grand final, and is set to perform a series of cover songs, including the Gerry and the Pacemakers' song and Liverpool FC anthem You'll Never Walk Alone.

Each musician's appearance fee is reportedly being donated to motor neurone disease causes.

World.title: Verstappen claims pole at Grand Prix in Malaysia
World.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed his first pole position of the season at the Formula One Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Saturday, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton joining him on the front row.

It is the first time two great rivals have shared the front row of the grid since the Hungarian Grand Prix in 2023.

Verstappen's teammate, Isack Hadjar, was third fastest but will start eighth due to a grid penalty, with championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third alongside Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Oscar Piastri was pipped to sixth by his teammate Lando Norris, but will move up a position as a result of Hadjar's penalty to start sixth as McLaren locked out the third row of the grid.

George Russell, who so spectacularly won the last Grand Prix in Azerbaijan last week, will start seventh in what was an alarming performance for Mercedes, who came to Malaysia with a big upgrade package.

"It's very difficult to understand," Mercedes boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports.

"We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year.

"But then you can say it's very hot, with the tarmac very different to all the tracks.

"[We] looked really good in the morning; we seemed to have, at least with Kimi [Antonelli], made a step in understanding. And then in qualifying, it was a little bit back to what we saw before — just no performance."

Verstappen was the last driver to win a Grand Prix in Malaysia in 2017, in what was his second career victory, before the race was taken off the calendar after the government said it could not justify the costs.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the front row of the grid together for the first time in three years. (Getty Images: Formula 1/Mark Sutton)

Nine years and four championships later, the Dutchman showed he was still the man to beat in Sepang with a time of 1 minute 35.130 seconds.

"It's fantastic, we've been trying for many Grands Prix to get more, sometimes a bit closer to the others. But to finally get it from where we started the season [it's] pretty incredible," said Verstappen as he eyes his first win of the season.

Hamilton, who also has one victory in Sepang, struggled with tyre degradation in practice sessions but the veteran Briton snatched second from Hadjar in the dying stages of the final qualifying session.

"It's so hot here, I keep saying it. But that's made it a massive challenge for the tyres, for the car, for the mechanics in the garage," Hamilton said.

"We made so many changes through all these practice sessions because the cars are sliding, these tyres are overheating. It was really, really hard to find a good balance. We made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot."

Hadjar had exceeded his seasonal allowance for engines, which resulted in a five-place grid penalty.

"It's a bit unfortunate we take the penalty on a track that fast," Hadjar said.

"But you know, from P8, I'm confident we can go through the field and come back for a good result."

Reuters/ABC

World.title: De Minaur fights into quarterfinals in China
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been pushed to the limit, before breaking the resistance of French qualifier Quentin Halys and advancing to his second consecutive China Open quarterfinal.

The Australian, who has had a seesawing second half of the year, lost the first set in Beijing on Saturday, before grinding his way back into the match.

After winning the first set 6-3, world number 50 Halys opened up a 5-3 lead in the second and was serving for the match, before de Minaur rallied to break back, then clinch a neck-and-neck tie break 7-5 to set up a decider.

The third set was another close affair, before de Minaur was able to break at 5-5 and secure a hard-fought 3-6 7-6 (5) 7-5 win in 2 hours 47 minutes.

Victory evened up their head-to-head record at 2-2 and put de Minaur into the quarters, where the world number 10 will play Andrey Rublev, currently ranked number 20 in the world, but a former top-10 player himself.

Rublev was also pushed to the limit before beating fellow Russian Roman Safiullin 6-2 3-6 6-4.

De Minaur will be looking to repeat or better last year's performance at the ATP 500 event, when he made the semifinals before losing to then world number 1 Jannik Sinner.

It has been an up-and-down year for de Minaur, who started 2026 off well by reaching the last eight at the Australian Open.

He continued that momentum into February, when he won the ATP 500 event in Rotterdam.

De Minaur followed that by reaching the French Open's third round and the fourth round at Wimbledon, before disappointingly bowing out in the second round of the US Open in September.

However, he bounced back impressively by steering Australia to victory over Poland in their Davis Cup clash in Brisbane, before beating in-from German Alexander Zverev at the Laver Cup in London.

Zverev, who has won two majors this year — at Roland Garros in June and Flushing Meadows in September — is top seed in Beijing and was scheduled to play China's Juncheng Shang later on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: David Fifita leads Australia in wild mismatch against PNG
World.content:
A rag-tag Australian side has outclassed Papua New Guinea 60-10 in the annual Prime Minister's XIII clash in Port Moresby.

The Australians scored 11 tries and exposed the PNG side's defensive frailties almost at will in what was the 20th men's Prime Minister's XIII match.

It was hardly a conventional game at the National Football Stadium on Saturday, with Australia switching on and off as players became accustomed to their makeshift position.

Ezra Mam spent time at fullback. Jock Madden appeared to be playing on an edge. Jamal Fogarty stood in the centres, and Josh Curran kicked a goal.

At one stage they had three regular hookers on the field.

In one piece of consistency, captain David Fifita started and finished the match as a devastating left centre.

Commentator Cooper Cronk mused it was coach Ben Teo's way of keeping the Aussies engaged after a long, hard season.

It was at times chaotic and they dropped the ball a lot, but it was fun. Less so for the PNG side, who were not just outclassed but also ill-disciplined, missing 47 tackles — 28 in the first half alone.

With the PNG Chiefs' arrival in the NRL fast approaching, it is clear the next level of local players are still a long way from that standard.

On a positive note, earlier on Saturday the Junior Kumuls scored a historic first win over the Australian Schoolboys, 18-10.

If Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters hasn't settled on his squad for this month's Rugby League World Cup, several players put their hands up.

Regular back-rower Fifita, who showed his class and power in the centres on Saturday, first appeared in the PM's XIII game seven years ago and looked destined for higher honours that never arrived. Maybe that time is approaching again.

Mam and fellow half Lachlan Galvin showed more than one glimpse of their brilliance, while hulking front-rower Tom Hazelton was one of the best players on the field.

For former NRL and current London Broncos coach Jason Demetriou, who will guide the PNG Kumuls at the World Cup, there was not a lot to love.

Sylvester Namo should be there, while uncapped centre Stanford Talita and fullback Sanny Wabo were dangerous at times and could find their way into Demetriou's squad.

In the women's game, Australia was also successful, dishing out a 66-6 thumping of their hosts.

The PNG women's Prime Minister's XIII scored a point for the first time in three years, but the Aussies still came out on top in a big way. (AAP: NRL Photos/Anthony Kourembanas)

PNG might have scored for the first time in three years, but Australia was a class above, crossing for 12 tries to one to rack up the biggest winning margin in the fixture's history.

While the standard of PNG's second-tier players has improved alongside the growth of the national women's competition, the Santos Cup, so too has that of the Australians.

Several showed they would not be out of place if called up to coach Jess Skinner's Jillaroos for this month's 2026 Rugby League World Cup.

Jada Taylor scored three tries and was almost impossible to handle at times, showing her versatility by playing on the wing, despite playing her club football at fullback.

Half Kasey Reh, centre Tahlia O'Brien, hooker Taneka Todhunter and back-rower Tayla Preston were others who impressed in what was effectively an audition in front of Skinner for a grander stage.

PNG Orchids coach Craig Sandercock, who this year guided Wests Tigers to their first NRLW finals series, would also have enjoyed the opportunity to see the next generation of PNG players.

There was no doubt they were outclassed, and they struggled for time with the ball, having just 37 per cent possession.

However, they had an 85 per cent completion rate and tried hard in defence, before tiring late in each half.

AAP

World.title: Saints hit rock bottom, Essendon, Suns, Port claim AFLW victories
World.content:
St Kilda have kicked just a single point, the club's lowest ever score in an AFLW match, as the Western Bulldogs scored a 30-point victory in Ballarat.

Incredibly, the Saints only managed the behind in the final 90 seconds of the game in a horror afternoon for the winless club.

The Bulldogs were barely better in tough conditions in Ballarat, with sideways rain and winds limiting the hosts to just three goals 13 on a day were accuracy in front of goal suffered.

Rylie Wilcox, Sarah Hartwig and Cleo Buttifant scored the goals for the Bulldogs, while Isabelle Pritchard (35 disposals, six clearances) was outstanding in the testing, cold conditions.

For the Saints, only Ashleigh Richards's point spared the cellar dwellers the ignominy of a bagel.

Earlier, star midfielder Madison Prespakis steered battling Essendon to an eight-point comeback victory over GWS for its first win of the season.

Essendon recorded its first win of the 2026 AFLW season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

The Giants got out to a game-high 25-point lead at the start of the third quarter and appeared on track for a second win of the season, before Prespakis kicked into overdrive and the Bombers lifted their pressure.

The star on-baller racked up 13 disposals, six contested possessions, three clearances and a goal in the third term to put Essendon on her back and inspire a terrific 6.7 (43) to 5.5 (35) comeback at Henson Park on Saturday afternoon.

"Genuinely just so proud of the resilience of the group," skipper Bonnie Toogood told Fox Sports.

"And it's been a challenging season, I suppose, and the persistence through adversity, particularly today.

"The first half wasn't what we were planning on, but to come out in the third like we did and just big moments by individuals — bloody inspiring."

The victory relieves some pressure on Bombers coach Natalie Wood and leaves St Kilda as the league's only winless team.

It was a devastating loss for Cam Bernasconi's Giants, who kicked five of the first six goals then only scored one point in a second half where they were completely overwhelmed by Essendon's manic pressure.

Madison Prespakis was sensational, with 13 disposals, six contested possessions, three clearances and a goal as the Bombers came from behind. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Essendon had trailed by just four points at the final change when star forward Toogood gave the Bombers a massive rev-up at the huddle.

"I'm passionate and emotional all the time — it could be the Italian in me," Toogood said.

"They were on the back foot … I was like, 'We've got 'em — lean into that, we've got them, our football is working.'"

Essendon hit the front when it went from end to end and Daria Bannister tumbled home a long-range goal.

Then Emily Gough kicked a terrific checkside from a forward-50 stoppage that sealed victory.

Prespakis finished with a mammoth 35 disposals and five clearances, and she was well supported by Maddi Gay (21 disposals) and Georgia Gee (15), along with ruck Steph Wales (20 disposals, 14 hitouts, eight clearances).

Later, the Gold Coast Suns finally secured their first victory over the Brisbane Lions, winning a fiery Q-Clash by 20 points in Brisbane.

Havana Harris kicked two as the Suns won their first Q-Clash. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Meara Girvan may have cause for concern after pinning the arms of Cathy Svarc in a tackle during the first quarter, while Charlotte Mullins was penalised for high contact on Niamh McLaughlin later in the game.

The Lions led by two points at the final change but failed to kick another point as the Suns booted three in the final term to win 5.10 (40) to 3.2 (20).

Havana Harris kicked two for the Suns, who recorded their sixth win of the season to sit fourth on the ladder.

In Saturday's final fixture, Port Adelaide ended a four-match losing run by winning the Showdown against Adelaide in front of a record crowd of 5,441 fans at Alberton Oval.

Port Adelaide completed a second Showdown victory in a row at Alberton Oval. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

The Power joined the Crows on 12 competition points thanks to a 5.6 (36) to 2.10 (22) victory.

Port (3-5) had five different goal kickers in the opening three quarters to open up a 34-7 advantage, but failed to hit the target in the fourth.

After going goalless for three terms, Caitlin Gould and Teah Charlton kicked straight for some respectability on the scoreboard for Adelaide (3-5).

AAP/ABC

World.title: FOMO and 4am wake-up call get Pallister in the ocean
World.content:
Is there anything Lani Pallister can't do?

On Friday night, Pallister wrapped up a hugely successful Australian short course championships with a fourth gold medal in the 800-metre freestyle to seal her spot in the 24-strong squad for the world championships.

Then, the 24-year-old rushed up to Queensland's Sunshine Coast to claim honours in the 1.2-kilometre Bluff to Bar ocean swim at Alexandra Headland on Saturday morning, after a 4am wake-up call.

"I'd get really bad FOMO [fear of missing out]," Pallister said when asked why she made the trip.

"It's important to give back … Alexandra Heads Surf Club helped make me the athlete I am today."

Lani Pallister won her third-straight Bluff to Bar race. (Supplied: Alexandra Headland Surf Lifesaving Club)

Pallister's dedication to her surf club cannot be doubted after she posted a story on her Instagram feed tagged at 4:38am to get her flight for an 11:20am race on the Sunshine Coast.

And the Paris Olympian made sure the early wake up was worth it, leading a stacked field from start to finish to claim a third-straight victory in the event.

Competing in a point-to-point ocean swim couldn't have been more different from the 125 tumble turns she completed in competition at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre in the past four days.

Pallister competed in every freestyle event from 100m to 1,500m, winning gold in all but the 100m, where she finished second.

That ensured that she would be the headline act for the Dolphins squad named for the Beijing world championships from December 1-6.

The squad includes six debutants: Amelie Smith, Mark Nikolaev, Marcus Da Silva, Emily Jones, Cameron Bladen and Alex Quach.

Lani Pallister (left) and Jenna Forrester both had excellent championships. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Head Dolphins coach Rohan Taylor noted Pallister's performance as a stand-out in Sydney, with Sam Short's clean sweep of the 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle and Jenna Forrester's four silvers and a gold also worthy of mention.

"Those three without a doubt have been stand-outs here," Taylor said.

"But also it's been great to see the likes of Amelie Smith and Marcus Da Silva come through the ranks and shift the dial.

"Also credit to Mark Nikolaev; it's a credit to his consistency and perseverance that he has earned his Dolphin number tonight.

"The international exposure in Beijing is an opportunity to come together and build towards LA 2028 and the meet presents a great opportunity for our younger swimmers to learn from established Dolphins."

Lani Pallister won the 200, 400, 800 and 1,500m freestyle events at the Australian short course championships. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Speaking of experienced Dolphins, Cam McEvoy is also set to join the Aussie team in Beijing, despite not competing at the national championships this week.

World Aquatics is offering wildcard spots for the world championships to any to any swimmer who finishes on the podium of an individual final during the the World Cup series.

The 32-year-old long course world record holder duly set a new national short course record of 20.22 for the 50m freestyle to win gold on the opening night of the 2026 World Cup series in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Friday.

Pallister will now head for an altitude training camp in Flagstaff, USA, before the world championships, which represents her ninth Australian Dolphins selection.

"Off to altitude in a couple of weeks' time, and then just pretty much getting back into full training, knuckling down and targeting world champs," Pallister said during the short course titles.

"I didn't really anticipate fast swimming this week. I was actually pretty shocked with the 200 being plus 0.2, so [I'm] pretty happy."

Dolphins World Championships squad

Iona Anderson, Ben Armbruster, Cameron Bladen*, Brittany Castelluzzo, Josh Collett, Isaac Cooper, Marcus Da Silva*, Jenna Forrester, Max Giuliani, Emily Jones*, Tara Kinder, Mark Nikolaev*, Lani Pallister, Alexandria Perkins, William Petric, Alex Quach*, David Schlicht, Sam Short, Amelie Smith*, Flynn Southam, Stuart Swinburn, Matt Temple, Olivia Wunsch, Josh Yong.

*debut Dolphins squad

Tech.title: Capcom is preparing for a ‘future where we create games together with AI’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.
